additions.text: Pablo is new in a parcel warehouse. He writes the labels and the cards: the parcel, the box, the book, the table. Today Elena, the supervisor, finds three mistakes on his cards. By the end of the class you know if a word is masculine (el, un) or feminine (la, una), even when the ending tricks you.
the book · a parcel
the table · a box
The problem is serious; the hand is small.
In Spanish, a table or a book is also masculine or feminine. It is not about meaning: it is grammar. The article (el, la, un, una) tells you the gender.
“La caja” (the box): masculine or feminine?
“Un paquete” (a parcel): masculine or feminine?
“El problema” ends in -a. Is it feminine?
Masculine: el, un
The phone is on the table.
A glass is for Elena.
The colour of the box is blue.
Feminine: la, una
The label is on the box.
The address is correct.
The destination city is Quito.
Do not learn “paquete”: learn “el paquete”. Do not learn “llave”: learn “la llave”. That way you never hesitate.
the television
the engine
the university
the flower
Tricky words: the ending lies
The problem is the address.
The language of the label is Spanish.
The day is long in the warehouse.
The photo of the parcel is on the card.
The delivery rider’s motorbike is in the street.
Look at the sentences: the problem is “serio”, the hand is “pequeña”. The describing word changes with the gender (-o / -a). Today you only notice it; you practise it in class 006.
the problem
a hand
the language
“Crema” (cream) ends in -ma. Is it masculine, like “problema”?
Feminine words that start with a stressed a
The water is cold.
Classroom 12 is new.
The shipping area is closed.
The school classrooms are big.
the water in the bottle
the warehouse alarm
the school classrooms
The map is in the box.
The photo is of Quito.
Area B is closed.
Good morning, Pablo. Are the cards ready for the shipping area?
Yes, here they are. There are three: a parcel for Quito, a box for Lima and another box for a school.
Let’s see. Card one: “la problema de la dirección”. No, Pablo: it’s “el problema”.
“El problema”? But it ends in -a!
Yes, but it’s masculine, like “el tema” or “el día”. Card two: “un mapa de Lima y un mano de madera”.
What’s wrong? “Un mapa” is correct, isn’t it?
Yes, the map is fine. But it’s “una mano”: “la mano” is feminine.
Oh, of course: like “la foto” or “la moto”. They end in -o, but they’re feminine.
Exactly. Card three: “paquete para la aula 12”. It’s “el aula”, Pablo.
“El aula”? So it’s masculine?
No, it’s feminine: “el aula nueva”. It’s like “el agua fría”: “el” only because of the sound.
Got it. I’ll correct the three cards now. Thanks, Elena!
How many cards does Elena check?
What is wrong on card two?
Why is it “el aula”?
Pablo prepares more labels for the warehouse. Which article does each word take?
Contents: an alarm system.
The climate in Lima is humid.
The catalogue photo is on the table.
Which is the customer’s language: Spanish or Portuguese?
Parcel for the University of Cusco.
Contents: a hand cream.
The system is new.
The motorbike is in the street.
Why does Elena call?
Where is the big parcel going?
What is in the parcel?
What is the problem?
Where is the water for the office?
Masculine: -o, -or (almost always)
Feminine: -a, -ción, -dad
Tricky words: learn them by heart
Feminine words with el: still feminine
The ending helps almost always, but the article is the boss. Learn every word with “el” or “la”: el problema, la mano, el agua fría.
Now in a school: a teacher prepares the list for her classroom. Correct her list.
You now know if a word is masculine or feminine. The natural next step: el, la, los, las and un, una, unos, unas, and when to use each one. With gender clear, choosing the article is easy.

Lucía works at a small company with two offices: one in the city centre and one by the harbour. Today she is preparing the supplies order: pencils, notebooks, folders, clocks… For the order she needs the plural: more than one thing.
a red pencil · a blue folder · a clock
two red pencils · two blue folders · two clocks
From “dos” (2) on, the noun is plural. The numbers themselves do not change: dos lápices, dos carpetas.
“Dos carpetas azules”: how many folders?
“A red pencil” → “two…”
To make the plural, look at the last letter of the noun. Is it a vowel (a, e, o)? Add -s. Is it a consonant (l, r, n, d, j…)? Add -es.
Does it end in a vowel? Add -s.
a chair → two chairs
a notebook → three notebooks
a table → four tables
the map → the maps
Does it end in a consonant? Add -es.
a city → two cities
a clock → two clocks
a sheet of paper → lots of papers
a computer → five computers (in Latin America: computadora)
a lamp → two…
a marker → three…
a city → two…
Does it end in z? Change z to c and add -es.
a pencil → two pencils
a light → three lights
once → twice (one time → two times)
a light → two…
the meeting → the…
Monday → Mondays
Is the noun plural? Then the article and the adjective are plural too.
the red pencil → the red pencils
a blue folder → some blue folders
the white lamp → the white lamps
a big clock → some big clocks
the green folders
some big clocks
the new maps
Which one is correct? (four small notebooks)
Which one is correct? (some green lights)
Hi, Diego! Are you at the office? I’m preparing the supplies order for the two offices.
Yes, I’m here. For the harbour office: eight pencils and two clocks for the wall.
Eight pencils? What colour?
Red. And some blue folders for the contracts.
Perfect. And for the meeting room? Some lamps?
Yes, three white lamps. The lamps we have now are broken.
Great. The city-centre office needs markers for the whiteboard and notebooks.
Big notebooks or small ones?
Small notebooks. And two city maps for the entrance.
And the lights in the corridor? Are they OK?
Yes, the lights are fine. The order goes out next Monday.
Great! Thanks, Lucía.
What does the harbour office need for the wall?
Why do they need new lamps?
What do they NOT need in the order?
a printer → two printers
a big box → two big boxes
the city maps
Ten red pencils.
The blue folders are on the table.
Two white clocks for the meeting room.
The corridor lights are fine.
Why is Diego calling?
How many pencils does the harbour office need now?
What are the clocks like?
What does Marta need?
What about the chairs?
after a vowel: add -s
after a consonant: add -es
z changes to c
the whole group agrees
Look at the last letter: vowel → -s; consonant → -es; z → -ces. Then make the whole group plural: article, noun and adjective. Gender does not change: el mapa → los mapas.
For the meeting room: three new lamps.
We need two clocks for the corridor.
Ten green pencils, please.
Some white papers.
Today you made short groups plural: “dos lápices rojos”. In class 006 you look closely at adjectives: how they describe things and how they agree in gender and number, even with two nouns together.

Irene Salas is an estate agent. Today she and her colleague Pablo are rewriting the listings for two apartments: one on calle Olivo and one on calle Río. To describe a home well, you need to know where the adjective goes.
It is a big apartment, with a white kitchen.
It is a great apartment in a good neighbourhood.
In “una cocina blanca”, the adjective goes…
“Un gran apartamento” mainly gives…
Noun + adjective: the neutral order
It is a small bedroom.
The listing has a nice photo.
It is a quiet street.
The owner is a Colombian man.
They are two big windows.
A listing for the website: “Living room with a green rug”.
Irene talks about the owner: “She is a Peruvian lady”.
“A round table” in Spanish is…
Adjective + noun: an opinion, a highlight
It is a good price.
It is a great terrace.
Today is a bad day to visit homes: it is raining.
It is a good area to live in.
It is a good apartment for a family.
It is a great kitchen!
It is a bad time to sell: the building is under renovation.
With a few adjectives, the position changes the meaning. After the noun, the basic meaning. Before the noun, another meaning. Today you learn four very frequent pairs.
Don Ramón is 85: he is an elderly friend.
Ana is 32, but she is an old friend of Irene: friends from school.
To talk about a person’s age, “viejo” can sound harsh. “Mayor” is kinder: “un señor mayor”. “Un viejo amigo”, on the other hand, is always something nice.
“Es el único apartamento con terraza” means…
“Un apartamento nuevo” is…
Irene and Carlos have been friends for twenty years. Carlos is…
Which sentence is right?
Pablo, look at the photos of calle Olivo. It is a great apartment.
Yes, and it is a big apartment: ninety square metres.
Exactly. With a bright living room and a white kitchen.
And the building? Is it new?
No, it is an old building, from 1950. But the kitchen is new.
And the owner? Is he a client of the agency?
It is don Ramón, an old friend of my family.
And the apartment on calle Río?
It is a brand-new apartment, small, but it is the only apartment in the building with a terrace.
So it is a unique apartment. And it is in a good neighbourhood!
Perfect. Now, the two listings: the normal adjective, after the noun.
How many square metres is the calle Olivo apartment?
Who is don Ramón?
Why is the calle Río apartment special?
Living room with a blue sofa.
It is a great offer!
It is a good price for the neighbourhood.
The owner is a Mexican lady.
It is the only apartment with a garage.
It is a bright living room.
It is the only apartment with a balcony.
Why is Irene calling?
What is the living room on calle Olivo like?
What does Irene say about the price?
What is special about the calle Río apartment?
After the noun: the neutral order to describe.
Before the noun: your opinion, with a short form.
Same adjective, another meaning before the noun.
After “es”: always the basic meaning.
If you describe, the adjective goes after: una cocina blanca. Before the noun only to give an opinion (gran, buen) or with a special meaning: un viejo amigo, el único apartamento.
The agency is also selling a small hotel on the beach. Write three pieces of its listing.

You can now describe and rate an apartment. Next you need to point: this apartment, that balcony, that building over there. In class 008 you learn to say which thing you mean, near or far from you, with the same agreement as today.

Marta Ríos hosts “Gente nueva”, a cultural centre’s podcast. Today she interviews three new members of the conversation group: Elena, Pablo and Ana. The game: each person introduces someone else. For that you need the verb ser.
She is Elena. She is a doctor.
She is from Chile. She is Chilean.
She is very calm.
“Es médica” tells you…
“Es de Chile” tells you…
For “she is calm” (her personality), you say…
to be: who, what, where from, what like
I am Marta Ríos and I am a journalist.
My sister is a doctor and she is from Chile.
Pablo and I are Colombian.
Ana and Elena are very nice.
Are you from Medellín?
As you know, the verb shows who: “Somos amigos” = “Nosotros somos amigos”. Use the pronoun to clarify or contrast: “She is Chilean and he is Colombian”.
We are from Valparaíso.
Are you Mr Herrera?
My parents are teachers.
Pablo and his brother are from Medellín.
jobs: no “a / an” in Spanish
Pablo is a teacher.
Pablo is a very patient teacher.
Ana is an engineer. Her brother is a lawyer.
I am a student. Leo is a journalist.
“Elena es de Chile” = “Elena es chilena”. With de you use the country or the city; without de, the nationality adjective, which agrees with the person.
Ana is an engineer.
Pablo is a very fun teacher.
Elena is Chilean.
Ana and her sister are Brazilian.
You know estoy from the first class. Today, just one contrast: ser says who a person is; estar says how they are today.
Elena is a doctor. She is calm.
Today Elena is tired.
After twelve hours at the hospital: “I am tired”.
Elena presents her job: “I am a doctor”.
Pablo talks about Ana: “She is very nice”.
Which sentence is correct?
Good afternoon and welcome to Gente nueva. Today there are four of us in the studio.
The introductions are crossed. Pablo, who is she?
She is Elena Rojas. She is from Valparaíso: she is Chilean. And she is a doctor.
How interesting! Elena, your turn: what is Pablo like?
Pablo is a music teacher and he is Colombian, from Medellín. He is an excellent teacher and he is very funny.
Thanks, Elena! And now Ana. Ana, you are from Brazil, right?
Yes, I am Brazilian, from Recife. I am an engineer. And today I am a bit nervous: it is my first interview in Spanish.
Relax, Ana! We are friends here. What are Elena and Pablo like?
They are very nice. Elena is calm and Pablo is very chatty.
Perfect! Three people, three countries and one group.
Where is Elena from?
What is Ana’s job?
Why does Ana say “estoy nerviosa” and not “soy nerviosa”?
My sister and I are doctors.
Pablo, are you from Medellín or Bogotá?
You are the host, right?
Ana and Pablo are very nice.
I am a journalist and I am Mexican.
She is an engineer.
Ana is Brazilian.
Elena is an excellent doctor.
We are from Colombia.
What is this audio?
What is Elena’s job?
Where is Pablo from?
How is Ana feeling today?
Who introduces Ana?
who someone is and their job
with an adjective, add un / una
where someone is from
what someone is like
how someone feels today
Name, job, origin, nationality and personality: ser. A bare job takes no “a”. Nationality agrees and is lowercase. How you feel today: estar.
A health conference in Lima. A participant’s name badge says: Dr Carmen Soto · paediatrician · Quito (Ecuador). You introduce her.
Carmen and her colleague Dr Ruiz, also from Quito: “They are Ecuadorian”.
You can now say who someone is with ser. Today you saw just one contrast: “Estoy cansada”. In class 012 you study estar in depth: how you feel and where you are. That completes the ser / estar pair.

Lucía is an engineer. This week she is in Monterrey for work. Her brother Daniel is in Mexico City, at home with their mum. On the call, the two key questions are “Where are you?” and “How are you?”. Both use the verb estar.
I am in Monterrey, at the hotel.
I am tired, but happy.
I am an engineer.
“Estoy en Monterrey” tells you…
“Estoy cansada” tells you…
“Soy ingeniera” uses…
Estar is irregular but easy: “estoy” is special, and the other forms carry an accent on the a (except estamos).
“Está” with an accent is the verb: Mum is at home. “Esta” without an accent means “this” (class 008): this house. You can hear it too: es-TÁ / ES-ta.
Daniel and Mum are at home.
I am in Monterrey.
Mum is in the kitchen.
how you are: feelings, physical state
Mum is nervous today.
Are you busy, Daniel?
My colleague Ana is sick.
Mum and I are calm.
Lucía: “Today I am very tired”.
Daniel and Mum are happy.
How are you? — I am fine, thanks.
where someone or something is
I am at the hotel.
Daniel is at home, with Mum.
The keys are here.
The hotel is near the station.
Monterrey is far from Mexico City.
Lucía, at the hotel: “I am here”.
Lucía asks about the keys, which are at Daniel’s place: “Are they there?”
In class 011 you learnt ser: who you are, your job, where you are from. With ser you also say what someone is like in general. With estar you say how they are today and where they are.
Mum is a calm person.
Mum is calm today.
Daniel is usually a very calm person.
Today Mum is not calm.
Lucía is from Mexico City, but now she is in Monterrey.
Which sentence is correct?
Hello? Hi, Lucía! Where are you?
Hi, Daniel. I am in Monterrey, at the hotel. It is a quiet hotel.
And how are you?
I am tired, but happy. And you? Are you at home?
Yes, I am here, at home, with Mum. Mum is a bit nervous today.
Nervous? But Mum is a very calm person.
Yes, but today she is not calm. Her keys are not on the table.
Relax. The keys are in the kitchen, near the window. Are they there?
Yes, they are here! Now Mum and I are calm.
Great! Monterrey is far away, but on Sunday I am home. A kiss for Mum.
Where is Lucía?
How is Mum today, and why?
Where are the keys?
Mum and I are at home.
Are you busy now?
Today I am sick.
My suitcases are at the hotel.
Are you all OK?
The hotel is not far.
Daniel and I are tired.
What is this audio?
What is the hotel like?
How is Lucía?
Who is sick today?
Where is Lucía’s passport?
how you are now
who someone is and what they are like
“Es tranquilo”: that is how he always is. “Está tranquilo hoy”: that is how he is right now. And a location always takes estar: “estoy en Monterrey”, never “soy en”.
Where are you now?
My parents are in Monterrey.
Daniel is a very calm person, but today he is nervous.
Lucía and Ana are tired.
You can now say where a person or a thing is: “The keys are in the kitchen”. In class 013 you learn “hay” (there is / there are) to say what exists in a place, and when to use hay or estar.
Paula Medina is at the San Rafael Clinic in Bogotá with her son Leo. At reception there is a form: name, age and symptoms. For almost the whole form, Paula uses one verb: tener (to have).
I am thirty (years old).
I am cold and I am sleepy.
I have an appointment at ten.
For age and for cold, heat, hunger, thirst and sleepiness, English uses “to be”: I am 30, I am cold. Spanish uses tener: literally “I have 30 years”, “I have cold”.
“Tengo treinta años” tells you…
“Tengo frío” tells you…
In “Tengo una cita”, Paula has…
Tener is irregular. “Tengo” has a g. “Tienes, tiene, tienen” change e to ie. “Tenemos” and “tenéis” are regular.
In Argentina and Uruguay, with “vos”, the form is “tenés”: “¿Vos tenés frío?”. It means the same as “¿Tú tienes frío?”. In this class you use “tú tienes”; “tenés” is just for recognising it.
Leo is six.
Paula and Leo have an appointment.
Madam, do you have your ID?
“¿Vos tenés frío?” means…
How old are you?
I am thirty.
The doctor is forty-five.
My mother is sixty-eight.
How old are you? — I am twenty-two.
Paula is thirty.
Paula is from Argentina.
You ask a friend his age:
My grandma is seventy.
What do you feel?
I am very thirsty. Is there any water?
Leo is hot.
We are very sleepy.
I am hungry: the cafeteria is on the first floor.
I am sleepy.
I am tired.
There is no food at home: Leo is hungry.
It’s a hard week: Paula is tired.
I am very thirsty.
Leo is very cold.
Which one is correct?
Good morning. Your name, please?
Paula Medina. I have an appointment at ten with Dr Ruiz.
Very good. Here is the form. How old are you?
I am thirty. I am from Argentina, but I live here, in Bogotá.
And the boy? Is he your son?
Yes, this is Leo. He is six.
Now, the symptoms. How are you today?
I am cold and I am sleepy. And I am tired.
And Leo? Is he cold too?
No, he is hot. And he is very thirsty.
There is water near the window. Do you have your ID, please?
Yes, here it is. And I have a question: where is the bathroom?
How old is Paula?
What symptoms does Leo have?
At the end, what does Paula have?
Good morning, Paula. What’s wrong today?
I have a headache and I am very cold.
And you are tired, right?
Yes, very tired. It’s a hard week.
Hi, Leo. And you, are you hungry?
Yes! I am very hungry. And I have a dinosaur.
How nice! Paula, it’s nothing serious: lots of water and early to bed.
Dr Ruiz is forty-five.
Paula and Leo are hungry.
Paula is very tired.
Are you thirsty? There is water here.
I am thirty-two.
Leo is very thirsty.
I am tired and I am cold.
What is this audio?
Who has priority?
Where do children under twelve wait?
What is there for people who are cold?
Where is the cafeteria?
Who has all the answers?
age: I am thirty. How old are you?
how your body feels: I am very thirsty. Leo is hot.
to have something: I have an appointment at ten.
origin and state: I am from Argentina. I am tired.

If in English you say “I am 30” or “I am cold / hungry / thirsty / sleepy”, in Spanish you say “tengo”. If it is an adjective ending in -o / -a (tired, nervous), use estar. And for “very” with a noun: mucho / mucha, not “muy”.
My son is eight.
I am from Colombia, but I live in Madrid.
Open the window, please: I am very hot.
The children are very hungry.
Today my father is very tired.
Now you are not at the clinic: you are at a new gym, filling in your registration form. The rule is the same.

Today you used “mucha hambre” and “mucho frío”: the word changes with the noun. In class 015 you see this rule across the whole noun phrase: article, noun and adjective together, in gender and number (“las manos frías”, “un niño cansado”).

Paula, Hugo and Rosa work in a small design studio in Guadalajara, Mexico. On Monday mornings they look at the week’s agenda together: who is who, where everyone is, where they are going and what meetings they have. For that they use four verbs: ser, estar, ir and tener.
Paula is the coordinator.
Hugo is in the office.
Rosa is going to the bank.
I have two meetings.
“I go to work and I have two meetings.” With these two forms you can already tell your Monday: where you go and what you have.
“Rosa va al banco” tells you…
“Hugo está en la oficina” tells you…
“Tengo dos reuniones” uses…

Ser, estar, ir and tener are irregular: they don’t follow the pattern of hablar, comer and vivir. But they are the most frequent verbs in Spanish, and you will use them every day. You already know ser, estar and tener; ir is new.
With “yo”, three verbs end in -oy: soy, estoy, voy. Tener is different: tengo. And watch the vowel: tienes, tiene, tienen, but tenemos.
In Argentina and Uruguay many people say “vos” instead of “tú”: vos sos, vos estás, vos vas, vos tenés. Today you only need to recognise it; you use tú: eres, estás, vas, tienes.
I am a designer.
We have a meeting at ten.
Paula and Hugo are in the office.
You are going to the bank today.
to go (where to?)
I go to the office at nine.
Are you going to the bank today?
On Tuesday Paula is going to Puebla.
We are going to the meeting room.
Hugo and Rosa go downtown by metro.
With ir, the question is “¿adónde vas?” (where are you going?). With estar, the question is “¿dónde estás?” (where are you?).
On Thursday we are going to the design fair.
Hugo goes to work by bike.
—Where are you going? —To the office.
I’m going to work. (on my way)
I’m at work. (already there)
It’s ten o’clock. Paula is already in the room.
At ten to nine, Hugo leaves home: he is going to the office.
Rosa isn’t answering the phone: she is in a meeting.
Look at the agenda: on Friday I have a meeting with a client.
Which sentence is correct?
Good morning, Hugo. Where is Rosa?
She’s at the bank, with the invoices. Today is Monday: bank day.
Oh, of course. Do you have the agenda for the week?
Yes, here it is. I have two meetings: on Tuesday and on Thursday.
On Tuesday I’m not here: I’m going to Puebla with a client.
And on Wednesday? Are the three of us going downtown?
Yes, to the design fair. Rosa has the tickets.
Hi! Sorry, I’m a bit tired. The bank is chaos on Mondays.
Don’t worry. Look: on Wednesday we’re going to the fair.
Perfect. And on Friday I’m not going to the office: I have the day off.
Great, team. There are three of us and we have a very full week.
Where is Rosa at the beginning?
Where is Paula going on Tuesday?
Who has the tickets for the fair?
I go to the office by bus.
Hugo and Rosa are in the meeting room.
Paula, do you have time today at five?
We are a small team.
Rosa is thirty-two.
Are you two going downtown on Thursday?
I go to work by metro.
We are in the meeting room.
Rosa has three meetings today.
Where are you going on Thursday?
Why is Paula speaking?
Where is Paula on Thursday morning?
When does Hugo have the meeting with the bank?
Where are Paula and Rosa going on Monday?
Where are the new keys?
to be (who / what)
to be (where / how)
to go (where to)
to have
With “yo”: soy, estoy, voy, tengo. And today’s pair: voy al trabajo (I’m moving) / estoy en el trabajo (I’m already there).
Now you use the four verbs outside work: your weekend with your family.

You can now use the four most frequent irregular verbs: soy, estoy, voy, tengo. In class 019 four more verbs arrive with a special “yo” form: hago, pongo, salgo, vengo. With them you can tell your full routine: what time you leave, what you do and where you come from.

Carla, Diego, Paula and Marcos are friends. On Saturday there is a dinner at Carla’s place and everyone has a task. To share out the tasks you need four very common verbs: hacer, poner, salir and venir.
Who does what?
I make the food.
Diego puts the music on.
Marcos leaves work at seven.
Paula comes at seven.
Today I go shopping and leave early.
“Pongo la mesa” means…
“Marcos sale del trabajo” means…
How does the “yo” form of these verbs end?
In class 017 you learned the regular present. Hacer, poner and salir are regular in every person except “yo”. With “yo” they end in -go.
Learn hago, pongo, salgo. For the other persons, use the regular endings.
Traer works the same way: yo traigo, tú traes. Today you only need to recognise it.
I make the dessert for the dinner.
You put the plates on the table.
Diego and Paula leave home at six.
Venir has two changes, just like tener (class 018): -go with “yo”, and -ie- with tú, él and ellos. With nosotros and vosotros it is regular.
In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America people say “vos”: hacés, ponés, salís, venís. In Spain, for several people, “vosotros”. You use tú and ustedes: everyone understands you.
Carla, are you coming to the dinner on Saturday?
We are coming at seven.
I am coming by bus.
I’m coming from the market. I have the bread.
I’m going to the market. Do you need anything?
When someone calls you and you go towards them, Spanish says “¡Voy!” (I’m coming!).
Carla gets home with the bags: “I’m coming from the market”.
Diego leaves home: “Now I’m going to the market”.
“Marcos is coming from work.”
Which sentence is correct?
Hi, guys! Saturday is the dinner at my place. I’m making the food.
Great! I’ll put the music on.
And I’m making the dessert. Marcos is setting the table, right?
Yes, sure. But on Saturday I leave work at seven.
No problem. What time are you coming?
I’m coming straight from work. I’ll arrive at half past seven.
Perfect. Diego and Paula, you’re coming at seven, right?
Yes. Diego and I leave home at half past six.
Carla, are you doing the shopping?
Yes, on Saturday morning I’m going to the market.
(Saturday, 12:00) I’m coming back from the market with two big bags. I have everything!
Who is making the dessert?
Why does Marcos arrive at half past seven?
In the last message, where is Carla coming from?
I’m making an omelette for the dinner.
What time do you leave work?
Paula and Marcos are coming at seven.
I put the glasses on the table.
I’m coming from the market. I have everything!
I set the table at seven.
I’m coming from the market.
Today I leave home early.
Paula and Diego are coming at seven.
What is the voice message for?
Why is there a change?
Who is setting the table now?
What is Carla making to eat?
What does Carla do in the morning?
What time are Diego and Paula coming?
only the “yo” form ends in -go
the other persons are regular
venir changes like tener
from / to
With “yo”, think -go. With the other persons, regular endings; venir adds -ie- except with nosotros.

You already know the change in vienes, viene, vienen. In class 020 you see that many verbs change their vowel like this: quiero, puedo, pido. With them you can say what you want, what you can do and what you order at dinner.

Clara and Diego are travelling together along the coast of Ecuador. They are in Puerto López, a fishing town. Every morning they decide three things: what to eat, what to do and how much money to spend. They have 100 dollars for two days.
Clara: “I want a coffee and some fruit.”
Clara: “I can’t pay much.”
Diego orders eggs with bread.
“Quiero un café” tells you…
“No puedo pagar mucho” is about…
In a restaurant, “pido una sopa” means…

Querer, poder and pedir have the regular endings from class 017. The special part is the stem: when the stress falls on the stem, its vowel changes. QUIE-ro, PUE-do, PI-do. In nosotros and vosotros the stress moves to the ending (que-RE-mos), so the stem does not change.

In Spain, vosotros does not change: queréis, podéis, pedís. In Argentina, Uruguay and parts of Central America people use vos, and with vos the stem does not change either: querés, podés, pedís. Today you only recognise it; class 021 covers tú, vos, usted, ustedes and vosotros.
I want to see the sea.
We can pay 100 dollars.
They order fish soup.
Why does “queremos” not change?
to want
I want a white coffee.
Diego wants to see the whales.
Do you want to eat at the market?
can / to be able to
I can pay 40 dollars.
I want a coffee, but I can’t stay long: the tour leaves at nine.
Can you book the hotel?
to order / to ask for
I’ll have a mango juice, please.
Clara always orders the local food.
At the end, we ask for the bill.
I want to eat at the market.
Can you book the tour?
Diego asks for the bill.
I want to order ceviche.
We want to order ceviche.
Clara and I want to see the whales.
Diego can pay for the tour.
Rosa and her boyfriend order rice with fish.
You can pay by card.
Which one is correct?
Good morning. I’m hungry. What do you want for breakfast?
I want a coffee and some fruit. And you, what are you ordering?
I’m having eggs with bread. Hey, there is a whale-watching tour today. Do you want to go?
Yes! We both want to see whales. But how much is it?
Forty dollars each. We have 100 dollars for today and tomorrow.
Phew. Then I can’t pay for the tour and an expensive restaurant.
Don’t worry. After the tour, we can eat at the market. It’s cheap.
Good idea. At the market people order ceviche, right?
Yes, and tourists order encocado: fish in coconut sauce. Can you book the tour?
Yes, I can book now. My friend Rosa and her boyfriend want to come too.
Perfect. Then we’ll ask for the tour for four people.
How much is the tour?
Where do they want to eat after the tour?
How many people is the tour for?
Clara and I want to go to the beach tomorrow.
Can I pay by card here?
Rosa always orders mango juice.
My friends can’t come today.
Diego, what do you want to do this afternoon?
We always ask for the bill at the end.
We want to see the whales.
I can’t pay much.
Clara always orders a coffee.
What is Diego talking about?
What do people order on the island’s beach?
What time does Diego want to meet Clara at the port?
Who else wants to come?
what you want
what you can do
what you order or ask for
outside the boot: no change

First look at who. Yo, tú, él, ella, usted, ellos and ustedes: the stem changes (quiero, puedes, piden). Nosotros and vosotros: no change (queremos, podemos, pedimos). And after querer or poder, the infinitive: quiero pedir.
Rosa and I want to go to the island.
Sorry, I can’t go out today: I’m tired.
In the café, Diego always orders eggs.
Can you (all) pay in cash?
We’d like the bill, please.

You can now say what you want, what you can do and what you order, and you saw that vosotros and vos keep the stem. In class 021 you see when to use tú, vos, usted, ustedes or vosotros, and how the verb changes with each one.

Sofía is organising a visit to the Museo de los Colores in Puebla with twelve colleagues from her office. She goes to the information desk with lots of questions: opening hours, price, address, people. Each question needs a special word, always with a written accent.
When does the museum open?
How much is the ticket?
What is the address?
How many people can go in?
The question word goes first, right after “¿”, and then the verb: “¿Cuándo abre el museo?”. You already know the ¿ ? signs from class 022.
“¿Cuánto cuesta la entrada?” asks about…
Sofía wants to know the time. Which word does she use?
What do all these words have in a question?
Each question word asks for one type of information: a thing, a person, a place, a time, a way or an amount. Choose the word for the answer you expect.

In a question these words are stressed, and the accent shows it. Without the accent, “que”, “cuando”, “donde” or “como” are different words that do not ask anything. The accent is not decoration: it changes the word.
—It is on Reforma Street. What is the question?
—Raúl, the guide. What is the question?
At what time does the shop open?
How much? How many?
How long does the tour last?
How many people are there today?
How many days does the museum open?
How many people are coming?
How many rooms does the museum have?
How many students are coming?
How much is the catalogue?
Which room is the nicest? · Which days does it open?
What is the price? · Which are the new rooms?
There are two tours. Which one do you prefer?

This is the general rule and the most useful one to start with. In some parts of Latin America you also hear “¿cuál sala?” in conversation. And careful: “¿Qué es…?” asks for a definition: “What is a museum?”.
What is the museum’s phone number?
Which days are there guided tours?
There is a big map and a small map. Which one do you want?
“¿Qué es una audioguía?” asks for…
Many question words have a “twin” without an accent that does not ask anything: it joins two ideas in a sentence. Today you only need to recognise them.
Some questions sit inside another sentence: “No sé qué sala es”, “¿Sabe dónde está la tienda?”. Exclamations too: “¡Qué bonito!” (How beautiful!). Today you only need to recognise them.
The sign says that the museum closes at six.
What is there in room three?
“No sé dónde está la tienda.” Why does “dónde” have an accent?
Which one is correct?
Good morning! What do you need?
Good morning. We are a group from my office and we want to visit the museum. When does it open?
Tuesday to Sunday, from ten in the morning to six in the evening.
And how much is the ticket?
Eighty pesos per person. How many people are you?
There are twelve of us. Which days are there guided tours?
On Saturdays and Sundays. There is a short tour and a full tour. Which one do you prefer?
The full one. Who is the guide?
Raúl. He is very nice. What is your name, for the booking?
Sofía Herrera. And where is the entrance for groups?
Here, on the right. The tour starts at eleven. See you on Saturday!
Great! Thank you very much.
How many people are in Sofía’s group?
Which tour does Sofía prefer?
How much is the audio guide?
What are the café’s opening hours?
Which room has the old photos?
Who are Saturday’s guides?
When does the guided tour start? —At eleven.
How many rooms are there in the museum?
Who gives the guided tour?
What time does the café close?
Which is the entrance for groups?
What is the audio?
Which day is the museum closed?
How much is a student ticket?
When are there guided tours?
How many people can go in a group?
Who gives the guided tours?
what / which
who
where / when / how
how much / how many
If it asks, it has an accent. “Cuánto” agrees with the noun (cuántas personas). And as a general tendency: “qué” + noun, “cuál” + es or to choose.
On Saturday, after the museum, Sofía and her group go to the Puebla tourist office. Ask their questions.

You can now ask about opening hours, prices, places and people. But sometimes the answer is “no”: “No, it does not open on Mondays”. In class 024 you learn to make negative sentences and where “no” goes in the sentence.

Nuria and Pablo work at a travel agency in Guadalajara, Mexico. They need two hours together to prepare a presentation for a client. They suggest three dates… and all three times the answer is “no”. Today you learn to say no: where “no” goes in the sentence and how to answer “no” briefly or in full.
Pablo: “I have time.”
Nuria: “I don’t have time.”
“Can you on Monday?” “No, I can’t.”
Today you will see many days: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. “El lunes” = on Monday. You only need to recognise them: the class on days and time comes later.
“No tengo tiempo” means…
In “No tengo tiempo”, where is “no”?
“No, no puedo”: how many times does it say “no”?
Where does “no” go?
I don’t have money; today I’m not working.
Pablo doesn’t work on Tuesday.
There is no free room on Wednesday.
The café is not a good place to work.
Nuria is not in the office on Monday.
In English you say “I don’t work”. Spanish has no word like “do / don’t”: just “no” + the verb. “I don’t work” = No trabajo. “She doesn’t work” = No trabaja.
I don’t work on Tuesday.
There is no room.
Pablo is not in the office.
And with two verbs?
I can’t come on Monday.
Pablo can’t work on Tuesday.
We don’t want to have the meeting in the café.
Don’t you want to wait until Friday?
I don’t work on Thursday.
I can’t work on Thursday.
Nuria doesn’t want to wait.
Where does “no” go in “Podemos trabajar el jueves”?

You can answer a yes/no question (class 022) briefly, just “No”, or in full, with the verb. In the full answer there are two “no”s: the first one answers the question; the second one goes before the verb.
“No.”
“No, I can’t.”
“No, I can’t. I have a doctor’s appointment.”
“Yes, I can.”
With only one “no”, “No, puedo” sounds as if you can. If you mean you can’t, you need the second “no”: No, no puedo.
“Do you work on Tuesday?” “No, I don’t.”
“Do you have time today?” Short answer:
“Can you on Wednesday?” Nuria can’t. She says:
“Can you on Thursday?” Pablo can. He says:
Which sentence is correct?
“Is there a room on Wednesday?” Full answer:
Pablo, we need two hours for the presentation. Can you this afternoon?
Yes, I can. And you?
I can’t today. I have a doctor’s appointment at four.
OK. What about tomorrow, Tuesday?
I can. Do you work on Tuesday?
No, I don’t. It’s my day off.
Wednesday at ten, in the big room?
Impossible: there’s no room on Wednesday. The big room isn’t free: there are meetings all day.
And in the café?
No. It’s very noisy. I don’t want to work with noise.
Thursday, then? I have no meetings on Thursday.
Perfect. Thursday at ten, in the big room.
Why can’t Nuria on Monday?
Why is Tuesday not possible?
Why is Wednesday not possible?
On Friday Pablo isn’t in the office: he works from home.
Sorry, I’m not free on Monday.
“Is there a projector in the small room?” “No, there isn’t.”
The client can’t come on Wednesday.
We don’t want to work with noise.
I don’t have time today.
The client can’t come on Monday.
No, I can’t.
Which day does Nuria suggest?
What happens on Wednesday?
What time is possible on Thursday?
Why not Friday?
positive sentence
no right before the verb
no before the first verb
short or full answer
Find the verb and put “no” right before it. With two verbs, before the first one. And if you answer “no” with the verb, say two “no”s: “No, no puedo”.
Today I don’t have money for the taxi.
“Do you work on Sunday?” “No, I don’t.”
Sergio can’t come to the presentation.
“Is there a projector?” You want to answer with the verb:
On Saturday a friend invites you to lots of plans. This week it isn’t possible. Answer “no” with the verb.

You can now say no. But Nuria and Pablo join ideas all the time: “I can, but there’s no room”. In class 025 you learn to join sentences with y, o, pero and ni, perfect for your “no”s: “I can’t on Monday or on Tuesday”.
«En» dice dónde está algo o alguien (in / at / on), sin movimiento. Si vas o llegas a un lugar, el destino lleva «a».
«En» dice dónde está algo o alguien, sin movimiento (in / at / on).

Mateo Ruiz is a courier in Córdoba. Today he has an important package: he leaves the Centro branch and goes to the Norte branch with Carla, a new colleague. To tell his day he needs five small words: a, de, en, con, sin. They are prepositions.
Mateo is at the Centro branch.
He is going to the Norte branch.
It is Mrs Molina’s package.
He is going with Carla.
The preposition goes before the place or the person: a Córdoba, en casa, con Carla. It is a short word, but it changes everything: “I am going to Córdoba” is not “I am in Córdoba”.
“Va a la sucursal Norte”: what does “a” say?
“Está en la sucursal Centro”: what does “en” say?
“Va con Carla” means…
The first decision is easy if you look at the verb. With movement towards a place (ir, llegar, venir), the place takes “a”. Without movement (estar, vivir, trabajar), the place takes “en”.
Where are you going? (to)
Mateo is going to the Norte branch.
We arrive in Córdoba by train.
At night, Carla goes home.
Where are you? (in / at / on)
Lucía works at the office.
The package is on the table.
Carla lives in Córdoba.
I am going to Córdoba.
I am in Córdoba.
Mateo is in Córdoba now.
Carla arrives at the office.
Lucía works at the Centro branch.
Where are you coming from? Whose is it?
Mateo leaves the Centro branch.
I am coming from home.
Carla is from Málaga.
It is Carla’s motorbike.
I am coming from the office.
I am going to the office.
A full trip has both: “Mateo goes from the Centro branch to the Norte branch”. First the origin with “de”, then the destination with “a”.
Mrs Molina’s package
Carla comes from Málaga.
Mateo leaves the office at nine.
Who are you going with? What don’t you have?
Mateo goes with Carla.
The package goes with the receipt.
Carla can’t ride a motorbike without a helmet.
Today Lucía works without help.
Carla rides with a helmet.
Carla rides without a helmet.
Who are you going with? —With Carla.
I don’t have the receipt: I am going without it.
The package goes with a note for Mrs Molina.

“En” also says the means of transport: by train, by motorbike, by bike, by car. Look: “Voy a Córdoba en tren”: “a” is the destination, “en” is how you travel. That is why “Voy en Córdoba” is wrong: Córdoba is not a vehicle.
Which sentence is correct?
Lucía’s office
Good morning, Mateo. Are you at the office already?
Yes, I am here. I am coming from home by bike.
Perfect. Today you have a special package: it is Mrs Molina’s package.
And where is it going?
To the Norte branch. It is on Colón Avenue.
Am I going alone?
No, you are going with Carla. It is her first day.
Very good. And where is the package?
It is on the table, with the receipt. Important: without the receipt, there is no delivery.
Understood. Carla and I are leaving the branch right now. See you later!
How does Mateo come to the office?
Where is the package going?
What is important for the delivery?
Today Carla works at the Centro branch.
I am from Málaga, but I live in Córdoba.
They are going to the Norte branch by motorbike.
I can’t ride a motorbike without a helmet.
Is it Mateo’s backpack? —Yes, it is his backpack.
I am coming from the Centro branch.
I am going home with Carla.
Mateo’s helmet is on the motorbike.
Why is Lucía calling?
Where does the package go now?
Why?
Where is Mrs Molina until two?
What can’t Mateo do?
Where is the receipt?
to (destination)
in / at / on (place)
from · of / ’s
with · without
Look at the verb first. Ir and llegar look for a destination: a. Estar says a place: en. Venir and salir look back to the origin: de. And for possession, never “’s”: el paquete de Lucía.
On Saturday, Mateo goes to Seville by train.
His parents live in Seville.
Mateo is from Córdoba, but his parents are from Seville.
He goes with Carla: she also has family in Seville.
He can’t travel without his ticket: he needs it for the train.

Today you always said “a la sucursal” and “de la oficina”. But what happens with a masculine noun, like “el hotel” or “el centro”? A + el joins into “al”, and de + el joins into “del”: “Voy al centro”, “Vengo del mercado”. It is the natural next step after today.

Ingrid is from Denmark and is on holiday in Valparaíso, Chile. Tomorrow she makes three trips: from the hotel to the port, from the port to the market and from the market to Cerro Alegre (a hill). To say where she is going and where she leaves from, she needs two small words: al and del.
I am going to the port.
I leave the hotel. (I go out from the hotel.)
I walk to the square.
“Voy al puerto”: what does “al” mean?
“Salgo del hotel”: what does “del” mean?
“Camino a la plaza”: why not “al plaza”?
to the
Ingrid goes to the port on foot.
I get to the market at eleven.
We go up to the hill in the funicular.
Ingrid says hello to the guide.
from the · of the
I leave the hotel at nine.
I come back from the market with fruit.
It is the guide’s map.
The funicular is near the market.
I am going to the centre.
I leave the museum at two.
I am coming from the station.
Contraction only happens with “a” or “de” + “el”. With other prepositions (en, con, por), with la, los, las, or with no article, everything stays the same.
I am going to the market.
I am at the market.
I talk with the guide.
“Casa” often goes without an article: “Vuelvo a casa” (I go back home), “Salgo de casa” (I leave home). No “el”, so no contraction.
Tomorrow I am going to the viewpoints on the hill.
Ingrid is at the hotel now.
At night I go back home.
The bus leaves from Plaza Sotomayor.
“el” without an accent is the article (the). “él” with an accent is the pronoun (he / him). The article contracts; the pronoun never does.
I ask the guide.
“Who are you asking?” “Him.”
The map is his.
When “El” is part of a proper name, it is not joined in writing: “Viajo a El Salvador” (I travel to El Salvador). It is an exception; today you only need to recognise it.
“Whose cap is it?” “It is his, Felipe’s.”
Ingrid says hello to the receptionist.
Can “del” be “de + él”?
Which one is correct?
Good morning, Carolina. Today I want to go to the port. Is it far?
No, it is close. From the hotel to the port it is ten minutes on foot.
Perfect! And then, how do I get to the market?
You walk to Plaza Sotomayor and take the bus. It is five minutes.
And is the market near the funicular?
Yes, very close. From the market you go up to Cerro Alegre in the funicular. It is very pretty!
And to come back from the viewpoints at night?
Better a taxi. Look, do you see the man in the cap? That is Felipe, the guide. The big map is his.
The guide’s map? Great! I will talk to him now.
Have a good trip, Ingrid! And at eight, dinner at the hotel.
How many minutes is it from the hotel to the port?
How does Ingrid go up from the market to Cerro Alegre?
Whose is the big map?
At ten I am going to the fine arts museum.
I am coming from the restaurant at the port.
The bus stop is near the cathedral.
Afterwards I walk to the beaches in the north.
Felipe is very nice. I have his phone number.
I go to the market on foot.
The funicular is near the port.
What is Carolina talking about?
How does Ingrid get from the hotel to the port?
Where does Ingrid take the bus?
Where is the funicular?
How does Ingrid get back from the hill to the hotel?
no contraction
him / his

There are only two contractions: a + el = al and de + el = del. Look at the next word: if it is “el” without an accent, they join; if it is la, los, las, él or there is no article, they stay separate.
After Valparaíso, Ingrid arrives in Santiago. Write her sentences.

You can now explain a trip: from the hotel to the port, near the market. To give full directions you now need words like aquí (here), allí (there), cerca (near), hoy (today) or despacio (slowly). In class 029 you learn adverbs of place, time and manner.

Lucía and Daniel work in the same office in Guadalajara. They both want to do sport, but alone it is no fun. To train together, they first talk about their habits: what they always do, what they sometimes do and what they never do.
Lucía: “I always have breakfast early.”
Lucía runs on Tuesdays.
Daniel: “I never have dinner late.”
“Siempre desayuno temprano” means…
“Lucía corre los martes” means…
“Nunca ceno tarde”: how many times?
Where do one-word frequency expressions go?
I always have breakfast early.
Daniel usually works late.
Sometimes we eat together at the office.
Lucía always runs in the same park.
Daniel usually works late: four days out of five.
Sometimes we eat together: once or twice a week.
Lucía runs in the same park every day. Lucía always runs in the same park.
How often? (longer expressions)
Lucía runs every day.
Once a week I swim in the pool.
Daniel goes to the gym twice a week.
On Saturdays I go out walking with my dog.
“Todos los días” = every day. “Todo el día” = all day long. “I work every day” is not “I work all day”.
Every Saturday, Lucía swims.
Monday to Sunday, no exceptions: I run every day.
I never go to the gym on Sundays.

In English one negative is enough: “I never go”. In Spanish, if “nunca” comes after the verb, the sentence needs “no” before the verb: “No voy nunca”. It is correct and very common. The same with “casi nunca”.
Which one is correct?
“Nunca voy” and “No voy nunca”…
On Saturdays I swim. Every day I run.
This Saturday I am not swimming. Today I run with Daniel.
Lucía has a special dinner only this Friday: “This Friday I have dinner late.”
“How often do you swim?” The natural answer is…
Daniel works at the office every Monday.
Lucía, you do a lot of sport, right?
Yes, almost every day. On Tuesdays and Thursdays I run in the park.
In the morning or in the afternoon?
In the morning. I always run early, before work. And you?
I go to the gym sometimes, about once a week. Alone it is no fun.
So, shall we run together? Can you do Tuesdays?
Tuesdays, yes. Thursdays I can hardly ever do: I work late.
OK. And the weekend? I usually swim on Saturdays.
Saturdays, perfect! But I never train on Sundays: it is my family day.
Great: Tuesday and Saturday. Shall we start this Tuesday?
Of course! Tomorrow, early, in the park.
Which days does Lucía run?
How often does Daniel go to the gym?
Why does Daniel not train on Sundays?
Lucía runs in the park on Tuesdays.
Daniel never swims in the sea.
I usually have breakfast at home, but today I have breakfast at the office.
We never have dinner after eleven.
How often do you go to the gym? — Twice a week.
Daniel never trains on Sundays.
Lucía never has dinner late.
I swim once a week.
Why does Lucía send the voice note?
What does Lucía do on Tuesdays and Thursdays?
Why can she not train on Mondays?
How often does Lucía train on Fridays?
What happens this Saturday?
One word, before the verb
Longer expressions, at the start or the end
Never after the verb needs “no”
One point in time, not a habit

Before you speak, think: does it repeat or happen once? If it repeats: los sábados, siempre, a veces. If it happens once: este sábado, hoy. And if nunca comes after the verb, put no in front: “No voy nunca”.
Lucía runs on Tuesdays: it is her habit.
We eat together twice a week.
I work all day: from morning till night.
How often do you swim? — Once a week.

You can now talk about your habits: “I always have breakfast early”, “I never have dinner late”. But many morning routines use verbs with me, te, se: “me levanto” (I get up), “me ducho” (I shower). In class 031 you learn these verbs to describe your whole routine.
Lucía is a nurse in a hospital. She works the morning shift: it starts at seven. Óscar is a new nurse and on Monday he starts on the same shift. Today Lucía explains how she gets ready.
“I get up at five.”
“Then I have a shower.”
“At night I go to bed at ten.”
“Me levanto a las cinco” means…
What does Lucía do at night?
In the three sentences, which word comes before the verb?

In the dictionary these verbs end in -se: levantarse, ducharse, acostarse. The “se” says the action goes back to the same person: Lucía gets herself out of bed. When you conjugate, the “se” changes with the person: me, te, se, nos, os, se.
You get up at six.
Óscar has a shower at night.
Lucía and I get up early.
Where does “me” go?
I have a shower and have breakfast.
Raúl doesn’t get up at five.
What time do you get up?
Me despierto = I open my eyes (I wake up). Me levanto = I get out of bed (I get up). Lucía wakes up at five to five and gets up at five.
Which one has the right order?
Which negative sentence is correct?
We get dressed at the hospital.
In the morning I wash my face.
On Saturday I wash the car.
Raúl wakes Alba up at half past seven.
After her shower, Lucía gets dressed quickly.
“Lavo el coche” has no “me” because…
Which one is correct?
Lucía, on Monday I start on the seven o’clock shift. What time do you get up?
I get up at five. It’s early, but it isn’t hard.
And what do you do first?
First I have a hot shower. Then I have coffee and bread for breakfast.
Do you get dressed in your uniform at home?
No. At home I get dressed in normal clothes. Here, in the locker room, I put on my uniform.
And your partner? Does he get up at five too?
No, Raúl gets up at seven. He wakes up Alba, our daughter, and makes breakfast.
I live with my brother Hugo. We go to bed very late, at twelve or one.
Phew! With the morning shift, that’s a problem. I go to bed at ten.
And at the weekend? Don’t you wake up early?
Yes, I wake up at six, but I don’t get up: I read in bed. And on Saturday I wash the car with Raúl.
What time does Lucía get up?
Where does Lucía put on her uniform?
Who wakes Alba up?
On Monday I get up at five.
Hugo, what time do you go to bed?
The nurses put on their uniform before the shift.
Raúl and I go to bed at half past ten.
Alba already gets dressed by herself.
Raúl wakes Alba up with a kiss.
I don’t get up early.
Lucía puts on her uniform.
Raúl and I go to bed at ten.
Why does Lucía send this message?
What time does Lucía go to bed?
Where do they put on their uniform?
Why doesn’t Hugo wake Óscar up?
What does Lucía do so she doesn’t wake up late?
What time is Lucía meeting Óscar tomorrow?
the action goes back to the same person
nosotros keeps the stem
the pronoun goes right before the verb
the action goes to someone or something else

Ask: who gets the action? If it is the same person, put that person’s pronoun before the verb: me levanto, te duchas, se viste, nos acostamos. If it is something or someone else, no pronoun: lavo el coche, despierta a Alba. Later you will see “quiero acostarme”: with an infinitive, the pronoun goes at the end.
On Mondays I wake up very early.
Do you get dressed at home or at work?
My brother and I go to bed late on Saturdays.
Raúl puts Alba to bed at nine p.m.

You now put me, te, se and nos before the verb to talk about your routine. In class 032 the pronouns me, te and nos come back with gustar and encantar: “me gusta el café”, “nos encanta viajar”. The order is the same, but the idea changes: the thing pleases you.

Carmen and Diego are on holiday in Veracruz, Mexico. Tonight they want to eat out. Valeria, the hotel receptionist, has three restaurants. To choose, everyone talks about tastes: what they like and what they don’t.
Salads, vegetables and soups. Vegetarian food.
Fish, seafood and live music.
Pasta, pizza and fish of the day. A quiet place.
Carmen says: “I like coffee and I like travelling.” In English it is “I like”; in Spanish the idea is “coffee pleases me”: the thing is pleasing to a person.
Where is there live music?
“Me gusta el café” means…
Diego doesn’t want noise. Which restaurant is good for him?
I like…
I like the book.
I like books.
I like vegetable soup.
I like salads.
I like having dinner late.
I like travelling and eating well.
I like the dessert. I like the beach.
I like desserts. I like beaches.
I like swimming. I like cooking.
For a general taste, Spanish uses the article: “Me gusta el pescado”, “Me gustan las sopas”. English doesn’t: “I like fish”.
I like Mexican food.
I like seafood.
I like walking on the beach.
I like fish.
The word before gusta says who likes it: me (me), te (you), le (him, her, you formal), nos (us). The verb still looks at the thing: gusta or gustan.
To react: “I like coffee.” — “A mí también” (me too) or “A mí no” (not me). Today they are fixed phrases; pronouns after “a” (a mí, a ti) are class 033.
Diego talks to Carmen: “Do you like fish?”
Valeria talks about Diego: “Diego doesn’t like noise.”
Carmen and Diego: “We like Veracruz.”
Valeria talks to Carmen (formal): “Madam, do you like music?”
I love…
I love the sea.
We love home-made desserts.
Carmen loves dancing.
I get up at seven.
I like coffee.
Diego: “I love pizza!”
Diego: “I don’t like noise at all.”
“Me encanta” is…
Which one is correct?
Good afternoon. I have three restaurants for tonight. Madam, what food do you like?
I love fish. And I really like seafood.
Then El Puerto is perfect: fish, seafood and live music. Sir, do you like fish?
No, I don’t like it at all. And live music, no thanks. I like having dinner in peace.
Diego! Don’t you like music?
Yes, but at home. In a restaurant I like talking and eating quietly.
And La Huerta? It’s vegetarian: salads, vegetables, soups…
Mmm, I like salads.
Not me. I eat vegetables, but I don’t love them.
Well, there’s also Casa Rosa: pasta, pizza and fish of the day. It’s a quiet place.
I love pasta and pizza!
And the fish of the day for me. And we love desserts! Casa Rosa, please.
What does Carmen love?
Why doesn’t Diego want El Puerto?
What do they both love?
Diego likes the pizzas at Casa Rosa.
Carmen, do you like the flan?
I like walking along the seafront.
I don’t like loud music.
Mmm, I really like this soup.
I like the sea.
We love desserts.
Diego doesn’t like noise.
What do you like to eat?
Why does Valeria call?
What time is the table at Casa Rosa?
What does Diego like, according to Valeria?
What does Valeria love?
What other option does Valeria give?
one thing or an action
several things
the person comes first
me too · not me
Always ask: what is being liked? One thing or an infinitive: gusta. Several things: gustan. The person (me, te, le, nos) doesn’t change the verb: never “me gusto”.
Carmen likes seafood.
Diego, do you like dancing?
We love Veracruz: it’s a beautiful city.
I love Mexican food.
—Do you like coffee? —Yes, I really like it.
My brother likes horror films.
We like going to the cinema on Sundays.
Do you like series in Spanish?

Today you say “a mí también” and “a mí no” as fixed phrases. In class 033 you see the whole system: a mí, a ti, para mí, con ella, and the special forms conmigo and contigo. Then you can say clearly “I like it, you don’t”.
Carmen runs a small team in an office. On Friday there is a team dinner. Today Carmen has a box with invitations, tasks and the Secret Santa papers, and she hands everything out.
“This envelope is for me.”
“Diego, this one is for you.”
“And this one is for her.”
“Esto es para mí” means…
Carmen gives Diego an envelope: “Diego, this is for you.”
After “para”, which form do we use instead of “yo”?

After a preposition (para, sin, de, a, en, con…) we use these pronouns. The rule is simple: yo → mí and tú → ti. The other pronouns are the same as the subject: él, ella, usted, nosotros, ustedes, ellos.
The box is for Pablo = The box is for him.
The flowers are for Rosa and Nuria = for them.
Which pronouns change after a preposition?
How do I say “with me” and “with you”?
Nuria, are you coming to the shop with me?
Yes, Diego, I’m going with you.
Rosa works with her in the office.
Write conmigo and contigo as one word, with no space. But “con él”, “con ella” and “con nosotros” are two words.
Diego, are you coming to the dinner with me?
Yes, Nuria, I’m going with you.
Nuria goes to the shop with him.
The invitation is for me.
It’s my invitation.
It’s my desk.
I bring the cake and the cake is for you.
Which one is correct?
Good morning, team! Here I have the invitations for Friday’s dinner. Diego, this one is for you.
Thanks, Carmen. And this other one? Is it for me too?
No, that one is for Pablo. He’s working from home today, but the invitation is for him and his partner.
And me? Isn’t there an invitation for me?
Of course! Here’s your invitation, Nuria. Without you there’s no party: you’re bringing the music.
Great! Diego, on Thursday I’m buying the lights. Are you coming to the shop with me?
Yes, I’ll go with you. And we’re also buying the present for Rosa, the new colleague, right?
Yes, please. For her it’s the first dinner with us.
I love buying presents. A book for her?
Good idea. Carmen, are you coming with us on Thursday?
No, I can’t on Thursday: you’re going without me. But on Friday I’m having dinner with you, of course!
Perfect. So, Diego, Thursday at six, you and me at the shop.
Who is the second invitation for?
Who is Nuria going to the shop with on Thursday?
Is Carmen going to the shop on Thursday?
Pablo, this box is for you.
Pablo isn’t here, but the task is for him.
Nuria, are you having lunch with me today?
Yes! I’ll have lunch with you at one.
On Thursday Diego and Nuria go to the shop without me.
Carmen, are you coming to the shop with us?
Are you coming to the shop with me?
We’re buying a book for her.
Without you there’s no party.
Why does Carmen send this message?
Where are the invitations?
Who is Rosa bringing the cake with?
Who is buying the lights on Thursday?
Who is Nuria going in the car with on Friday?
after a preposition: mí (accent), ti (no accent)
one single word
él has an accent: it is not the article
yo and tú go before the verb; mi and tu go with a noun

Ask: is there a preposition just before? If so, yo → mí and tú → ti; with “con”, conmigo and contigo. The other pronouns don’t change. One exception: “entre tú y yo” (between you and me) uses yo and tú.
Pablo, these flowers are for you.
Rosa, are you having dinner with me on Friday?
Diego isn’t coming: the meeting is without him.
I love chocolate cake.

You can now hand out invitations, tasks and presents: for me, for you, with me, with you. Now the question is how many: in class 034 you count people, invitations and things with numbers, mucho, poco and bastante, exactly what you need to organize a party.
It is Saturday, eight in the evening. Clara and Sergio share a flat. There is a concert at nine, but Clara is unwell. Sergio is getting ready to go out with his friend Pablo.
“My head hurts.”
“I’m putting on my coat.”
“Where is my coat?”
What is wrong with Clara?
In “me duele la cabeza”, whose head is it?
In English we say “my coat”. Which word goes in “me pongo ___ abrigo”?
Doler (to hurt) works like gustar (class 032). The body part is the subject: one part, duele; two or more, duelen. The person goes first: me, te, le, nos, les.
What hurts?
My throat hurts.
My eyes hurt in the light.
Sergio’s back hurts.
Do your feet hurt?
My stomach hurts.
After the concert, Sergio’s legs hurt.
What does “nos duele la cabeza” mean?
With a pronoun, use the article
Before eating, I wash my hands.
Sergio puts on his white shirt.
At home, Clara takes off her shoes.
Do you brush your teeth after dinner?
With other verbs, when it is clear whose it is, Spanish also uses the article: “I open my eyes”, “I raise my hand”, “I have green eyes”. Today you only need to recognise it.
It’s cold. I put on my gloves.
Clara washes her hands.
“Sergio se quita los zapatos” means…
My head hurts.
My head is big.
Sergio: “Where is your scarf, Clara?”
Which sentence is natural?
Which one is correct?
Clara, the concert starts at nine. Are you ready?
No, Sergio. I don’t feel well: my head hurts and my throat hurts.
Oh no! And do your ears hurt too?
No, not my ears. But my eyes hurt in the light.
Then you’re not going out. I’m going with Pablo. Just a moment: I’ll wash my hands and put on my new shirt.
It’s cold tonight. Are you putting on your coat?
Yes, of course. But… where is my coat?
Your coat is on the chair in the living room. And my scarf is on the sofa: it’s big and very warm.
Thanks! Then I’ll put on your scarf for the concert.
Sure. Hey, why are you walking like that?
My shoes are new and my feet hurt. OK, I’ll take off the shoes and put on my trainers.
Good idea. Enjoy the concert, Sergio!
What hurts Clara?
Where is Sergio’s coat?
Why does Sergio take off his shoes?
Doctor, my throat has hurt since today.
My eyes also hurt in the light.
With his new shoes, Sergio’s feet hurt.
Clara, your coat is very nice.
I put on my gloves and my hat.
Sergio puts on his coat.
We wash our hands.
My coat is blue.
Why is Clara calling?
When do her eyes hurt?
What does Clara put on at home?
Why does she wash her hands so often?
one body part hurts
two or more hurt
the pronoun says whose it is
describing, location, someone else’s

Look at the verb: if there is me, te, se, le or nos and the thing belongs to that person, use el, la, los, las: my head hurts, I put on my coat. If you describe it, say where it is, or it belongs to someone else, use mi, tu, su. And with doler: one part, duele; two or more, duelen.
After the gym my legs hurt.
At the door, Clara takes off her boots.
My jacket is red and Sergio’s jacket is black.

You now know when to use the article and when to use mi, tu, su with clothes and the body. In class 036 you describe an object with several clues so someone can find it among others: “the grey scarf, the big one, is on the sofa”. Article, noun, adjective and place, all together.
It is Monday morning at a language school. Carmen works at reception. There are four lost objects: two folders and two notebooks. Many students ask: “Is my folder here?” But which one is it?
A student says: “I’m looking for a folder.” Does Carmen know which one?
What is in the box?
How many things are on the shelf?
How do I say exactly which thing I am looking for?
I’m looking for my blue folder.
It is a small red notebook.
I’m looking for the blue folder that is on the shelf.
Which object is “something blue and big”?
What is the normal order?
Which clue is enough for the red folder?
The red folder is on the desk.
The red notebook is on the shelf.
Look at the article, not only the last letter: el paraguas is masculine and singular: el paraguas negro. El aula (classroom) is feminine: el aula pequeña.
I’m looking for the black backpack.
I’m looking for some blue notebooks.
It is a big folder.

When the other person already knows what you are talking about, you don’t repeat the noun. You say el or la + one clue: “Which is your folder? — The blue one.” Also: “The one that is on the shelf.” The article tells you which thing it is: la = the folder, el = the notebook.
Which is your notebook? — The red one.
Which is your folder? — The one that is on the desk.
“The one (fem.) that is on the shelf” is…
Which one is correct?
Good morning, Pablo. What do you need?
Hi, Carmen. I’m looking for my folder. It isn’t in my backpack.
Well, there are two folders and two notebooks here. What is your folder like?
It’s blue and small. It has my class notes.
Look: there is a red folder on the desk and a blue folder on the shelf.
The blue one, please. The one on the shelf.
This one? The small blue folder?
Yes, it’s this one! Thanks. Oh, my classmate Lorena is looking for her notebook. It’s red.
There is a red notebook and a blue notebook. Is it big or small?
Small. It’s a small red notebook, with a photo of Lima.
Then it’s the one on the shelf. The big one is blue and it’s in the box.
Perfect. Lorena is in class: I’ll take the notebook. See you later!
What is Pablo’s folder like?
Where is Lorena’s notebook?
I’m looking for a green scarf.
I’m looking for my big black umbrella.
I’m looking for some small keys.
Which is your jacket? — The grey one.
My backpack is the one that is on the chair.
They are some white gloves.
I’m looking for the big red folder.
My backpack is the one on the chair.
Why does Lorena call?
What is Lorena’s scarf like?
Where is the scarf, probably?
Whose is the small green scarf?
What are the keys like?
colour and size go after the noun
-o changes; -e and consonants don’t change for feminine
es = what it is like · está = where it is
the article tells you which thing it is

One clue is almost never enough. Give several clues that agree with the noun: la carpeta azul pequeña, el cuaderno rojo pequeño. And when the other person already knows what you mean, drop the noun and keep the article: la azul, el que está en la caja.
I need the red folder.
I’m looking for some blue books.
Which is your umbrella? — The black one.
My scarf is the one that is next to the window.

You can now pick out a thing with several clues: the small blue folder, the one on the shelf. In class 037 you use the same adjectives to compare two things: “the red folder is bigger than the blue one”, “the red notebook is as small as the blue folder”.

Clara and Julio arrive at the Hotel Mirador in Cádiz without a booking. Nuria, the receptionist, has three free rooms: 12, 20 and 31. Which one do they choose? To decide, they compare three things: size, price and noise.
Room 12 is bigger than room 31.
Room 31 is less expensive than room 12.
Room 20 is as big as room 31.
“La 12 es más grande que la 31” means…
Which room is quiet?
“Tan grande como” says that the two rooms are…
more … than / -er than
Room 12 is more expensive than room 20.
Room 31 is quieter than room 12.
The courtyard is prettier than the street.
The beds in 12 are bigger than the beds in 20.
In English you say “bigger” or “more expensive”. In Spanish it is always the same: más + adjective. Más grande, más caro, más tranquilo.
Room 20 is noisier than room 31.
Room 12 is bigger than room 20.
The reception is prettier than the bar.
less … than
Room 20 is less quiet than room 31.
The street is less pretty than the courtyard.
Room 20 is less expensive than room 31.
“La 31 es menos cara que la 12” = …
The bar is less quiet than the terrace.
as … as
Room 20 is as noisy as room 12.
Room 31 is not as big as room 12.
The museum is cheaper than the aquarium.
The museum is as cheap as the castle.
The castle is as cheap as the museum.
The aquarium is more expensive than the museum.
“La 20 no es tan tranquila como la 31” means…
With a number you say “más de”: “Room 12 costs more than 80 euros”. And bueno / malo have special forms: mejor / peor (better / worse). You will practise them in another class.
Which one is correct?
Room 12 costs more than 80 euros.
Good afternoon. We have three free rooms: 12, 20 and 31.
Which one is bigger?
Room 12. It’s bigger than the other two: it has thirty square metres. But it is also more expensive: ninety euros a night.
And 20 and 31?
Room 20 is as big as room 31: twenty square metres. Room 20 costs sixty euros and 31, seventy-five.
So room 20 is cheaper than 31. Is it quiet?
Not very. It faces the street: it’s as noisy as 12. Room 31 faces the courtyard and is quieter than the others.
For us, silence is important. And 31 is less expensive than 12.
Yes. It’s not as big as 12, but for two nights it’s fine.
Perfect. We want room 31, please.
Very good. Here is the key. It’s on the third floor.
Why is room 12 more expensive?
Why don’t they want room 20?
Which room do they choose?
The wardrobe in 12 is bigger than the wardrobe in 31.
The bed in 20 is as big as the bed in 31.
Breakfast at the bar is cheaper than breakfast at the hotel.
The hotel pool is smaller than the gym pool.
The car park in the square is less expensive than the hotel car park.
Room 20 is not as bright as room 12.
Room 12 is more expensive than room 31.
The courtyard is as pretty as the terrace.
Room 31 is less noisy than room 12.
Room 20 is not as big as room 12.
Why does Nuria call?
Room 40 and room 31: which one is bigger?
Why is room 40 quiet?
How much does room 40 cost?
How much is breakfast tomorrow?
Until what time can they call?
less … than / not as … as
Más and menos go with que; tan goes with como. The adjective agrees with the first thing: la 31 es más tranquila, el patio es más tranquilo.
Room 12 is noisier than room 31.
Room 40 is as quiet as room 31.
Room 40 is less expensive than room 12.
Room 31 is as big as room 20.
The bed in room 40 is more comfortable than the bed in room 20.
On Monday, Clara and Julio go from Cádiz to Seville. They can go by train or by bus. Compare the two.

You can now compare rooms with más, menos and tan. In class 038 the trip goes on: you buy a train ticket and confirm the time, the day and the date: “Son las ocho”, “el martes 20 de octubre”. Today’s numbers (prices and sizes) help you again.

It is Tuesday morning at the station in Madrid. Elena wants a train ticket to Valencia: on Friday it is her mother’s birthday. At the ticket office she needs three things: the time, the day and the date.
What time is it? It’s eight o’clock.
The train leaves at half past six.
Today is Tuesday. I travel on Friday 23 October.
“Son las ocho” tells you…
What day is it today?
What time does train 3 leave?
What time is it?
It’s one o’clock.
It’s two o’clock.
It’s eight o’clock sharp.
It’s half past one.
It’s twelve. / It’s midday.
It’s quarter past one.
It’s quarter past three.
It’s four o’clock.
It’s quarter to seven.
At what time…?
What time does the train leave?
The train leaves at one.
It arrives at quarter to three.
Elena works until two.
Dinner is at half past nine in the evening.
What time is it? It’s six.
The train leaves at six.
Tickets and screens use the 24-hour clock: 18:30. In normal conversation we say “las seis y media de la tarde”. In station announcements you will hear “las dieciocho treinta”.
Elena’s train leaves at half past six.
Excuse me, what time is it? · It’s nine.
The train arrives at quarter past eight in the evening.
Which day? What date?
Today is Tuesday, 20 October.
Elena travels on Friday.
She comes back on Sunday 25 October.
Elena works at the office on Mondays.
Her mother’s birthday is on 23 October.
Elena travels on Friday (this Friday).
Elena works until two on Fridays.
Which date is correct?
Today is Tuesday.

In Mexico and other Latin American countries: “Son cuarto para las nueve” (8:45) or “Son quince para las nueve”. In some areas people also ask “¿Qué horas son?”. They are all correct; you can use “son las nueve menos cuarto”.
Which one is correct?
Good morning. How can I help you?
Good morning. A return ticket to Valencia, please. For Friday.
Friday 23 October? There are three trains: at ten past nine, at one, and at half past six in the afternoon.
On Friday I work until two. What time does the half past six train arrive?
It arrives at quarter past eight in the evening.
Perfect, that one. And the return, on Sunday afternoon.
On Sunday the 25th there is a train at five. It arrives in Madrid at ten to seven.
Very good. Excuse me, what time is it? I start work at nine.
It’s five past eight. Don’t worry, you have time.
So: outward, Friday 23rd, at half past six; return, Sunday 25th, at five.
Exactly. Here is your ticket. Have a good trip!
Why doesn’t Elena want the one o’clock train?
What time does Elena arrive in Valencia?
Which day does Elena come back?
It’s twenty past one.
It’s half past ten.
The bus leaves at three in the afternoon.
It’s quarter to eight.
The appointment is on Thursday.
Pablo’s birthday is on 4 May.
It’s quarter past eight.
Elena arrives on Friday at eight.
Why does Pablo call?
What day is it today in the message?
What time does Pablo leave work?
What time is the birthday dinner?
When is there a market in the square?
What time does the Sunday train leave?
What time is it? It’s five past eight.
The train leaves at half past six in the afternoon.
I come back on Sunday 25 October.
One o’clock is singular: es la una, a la una. All other hours are plural: son las dos, a las dos. For a specific day, el viernes, without “en”. And the date: el 23 de octubre.
It’s three o’clock.
The yoga class is at one.
It’s quarter to twelve.
Elena works on Mondays and goes back to Valencia on Saturday the 31st.
The New Year’s Eve party is on 31 December.
Back in Madrid, Elena has a busy week: a doctor’s appointment, a class and a concert. Write each one with day, date and time.

You can now say when something happens: on Friday, at half past six, on 23 October. In class 039 you use these times and dates to talk about your plans: “On Saturday I’m going to visit my mother”, “At nine we’re going to have dinner”. With ir a + infinitive, your diary talks about the future.

It is Friday night. Lucía and Daniel are friends and share a flat. They talk about tomorrow, Saturday: what are they going to do? To talk about a plan, Spanish has a very easy structure: ir a + infinitive.
On Saturdays Daniel works at the library.
Tomorrow I am going to visit Marta.
Tomorrow · tonight · on Saturday
“Mañana voy a visitar a Marta” talks about…
“Los sábados Daniel trabaja” talks about…
Which word talks about the near future?
going to + verb
Tonight I am going to cook rice with vegetables.
Tomorrow Daniel is going to sleep until nine.
On Saturday we are going to buy fruit at the market.
Marta and Felipe are going to come to dinner.
Tonight Daniel is going to cook.
Tomorrow we are going to have breakfast with Marta.
On Saturday I am going to clean the flat.
The present tells what is normal: what you do every day, on Saturdays, always. Ir a + infinitive tells a plan: what you are going to do tonight, tomorrow, this Saturday.
You will also hear the present for a fixed plan: “Mañana trabajo”. It is correct. Today you practise ir a + infinitive, the clearest way to tell a plan.
Every day Lucía has coffee at eight.
Tonight Lucía is going to watch a film.
“I normally work on Saturdays, but this Saturday…”
Tomorrow we are going to the market.
Tomorrow we are going to buy fish.
Tomorrow we are going to go to the market.
“No” goes before ir: “No voy a trabajar”. To ask, the word order stays the same; only the intonation changes: “¿Vas a venir?”, “¿Qué vas a hacer?”.
This afternoon I am going to the cinema.
This afternoon I am going to watch a film.
Which question is correct?
Which one is correct?
Lucía, what are you going to do tomorrow?
In the morning I am going to visit Marta. We are going to have breakfast at her place at ten.
I normally work at the library on Saturdays. But this Saturday I am not going to work.
Great! In the afternoon, shall we go to the market? We need fish for dinner.
Perfect. And at night I am going to cook: fish with rice.
Marta and her brother Felipe are going to come to dinner. But Marta does not eat fish: she always eats vegetables.
No problem. I am also going to make a big salad.
And the film? On Saturday nights we watch a film.
Yes, but not tomorrow. We are going to talk with Marta and Felipe all night.
Very good. And are you going to come to the breakfast too?
Yes! But first I am going to sleep until nine.
What is Lucía going to do in the morning?
What does Daniel normally do on Saturdays?
Why is Daniel going to make a salad?
On Saturday I am going to bring dessert.
Are you going to come to the market with me?
Marta and Felipe are going to arrive at eight.
On Sunday we are going to rest at home.
Madam, are you going to come to dinner?
Felipe is going to bring dessert.
We are not going to watch a film.
What are you going to do on Sunday?
Tomorrow I am going to rest.
Why does Marta send the message?
What is Marta going to make?
What time is Felipe going to come?
Why can’t Marta make it at two?
What are Marta and Felipe going to bring to dinner?
What does Marta ask at the end?
going to + verb: a plan
present: what you usually do
going to a place
Three pieces, always: ir conjugated + a + infinitive. Only ir changes. What is normal goes in the present: “Trabajo hoy”; the plan goes with ir a: “Voy a trabajar mañana”.
Tomorrow Felipe is going to bring dessert.
Tonight I am going to cook.
On Saturdays Marta walks in the park.
Lucía and Daniel are going to buy fish.
In the afternoon we are going to the market.
It is Monday. At work, Elena, a colleague, asks Daniel about his plans for the week. Write Daniel’s answers.

You can now tell your plans with ir a + infinitive. In class 040 you use the same idea, a verb + infinitive, with querer, poder and tener que: what you want to do, what you can do and what you have to do. “Quiero salir, pero tengo que estudiar”.

Laura lives in Bogotá. She and her brother Gabriel want to travel to Cartagena on the long weekend. But there are limits: time, money, work. Laura asks her friend Julio, who works at a travel agency, for help.
Laura wants to see the sea.
Laura can leave on Friday.
Gabriel has to work on Friday.
“Laura quiere ver el mar” is…
“Gabriel tiene que trabajar” means…
“Laura puede salir el viernes” means…
want to · can · have to + verb
Laura wants to visit the Rosario Islands.
Gabriel cannot leave before two.
The two of them have to book the hotel this week.
We want to eat fish on the beach.
Laura and Gabriel want to travel in November.
I can pay for the hotel.
The action is the same: salir (to leave). The first verb changes, and the meaning changes.
