A month later, Gabriel moves into a new home. Tell how the move is going: transform the sentences.

Three more constructions with the infinitive: dejar de + infinitive (to stop doing something: “Rubén stopped smoking”), seguir sin + infinitive (still not: “The printer still isn’t working”) and ponerse a + infinitive (to start suddenly: “It started to rain”).
Marina stopped working on Sundays: now she rests.
I called the technician, but the printer still isn’t working.
We were on the terrace and suddenly it started to rain.

You can now join one verb with another and describe states: “Acabo de llegar”, “Sigue pintando”, “La puerta está cerrada”. In class 083 you learn to put a question inside another sentence: “I don’t know where the print shop is”, “Do you know what time the bookshop opens?”. It is the natural next step: from joining two verbs you move on to joining two ideas in one sentence.

Marta Rojas has just arrived in Medellín. She lives in the Los Almendros building, apartment 502, and has lots of questions for Héctor, the doorman. Sometimes she asks directly: “Where is the laundry room?”. But often she puts the question inside another sentence: “Can you tell me where the laundry room is?”, “I don’t know where it is.” These are indirect questions.
Where is the laundry room?
Can you tell me where the laundry room is?
I don’t know where the laundry room is.
The question word stays the same, with its accent, and the verb comes right after it: “dónde está la lavandería”. You only add a phrase at the start: “no sé”, “¿me puede decir…?”.
“¿Me puede decir dónde está la lavandería?” is…
“No sé dónde está” means…
In “No sé dónde está”, does “dónde” have an accent?
Do you know where Elena lives?
I don’t know where Elena lives.
Do you know when the bank opens?
Tell me what you want for dinner.
I don’t remember what the night doorman is called.

“¿Dónde está el baño?” is correct. But with a stranger, “Can you tell me where the bathroom is?” or “Do you know where the bathroom is?” sounds softer. To answer without the information: “No, no lo sé” (No, I don’t know).
Choose the correct sentence.
With usted: “Do you know when the technician is coming?”
Which is the most natural order?
Do you know if there is a lift?
Is the technician coming? → I don’t know if the technician is coming.
Do you have to pay? → Do you know if you have to pay?
Does the dryer work? → Tell me if the dryer works.
I don’t know if there is a lift.
If it rains, I don’t go out.
—Is there a lift? —Yes, there are two.
Do they have a gym? → I don’t know if they have a gym.
Which “si” introduces an indirect question?
—Do you know if there is a lift? —Yes, there is one.
Do you know what his number is?
I don’t know which bus goes to the city centre.
Do you know what Elena’s number is?
There are two keys and I don’t know which one is for the garage.
I don’t know who Elena lives with.
Can you tell me how much the laundry room costs?
Where is Elena from? → I don’t know where Elena is from.
There are two washing machines. Do you know which one works?
How many apartments are there? → I don’t know how many apartments there are.
Do they open on Sundays? → I don’t know if they open on Sundays.
Which sentence asks “what do you need”?
Good morning, Héctor. Excuse me, can you tell me where the building’s laundry room is?
Of course, Marta. It’s in the basement, next to the garage. It opens at seven in the morning.
Perfect. And do you know if you have to pay with coins?
Yes, with thousand-peso coins. But careful: I don’t know if the dryer works. Yesterday it wasn’t working.
Oh dear. And do you know when the technician is coming?
This week, but I don’t know which day. I’ll ask the building manager and let you know.
Thank you very much. Another thing: I’m expecting a parcel. Tell me what the best time to receive it is.
I’m here from seven to three; after that my colleague Julián is here. And do you know what time the parcel arrives?
No, I don’t know. The shop only says “between Monday and Wednesday”.
Don’t worry. If it arrives in the afternoon, Julián will take it and keep it for you.
Very kind. One last question: I don’t know who lives in 503. Yesterday a very friendly woman said hello to me in the lift.
That must be Elena Cardona! She can explain to you how everything works in the building.
What doesn’t Héctor know?
Who can explain to Marta how the building works?
Marta writes the questions for Elena in her notebook. Look at each direct question: inside “No sé…”, does it go with “si” or with a question word?
Do you know where the nearest cash machine is?
I don’t know if the building has a doorman at night.
Do you know what the night doorman is called?
I don’t know which one is the garage key.
Can you tell me how much the local gym costs?
I don’t know where the pharmacy is.
Tell me which day you are free.
Can you tell me what time the bank opens?
What is the main idea?
Where is there a supermarket?
What doesn’t Elena know about Friday’s meeting?
What does Elena ask Marta?
Why does Elena want to know which day Marta is free?
introduces the question; ¿ ? only if the whole sentence asks
the same word, with its accent, then the verb
yes/no questions: si, no accent, no “que”

Think of the direct question. If it starts with a question word, keep it with its accent: “¿Dónde está?” → “No sé dónde está”. If the answer is yes or no, use “si”: “¿Viene?” → “No sé si viene”. Never “que si” or “que dónde”. And the verb stays in the indicative.
Excuse me, do you know what time the next bus to Bogotá leaves?
I don’t know if my sister is coming to dinner tonight.
There are three T-shirts. Tell me which one you like best.
Can you tell me who you are going to the concert with?
A month later, Marta goes on a trip and arrives at the bus station in Cali. She doesn’t know anything there. Turn her direct questions into polite questions for the information desk.
In Spain people say “billete”; in many Latin American countries, “boleto” or “pasaje”. The grammar of the question is the same.

In an email or an office: “I would like to know if there are places available”, “Could you tell me when the office opens?”. For a real doubt, add “o no”: “I don’t know whether he is coming or not.” And to report someone else’s question in the present: “Elena asks if there is a meeting”, “Héctor asks where the parcel is.”

You can now ask for information politely and say what you don’t know: “Can you tell me what time it opens?”, “I don’t know if he is coming.” These questions also work for the past: “Do you know how long she lived in Cali?”, “I don’t remember how many times I went.” In class 084 you learn to answer: “I was there for three days”, “I used to go every summer.” It is the natural next step: you know how to ask “how long” and “how often”; now you tell it in the past.

Marta Ruiz runs a small hotel in Cartagena, Colombia. She needs a receptionist. Today she is interviewing Julián Mora. Julián talks about his experience: how long he worked in each place, what he always did and when he came back to Colombia.
I worked in a hostel for five years. (a finished period)
Every Saturday I organised a walk. (a habit of that time)
I came back to Colombia two months ago.
“I worked in a hostel for five years.” Does Julián work there now?
“Every Saturday I organised a walk” is about…
“I came back two months ago.” When did Julián come back?
How long were you / did you work / did you live there?
Last summer I was in Santa Marta for three days.
Marta lived in Bogotá from 2010 to 2015.
For two months I worked nights.
Yesterday we studied all afternoon.

In class 230 you saw “Vivo aquí desde hace dos años” (it is still going on). Today the situation is over: “Viví allí dos años”. Present + desde hace: still going. Indefinido + amount of time: finished.
Last year Julián was out of work for six months.
Marta worked in a bank from 2008 to 2010.
My sister lived in Quito for three years. Now she lives in Cali.
How often did you do it? What did you always do?
At the hostel, Julián always started at six.
In Toronto he spoke English every day.
As a girl, Marta went to the beach every Sunday.
How many times did you go? How many times did it happen?
Before living here, Julián had been to Cartagena three times.
Marta went to Lisbon once, in 2018.
In Toronto, Julián rode his bike almost every day.
Marta went to Lisbon twice in her life.
As a student, I visited my grandparents twice a month.
When did it happen? When was it?
I saw him two days ago.
Julián came back from Canada two months ago.
Five years ago, Julián lived in Medellín.
I was in Medellín for three days. (how long it lasted)
I was in Medellín three days ago. (when it was)
I met Marta two years ago.
“Estuve en Bogotá hace una semana” means…
Last year Marta was in hospital for two weeks.
At university I often went to the library.
Good morning, Julián. Please sit down. I see a hostel in Medellín on your CV. How long did you work there?
I worked there for five years, from 2019 to 2024. I was a receptionist.
And what was a normal day like at the hostel?
I always started at six in the morning. And every Saturday I organised a walk around the centre with the guests.
Did you speak English at work?
Yes, often. And then I lived in Toronto for a year and a half. There I spoke English every day.
Do you know Cartagena well?
Quite well. Before living here, I was in Cartagena three times on holiday.
And when did you come back from Canada?
I came back two months ago. You know what? I already know this hotel: I stayed here once, five years ago.
How nice! And how long did you stay?
I stayed for a week, with my family. Every afternoon we went to the beach.
How long did Julián live in Toronto?
What did Julián do every Saturday at the hostel?
When was Julián at the Casa Bahía hotel?
Julián worked in a hostel in Medellín for five years.
At the hostel, he often spoke with foreign guests.
He came back to Colombia two months ago.
In Bogotá, I went to the theatre twice a month.
In 2012 I spent a week in Lisbon with my mother.
In my whole life, I have travelled to Europe only twice.
Julián lived in Toronto for a year and a half.
Every Saturday he organised a walk.
I came back to Cartagena two months ago.
Marta went to Lisbon twice.
What is the main idea?
How long did Julián work at the hostel?
What did Julián do every Saturday?
Why was Julián the manager for three months?
When did Rosa last talk to Julián?
a period with a start and an end, short or long
a counted total
a habit of that time
ago: “hace” always goes first

Ask yourself what you want to say. How long did it last? or How many times in total? → indefinido: “estuve tres años”, “fui dos veces”. How often did you do it? → imperfect: “iba cada verano”, “iba dos veces por semana”. When? → hace + time: “lo vi hace dos días”. And if the situation is still going on, present + desde hace (class 230).
Last night I was at the office until eleven.
When I was a child, my father read me a story every night.
I started studying Spanish a year ago.
Last month I went to the doctor three times.
My grandmother lived in Mendoza for forty years. Now she lives with us.
Julián got the job. On his first day, Marta tells him about her life before the hotel. Write her sentences with the right form.

Two details for fast learners. First: “Volví hace dos meses” can also be said “Hace dos meses que volví”. Second: a habit normally goes in the imperfect, but if you give the limits of the whole series, you can also use the indefinido: that way you present it as a closed period.
As a girl, Marta went to Santa Marta every summer. (describing that time)
From 2010 to 2015, Marta went to Santa Marta every summer. (a closed, dated period)
“Hace un año que terminé la carrera” means…
Are both sentences correct?

You can now say how long something lasted (“Estuve tres años”), how often you did it (“Iba cada verano”), how many times it happened (“Fui dos veces”) and when (“Lo vi hace dos días”). In class 085 you put together everything you know about the past to tell complete stories and write practical messages: “Ayer llegué tarde porque había tráfico”. It is the natural next step: now that you measure time precisely, you tell whole stories.

Elisa Navarro is a designer at Estudio Faro, a small design studio in Zaragoza. On Monday she had a presentation at nine with a client, Mrs Ibarra. But she arrived late: there was a lot of traffic. Today, Tuesday, Elisa tells what happened and writes messages to organise the week. This class is the final A2 review: there is no new grammar. You put together everything you know to tell a story and write practical messages.
Yesterday I arrived late… (what happened)
…because there was a lot of traffic. (the situation behind it)
Could you send me the notes? (a polite request)
“Ayer llegué tarde” tells…
“…because there was a lot of traffic” is used to…
Elisa needs the meeting notes. What does she write to Ramón?

“Llegué tarde porque había mucho tráfico” gives the reason as a situation. “Llegué tarde porque hubo un accidente” gives the reason as an event that happened. Both are correct: “porque” does not choose the tense; you do.
When Elisa left home, it was raining hard.
The bus was stopped for twenty minutes.
It was twenty to ten when Elisa went into the room.
Today Elisa has already spoken to the client on the phone.
Elisa used to come to the studio by bike.
The bike is at the repair shop. Elisa took it there two weeks ago.
In what order did it happen? Why? And what happened as a result?
First I took the bus; then the bus stopped on the avenue.
My phone had no battery, so I couldn’t call.
In the end, the client really liked the logo.
Noelia started the presentation because Elisa wasn’t there.
Elisa wasn’t there; that’s why Noelia started the presentation.
It was raining hard, so Elisa didn’t go by bike.
Noelia wanted to wait for Elisa, but the client was in a hurry.
In the end, everything went well and the client signed.
With Noelia and Ramón, Elisa uses tú: “¿Puedes llamarme?”, “Envíamelo”. With the client she uses usted: “¿Podría llamarme?”, “Envíemelo, por favor”. You practise usted in the extension step.
The photos of the logo, Ramón: can you send them to me?
At the studio, the meeting room is booked at reception.
Thank you very much for your help, Noelia.
On Monday there was an accident on the avenue.
Ramón wants the logo. Elisa: “I’ll send it to him now.”
Good morning, Elisa. You’ve arrived very early today. Hey, what happened yesterday?
I’m really sorry, Ramón. Yesterday I arrived late because there was a huge amount of traffic.
But you used to come by bike, didn’t you?
Yes, but the bike has been at the repair shop for two weeks. Yesterday I took the bus, it was raining and there was an accident on the avenue.
Oh dear! And why didn’t you call?
My phone had no battery, so I couldn’t call. And the bus was stopped for twenty minutes.
Well, never mind. Noelia started the presentation and, in the end, Mrs Ibarra really liked the logo.
Great! I’ve already spoken to her on the phone this morning, but I haven’t sent her the quote yet.
Don’t worry, it’s for Friday. Do you need anything?
Yes. Could you send me the notes from the meeting?
Sure, I’ll send them to you now. And tomorrow, are you here at nine?
No, I have a dentist appointment. I’ll leave Noelia some instructions: the room is booked at reception and the samples are on my desk. Thanks for your patience, Ramón.
Why didn’t Elisa call?
What has Elisa done this morning?
Why won’t Elisa be there tomorrow at nine?
When I went into the room, Mrs Ibarra was already there.
The meeting lasted two hours, from nine to eleven.
This morning Ramón has already sent Elisa the notes.
As a student, Noelia used to work on Saturdays in a bookshop.
Elisa didn’t go to the studio at nine because she had a dentist appointment.
I used to come to the studio by bike.
This week I’ve already finished two logos.
Can you send them to me before Friday?
There was a lot of traffic, so I took the metro.
What is the main idea?
How was Mrs Ibarra when Noelia arrived?
What did Noelia do after waiting ten minutes?
What has Noelia done today?
What does Elisa have to leave at reception?
what it was like, why, what you used to do
what happened, in order; periods with limits
taking stock of today or this week
ask, instruct, thank, give a deadline

To tell a story, ask three questions: what was it like? (imperfect), what happened? (indefinido), what have you done today? (perfect, or indefinido in much of Latin America). For a practical message: ask with “¿podrías…?”, attach the pronoun to the command (“dáselas”), use “se” for rules and thank with “gracias por”.
Last night there was a two-hour power cut in the neighbourhood.
When Ramón opened the studio, it was very cold.
This week Noelia has already given three presentations.
The room key, can you leave it for me at reception?
Thank you very much for coming so early.
A month later, Elisa travels to Valencia to see a client. There are problems at the station: a taxi strike. Tell the story and organise things with what you know.

With a client, Elisa writes with usted: the verb is in the third person and the possessive changes. “¿Puedes enviarme…?” becomes “¿Puede / Podría enviarme…?”; “Llámame” becomes “Llámeme”; “tu paciencia” becomes “su paciencia”. And she starts with “Estimada señora Ibarra:”.

You can now tell a complete story at A2: the scene, the events, the reason and how today has gone, and you can write practical messages. In class 086 you start B1: you go back to the past tenses with more intention, to describe better, build suspense and decide what matters in your story. It is the natural next step: now that you choose the right form, you learn to use it to tell stories better.

Daniel is moving to Montreal: in three weeks he starts working in a lab. His friend Valeria is organising a farewell party, and everybody talks about wishes: what they want, what they hope, what they wish for Daniel. In lesson 088 you learned the forms of the present subjunctive; today you use them to make wishes.
Daniel finds a flat near the lab. (a fact)
Valeria hopes Daniel finds a flat.
I really hope Daniel finds a flat. / Let’s hope he does.
“Valeria hopes Daniel finds a flat.” Does Daniel already have a flat?
Which sentence states a fact?
Who has the wish, and who does the action?
I want to go to the party. / I want you to come to the party.
Daniel hopes to find a flat soon. / His mother hopes he calls her on Sundays.
We hope to see you soon. / We wish you every happiness there.
Valeria wants to have a party at her place.
Valeria wants Daniel to invite his colleagues from the lab.
We hope you like the new city.
How do you express a strong wish?
I really hope you find a nice flat.
Let’s hope it doesn’t rain on Saturday.
Tomorrow I have my French exam. I really hope I pass.
“Do you think you’ll have holidays in December?” “I hope so!”
I want to pass the exam.
I really hope I pass the exam.
I really hope I have time to say goodbye to everyone.
“Are you going to come and see me in Montreal?” “I hope so!”
What do you say to someone who is leaving?
All the best! / Good luck! (literally: may it go well for you)
Have a good trip!
Have a good rest! / Sleep well!
Before a meal, in Spain people very often say “¡Que aproveche!”; in many Latin American countries they say “¡Buen provecho!” (Enjoy your meal!). Both are understood everywhere.
Your colleague has the flu and is going home. You say: “Get well soon!”
Your friends are going on holiday. You say: “Have a great time!”
“Te espero en la puerta” means I’ll wait for you at the door. “Espero que llegues bien” means I hope you arrive safely. When esperar means hope, esperar que takes the subjunctive, never the future.
I hope my sister comes to see me in December.
Daniel hopes to see all his friends before the trip.
I really hope my parents come to Montreal in the summer.
I want to do an intensive French course.
Right, Daniel, it’s decided: on Saturday we’re having your farewell party at my place. I want all your friends from the lab to come.
Thanks, Vale. But I just want to spend a quiet afternoon with you all.
Quiet, yes, but with music. Hey, have you got a flat in Montreal yet?
Not yet. Next week I have two viewings by video call. I really hope I find something near the lab.
Let’s hope so. And your French? How’s it going?
So-so. My boss expects me to speak a bit in meetings from the first month.
You’re going to learn really fast! And I hope to visit you in spring, OK?
Of course. And I want you to bring me some good coffee from here.
Done. Oh, Irene can’t come on Saturday: she’s on shift at the hospital. But she sends you a message: All the very best!
How kind! Tell her I hope her shift goes well too.
I’ll tell her. Well, I’m off home. See you on Saturday. Have a good rest!
You too. And thanks for everything, really.
What kind of party does Daniel want?
What does Daniel’s boss expect?
Why isn’t Irene going to the party?
I want everyone to bring something to eat.
Hugo wants to choose the music for the party.
I hope Daniel isn’t sad at the party.
We want to give him a coat. We hope it fits him well.
I want you to write to me from Montreal.
I hope to see you in the summer.
My parents hope I visit them soon.
What is the main idea?
What does Daniel’s mother hope?
When does Paula want to go and see Daniel?
What does Paula wish about the flat?
What does Paula hope about Spanish?
your wish for yourself: one person
your wish for someone or something else; never the future
always subjunctive, even for yourself
short goodbye wishes
Always ask: one person or two? One: infinitive. Two: que + subjunctive. And two shortcuts: ojalá and ¡que…! always take the subjunctive.
My colleagues want me to give a presentation on Monday.
Let’s hope it’s sunny on the day of the trip.
We hope to catch the eight o’clock train.
Your friend has an interview tomorrow. You say: “Good luck!”
I hope my children have a good time at camp.
Marta, Valeria’s neighbour, is retiring after thirty years as a teacher. Her colleagues have a lunch for her. Choose the right form for each wish.
Her colleagues: “We hope you enjoy your free time a lot.”
Marta: “I want to visit my sister in Chile.”
Her grandson: “I really hope you’ll have more time to play with me!”
At the end, Marta says goodbye to everyone: “All the best, everyone!”

In formal messages (a hotel, a company, a card for a client), desear and esperar are used with usted or ustedes. You will also hear “Ojalá estuvieras aquí” (I wish you were here): that is another form, the imperfect subjunctive, for impossible or unlikely wishes. You will study it at B2; for now, just recognise it.

You can now express wishes for yourself and for others. In lesson 090 you use the same structure (verb + que + subjunctive) with a different purpose: influencing what others do with advice and suggestions. It is the natural next step: from wishing to advising.

Rafael Ortega lives in Bogotá. In March he starts a new job in Santiago, Chile, and he has a thousand questions: where to live, what clothes to take, what his new boss is like. His Chilean friend Carolina Fuentes gives him advice. Today you learn to give advice and make requests with “te recomiendo que…”, “te sugiero que…”, “te pido que…”, and to report what another person says.
Look for a flat near the metro. (direct)
I recommend (that) you look for a flat near the metro.
My brother says there are free flats in March.
A flat is “departamento” in Chile, Argentina or Mexico, “piso” in Spain and “apartamento” in Colombia. Carolina is Chilean, so she says “departamento”.
Who is going to look for a flat?
This sentence…
Why “busques” and not “buscas”?
Advice and requests: what you want another person to do
I recommend you look near the metro.
I advise you to bring a jacket.
I suggest you look at other neighbourhoods too.
The company asks me to send a copy of my passport.
My boss tells me to arrive at nine.
I suggest you take the night bus.
I ask you to call me on Sunday.
Carolina advises him to open an account in a Chilean bank.
Before the verb there is almost always an indirect object pronoun (class 063): it says who gets the advice. That person is also the one who does the action in the subjunctive.
Before the conjugated verb: “te recomiendo”, never “recomiendo te”. With an infinitive, after it and joined: “Quiero recomendarte que…” (class 065).
The boss asks us to arrive on time.
Madam, I recommend you try the pastel de choclo (corn pie).
I advise you to rest.
When can I use the infinitive?
I recommend you take cash for the first day.
I suggest you visit Valparaíso one weekend.
I recommend this neighbourhood: it’s quiet and has parks.
No preposition between the verb and the infinitive or “que”: never “te aconsejo de llevar”.
Which sentence is NOT correct?
Carolina wants Rafael to visit her in April.
I suggest you leave the big coat in Bogotá.
Carolina says (that) the metro is fast.
Carolina says I should buy a transport card. / Carolina tells me to buy one.
“Pedir” = ask someone to do something. “Preguntar” = ask a question. In English both are “ask”.
“She says it’s cold at night.”
“Carolina says I should take a light jacket.”
Rafael asks Carolina if the metro opens on Sundays.
I’m asking you to wait for me at the exit.
My brother says rents go up in March.
Carolina, thanks for calling! I have a thousand questions. First: where should I look for a flat?
I recommend you look near the metro. That way you don’t lose hours in traffic.
Perfect. My new boss says the Providencia area is very quiet.
Yes, it’s quiet, but expensive. I suggest you also look at Ñuñoa: it’s cheaper and has lots of parks.
And the weather in March? Should I take winter clothes?
No, it’s still hot. But I advise you to bring a jacket: it gets cool at night.
Noted. The company is asking me to send a copy of my passport this week. Is that normal?
Yes, it’s normal. And another thing: your boss is very punctual. I recommend you arrive early on the first day.
Phew, thanks. By the way, my mum is telling me to bring you a present from Colombia. What do you like?
How kind! Coffee, of course. And now I’m asking you for one thing: write me the date of your flight. I want to pick you up at the airport!
Which area does Carolina suggest?
What does the company ask Rafael for?
Is it information or an errand Rafael must do?
After the call, Rafael writes notes on his phone. Is each note advice with “que”, advice with an infinitive or information?
“I recommend you go early on Saturdays: there are fewer people.”
The company asks Rafael to sign the contract before Monday.
“Carolina says there are lots of parks in Santiago.”
Carolina suggests he get to know the area by bike.
“I’m asking you to arrive at nine sharp.”
“I advise you to leave the big coat in Bogotá.”
I recommend you book in good time.
Carolina suggests I visit Valparaíso.
Why does Carolina send the message?
Why does she recommend living near the metro?
What does Carolina’s brother say?
What clothes does she advise him to bring?
What does Carolina ask Rafael to do?
“My mum says you should come for lunch.” The mum…
Advice or request + que + subjunctive
Same advice with the infinitive (not with querer or decir)
Decir que + subjunctive: an instruction
Decir que + indicative: information

Ask yourself: does someone have to do something? If yes, advice or request: que + subjunctive (or the infinitive with recomendar, aconsejar, sugerir). If not, information: indicative. And to ask for an action, use “pedir”, not “preguntar”.
Rafael now lives in Santiago and takes a Chilean cooking class. The teacher, Ximena, gives the group instructions. Later Rafael tells Lucía about them on the phone.

In notices, formal emails and signs, advice uses ustedes (les pedimos que…), the company “we” (les recomendamos que…) or se + infinitive (se recomienda llegar…). In Spain, with friends, also vosotros: os aconsejo que vayáis. And “insistir en que” is very strong advice or a strong request: it takes “en”.
“We ask passengers to have their passport in their hand.”
“We recommend you check the contract before signing it.”
“I advise you all to visit the museum in the morning.”
“It is recommended to have breakfast before ten.”
“Rafael, I insist that you come for lunch on Sunday.”

You can now give advice with “te recomiendo que…” and report what others say. The natural next step: evaluating an action with “es importante que”, “es bueno que”, “es mejor que” + subjunctive, another very common way to give advice without “te recomiendo”.

Lorena Vidal runs the Pasos Largos hiking club. On Saturday they are doing the Cascades route, and Óscar, a new member, is going for the first time. Lorena gives advice and gives her view: “It’s important that you wear hiking boots.” She also states facts: “It’s true that the route is long.” Today you learn to judge and to state, and to choose the right mood.
It’s important that you wear hiking boots. (her judgement)
It’s true that the route is long. (a fact she states)
In “Es importante que lleves botas”, Lorena…
In “Es verdad que la ruta es larga”, the verb “es” is in…
What do you think of it? Is it important, better, normal, a shame?
Everyone needs to bring a raincoat.
It’s better if we leave at seven.
It’s a shame that Nuria can’t come on Saturday.
I think it’s good that you’re coming with us.
Everyone needs to bring water.
It’s a shame that Nuria can’t come.
I think it’s great that Óscar is coming to the club.
Are you talking about anyone, in general?
In the mountains it’s important to drink plenty of water.
It’s better not to walk alone at night.
You need to check the weather before setting off.
Club rule: “On a long route, it’s good to rest every two hours.”
Lorena to Óscar: “It’s important that you sleep well on Friday.”
Are you saying something is true?
Clearly the weather changes fast in the mountains.
It’s obvious that Lorena knows a lot about routes.
It’s true that the climb is hard.
“Me parece que” = I think (an opinion about a fact): indicative. “Me parece bien que” = I think it’s good that (a judgement): subjunctive.
Clearly the route is beautiful.
It’s normal for Óscar to be a little nervous.
I think the bus leaves at seven.
Today you use these expressions in the affirmative. Sentences like “no es verdad que…” or “es posible que…” work differently: you will see them in classes 093 and 094.
It’s obvious that Óscar is keen to go.
It’s better if we leave together from the square.
Hi, Lorena. I’m Óscar, the new member. I want to do Saturday’s route, but it’s my first time in the mountains.
Welcome! I think it’s great that you’re coming. But it’s true that the route is a bit hard: it’s twelve kilometres.
Twelve? Phew. And what do I need? Do you have to buy new boots?
They don’t need to be new, but it’s important that you wear hiking boots. In trainers, on wet stones, it’s easy to slip.
OK. And food? Do we stop at a restaurant?
No, there’s nothing on the way. It’s better if you bring your own food and two litres of water.
Got it. What time do we leave? At nine?
No, at seven. I know it’s early, but in summer it’s better to leave early, before the heat.
And what if it rains? The forecast isn’t very clear.
Look, clearly the weather changes very fast up there. That’s why everyone needs to bring a raincoat.
One last thing: I don’t know anyone in the group. Is that a problem?
Not at all! It’s normal not to know anyone on the first day. And the group is obviously very friendly: you’ll see.
Does Óscar have to buy new boots?
Why are they leaving at seven?
What worries Óscar at the end?
It’s a good idea for Óscar to walk around in the boots a bit before Saturday.
It’s true that the path has a lot of stones.
In the mountains you need to walk carefully.
Lorena: “I’m fine with you bringing Lúa, but on a lead.”
It’s clear that Lorena knows a lot about the mountains.
It’s important that everyone wears a hat.
Clearly the path is difficult.
It’s better not to walk at night.
I think it’s good that Nuria is coming with us.
Why does Lorena send the voice message?
Where and what time are they meeting?
Why is it important to bring food?
What does Lorena say about city trainers?
Who can’t go, and why?
you judge an action, even a real one
for anyone, with no “que” and no “de”
you state that something is true

Ask yourself: am I judging or stating? “Es una pena que llueva”: you judge (subjunctive), even though it really is raining. “Está claro que llueve”: you state (indicative). And if you speak about everyone, with no specific person: “Es importante llevar paraguas.”
It’s a pity that the museum closes on Mondays.
Marta is obviously tired today.
To learn a language, you need to practise every day.
I think the train leaves at ten.
I think it’s good that your children do sport.
Héctor, from the club, also volunteers at the neighbourhood food bank. On Saturday a new volunteer starts. Transform the coordinator’s sentences.

On signs and in official texts, judgements are more formal: es imprescindible que, es fundamental que, conviene que, resulta evidente que. The rule is the same: judgement + subjunctive, certainty + indicative, general + infinitive.
It is essential that visitors keep to the marked paths.
It is advisable to check the weather forecast before setting off.
It is evident that the number of visitors increases every year.

You can now judge plans and facts: “Es una pena que Nuria no pueda venir”, “Es importante que todos lleven agua”. In class 092 you go one step further: you express how you feel about what others do: “Me alegra que estés aquí”, “Me molesta que llegues tarde”. It is the natural next step: the same structure with “que” + subjunctive, now to react with emotions.

Sara Molina shares a flat in Mexico City with Bea, a nurse, and Iván, who moved in a month ago. It is Sunday and they are having a meeting in the kitchen. Iván says: “I’m very happy here.” Sara reacts: “I’m glad you’re happy.” Today you learn to react with emotion to what other people do or go through.
Iván is happy in the flat. (a piece of information)
I’m glad that Iván is happy in the flat. (her emotional reaction)
In “Me alegra que Iván esté contento”, Sara…
Iván is happy. Is it true?
How do you feel about what someone else does or goes through?
I’m surprised that Iván cooks so well.
We’re worried that the landlord doesn’t answer messages.
It bothers Bea that the neighbours make noise during the day.
It’s a shame for me that we’re almost never at home at the same time.
I love it that Bea makes bread on Sundays.
It bothers Iván that the neighbours make noise.
We’re worried that Sara is so tired.
How do you feel about what is happening?
I’m fed up with the washing machine not working.
We’re delighted that you’re staying the whole year.
I’m glad you have a new job.
I’m sorry you have to wash your clothes by hand.
Do you want to react quickly to some news?
How great that you’re coming to dinner!
How strange that Bea isn’t answering!
What a shame that you’re leaving in June!
“Es una pena que…” judges the fact (class 091). “Me da pena que…” says how you personally feel. “¡Qué pena que…!” is the quick reaction. All three take the subjunctive.
I’m tired of Iván leaving the dishes for the next day.
How lucky that there’s a market next to the house!
I’m sorry you can’t come to the meeting, Bea.
It bothers me that the landlord doesn’t fix it.
I’m fed up with washing my clothes by hand.
I’m annoyed because the washing machine isn’t working.
“Siento que no puedas venir” = I’m sorry you can’t come (subjunctive). “Siento que no me escuchas” = I feel you’re not listening to me (indicative). The context tells you which one it is.
Iván talks about his life: “I love living in Mexico City.”
Sara is sad because Bea is leaving in June.
Sara is sad that Bea is leaving in June.
We’re surprised there are so many cars in the street.
Bea is delighted that Iván lives with them.
So, Iván, you’ve been with us for a month now. How’s it going? Are you comfortable?
Yes, very comfortable. Honestly, I love living with you two.
How great that you feel at home! Bea and I are really glad that you’re happy.
Thanks. Hey, one thing: I’m surprised Bea is never at home. Is everything OK?
Yes, she’s a nurse and works nights. But it makes me sad that we’re almost never home at the same time.
Right. And another thing… what’s going on with the washing machine? I’m fed up with washing my clothes by hand.
Me too! It really bothers me that the landlord doesn’t answer. I sent him a message two weeks ago.
How strange that he doesn’t say anything! Isn’t he away?
I don’t think so. And on top of that, I’m worried the rent will go up in September: he mentioned it in January.
Well, I’m happy because I pay less here than in my old flat.
That’s true. Look, I’m sorry you have to wash by hand. Tomorrow I’ll call the landlord again.
Don’t worry, it’s fine. And thanks for asking: I’m glad you care.
Why is Bea hardly ever at home?
What problem does the flat have?
What is Sara worried about?
It bothers me that the neighbours play their music so loud.
Iván is surprised that it rains so much in the afternoons.
I’m delighted that my sister is coming to live nearby.
I love having breakfast on the terrace on Sundays.
How lucky that there’s such a good bakery on the corner!
It bothers me that the landlord doesn’t answer.
We’re glad that Iván is staying the whole year.
What does Bea do in the voice message?
Why is Bea surprised that the landlord isn’t answering?
What is Bea’s news?
Why do they see each other so little?
What does Bea suggest?
like gustar: the emotion verb stays singular
with estar + adjective, don’t forget “de”
the quick reaction to some news
I feel it and I do it: no “que” (class 095)
you give the cause as information

Ask yourself: who feels it and who does it? If they are different people, or it is something that happens: que + subjunctive. If it is the same person: infinitive. And if you only report the cause: porque + indicative.
I’m surprised Lucía doesn’t know anything about the party.
My parents are happy that I have a new job.
I’m glad to be here with you.
I’m tired because my son wakes up at six every day.
It bothers my neighbours that my dog barks at night.
Sara works at a design studio. There is a lot of news at the office this week. Turn what is happening into reactions.

When the emotion is about something that has already happened, you will hear the perfect subjunctive: “Me alegra que hayas venido” (I’m glad you came). Today you only recognise it; you study it in class 097. In formal texts “lamentar” is common: “We regret that the service is not available.”
For anger, “me da rabia que…” is very common in Spain, and “me da coraje que…” in Mexico. The structure is the same: que + subjunctive.
Bea to Iván: “I’m glad you’ve come to my farewell party.” When did Iván come?
Company email: “We regret that the order is arriving late.”
Iván, in Mexico City: “It makes me angry that the metro is so packed.”

You can now react with emotion: “I’m glad you’re here”, “What a shame you’re leaving!”. In class 093 you move from what you feel to what you think: “Creo que el alquiler va a subir” versus “No creo que suba”. It is the natural next step: again indicative or subjunctive after “que”, now depending on whether you affirm or deny an opinion.

In the Mercado neighbourhood there is a proposal: to close calle del Mercado to cars. Inés Molina, chair of the residents’ association, organises a meeting. Paula Ríos, a teacher, says: “I think it’s a great idea.” Ramiro Lara, who runs a hardware shop on that street, replies: “Well, I don’t think it’s a good idea.” Today you learn why the verb changes.
I think it’s a great idea. (she asserts it)
I don’t think it’s a good idea. (he doesn’t assert it)
In “Creo que es una idea estupenda”, the verb “es” is in…
What changes in Ramiro’s sentence?
Are you saying what you think, with no “no” in front?
I think the street is too narrow for so many cars.
I think there are few trees in the neighbourhood.
Paula thinks children need more space.
I’m sure people are going to walk around more.
I think the market gets more customers on Saturdays.
I think Ramiro is a bit worried.
I’m sure the residents are going to vote in favour.
Is there a “no” in front of creo, pienso, me parece or estoy seguro?
I don’t think the city council wants to spend money on this.
I don’t think the street is dangerous.
I’m not sure the residents are informed.
I think it isn’t the best time.
I don’t think it’s the best time.
I don’t think the project is very expensive.
I think there isn’t enough parking.
I’m not sure Paula is right.
Are you asking someone’s opinion or correcting what they understood?
Do you think the residents are going to vote in favour?
Don’t you think it’s better to try it for a few months?
It’s not that Ramiro is against it; it’s that he’s afraid of losing customers.

In Mexico and other parts of Latin America you often hear the subjunctive in questions: “¿Crees que venga Ramiro?” It shows the speaker has doubts. It’s correct but not required: the indicative is used everywhere.
It’s not that I don’t like cars; it’s that there are too many.
Don’t you think the square looks nicer with trees?
It’s not that Inés is in a hurry; it’s that the vote is on Thursday.
Ramiro thinks differently. What does he say politely?
I don’t agree with the council closing the square.
I assert my opinion → indicative. I deny the opinion verb → subjunctive. What decides it is the “no” in front of creo, pienso, me parece or estoy seguro.
I don’t think there’s that much noise at night.
Paula thinks the street is going to be safer.
Good evening, everyone. Today’s topic: closing calle del Mercado to cars at weekends. What do you think?
I think it’s a great idea. Children will be able to play in the street and people will walk around more.
Well, I don’t see it that way. My hardware shop is on that street, and I don’t think my customers will come on foot carrying a ladder or a bag of cement.
It’s not that we want to shut your business, Ramiro. It’s that there’s too much noise and too many fumes.
Sure, I agree there’s a lot of traffic. But I don’t think closing the street is the answer.
Ramiro, do you think customers are going to stop coming?
I’m sure some of them will. Especially older people, who come by car.
I think you’re exaggerating a bit. There’s a car park two hundred metres away.
I’m not sure it has free spaces on Saturdays. It’s always full.
And what if we close it only on Sundays? Most shops are closed that day. Don’t you think that’s a good starting point?
Well, that’s a different matter. I’m fine with them closing it on Sundays.
Me too. I’m sure the residents are going to like it.
Why does Ramiro have doubts?
What does Ramiro agree with from the start?
What does Inés suggest at the end?
I don’t think the residents know how much I sell on Saturdays.
I think the square is going to be much livelier.
I’m not sure the budget will stretch to new benches.
I think you’re right: there are too many fumes.
It’s not that Ramiro is against everything; he’s scared.
I don’t think the corner is dangerous.
I’m sure the idea is going to work.
It’s not that I don’t like it; I just have doubts.
I think there aren’t enough benches in the square.
Why does Ramiro send the voice message?
What does Ramiro think about closing the street on Sundays?
Why is he worried about Saturdays?
What does he agree with Paula about?
What does Ramiro propose?
you assert what you think
you don’t assert what follows
you ask for an opinion or reject an interpretation
you agree or disagree politely

Check for a “no” in front of the opinion verb. “Creo que viene”: you assert (indicative). “No creo que venga”: you deny (subjunctive). But “Creo que no viene” and “¿No crees que viene?” take the indicative: the “no” doesn’t deny “creer”.
I don’t think my boss is coming back to the office today.
I think this book is better than the film.
It’s not that I’m not hungry; I’ve just eaten.
I’m sure you’re going to pass the exam.
I don’t think the exam is that hard.
Paula also has a meeting at her school: they are discussing an end-of-year trip. Transform her colleagues’ opinions.

Three uses you will hear a lot. “No pienso + infinitive” is not an opinion: it means “I have no intention of”. “No creas que…” is a negative command: you warn someone that an idea is wrong; the indicative often follows. And in Mexico and other parts of Latin America, “¿crees que + subjunctive?” shows doubt.
Ramiro, angry: “I’m not going to close my shop on Saturdays.”
Inés: “Don’t think it’s easy to organise a vote.”
A neighbour from Guadalajara: “Do you think it’ll rain on Sunday?”

You can now assert and deny opinions: “Creo que es buena idea”, “No creo que sea buena idea”. In class 094 you take the next step: you express degrees of certainty with “quizás”, “es posible que”, “dudo que” or “seguro que”. It’s the natural next step: from saying yes or no to an idea to saying how much you believe it.

Irene Salas organises the Book Fair in the main square on Sunday. Rodrigo Peña is volunteering for the first time and has lots of questions: will it rain? Is the guest author coming? How many people will come? Irene doesn’t know everything. Sometimes she is sure: “It’ll definitely be sunny in the morning.” Sometimes she only sees a possibility: “It may rain in the afternoon.” Today you learn to say how sure you are and which mood goes with each expression.
It’ll definitely be sunny in the morning. (she is sure)
It may rain in the afternoon. (only a possibility)
In “Seguro que hace sol”, Irene…
In “Es posible que llueva”, the verb “llueva” is in…
Are you sure? Is it obvious?
I’m sure Pilar is bringing the children’s books.
I’m sure the fair is going to be a success this year.
Clearly the square is small for so many tents.
Is it a possibility, in everyday conversation?
Maybe we’ll put the tents up on Saturday.
Maybe Mateo can’t come in the morning.
Maybe Elena is coming on the eight o’clock train.
I’m sure the children enjoy the storytelling.
Is it only possible? Do you doubt it?
More than five hundred people will probably come.
Elena may arrive a bit late.
I doubt the town hall will give us more tents.
I’m not sure the microphone works.
There will probably be a lot of people on Sunday.
I doubt Rodrigo can put up a tent on his own.
We may have to change the programme.
Does the adverb come before the verb?
Maybe we’ll change the order of the activities. (a real option)
Perhaps it’ll be too windy for the tents. (more doubt)
Pilar is probably right.
Elena will probably arrive at twelve. (adverb after the verb: indicative)
“Quizás vienen” and “Quizás vengan”…
Rodrigo is coming with his sister, maybe.

Ask yourself: am I stating it or only imagining it? If you state it, indicative. If it is possible, probable or doubtful, subjunctive. Two special cases: “a lo mejor” always takes the indicative; “quizás / tal vez” before the verb takes either.
It’s obvious that Irene has a lot of experience.
I’m not sure the tables will fit in the square.
Irene, have you seen the forecast? They say there’s a storm on Sunday.
Yes, I’ve seen it. It may rain in the afternoon, but in the morning the weather will definitely be good.
And the tents? When do we put them up?
Maybe we’ll put them up on Saturday afternoon. It depends on the town hall: I’ll confirm tomorrow.
OK. And Elena Mora? Is she definitely coming?
I’m sure she’s coming, but she’s coming by train and there are works on the line. She may arrive a bit late.
Then maybe we’ll have to change the order of the activities, right?
Yes. Maybe we start with the children’s storytelling, and then Elena’s book presentation.
And how many people are you expecting? A thousand?
Phew, I doubt a thousand will come. Last year about four hundred came. But there will probably be more this year: there are more bookshops.
Another thing: Pilar says the microphone doesn’t work properly.
Pilar is probably right: it’s old. I’ll test it tomorrow. Well, it’s clearly going to be a long Sunday.
What weather does Irene expect on Sunday?
Why might Elena Mora arrive late?
How many people does Irene think will come?
Look at those clouds: it may rain tonight.
Pilar is very organised. I bet she already has everything ready.
I don’t know where Mateo is. Maybe he’s at the library.
I doubt the children will sit still for two hours.
Elena will probably arrive late, because of the works.
The train may arrive late.
Maybe we’ll close early because of the rain.
I doubt the town hall will give us more chairs.
I’m sure Pilar is bringing the posters.
Why does Irene send the message?
What time are they closing the fair, and why?
Which activity do they start with?
What is the problem with the sound?
What time do the volunteers have to be in the square?
you present it as true
a possibility, in conversation
both are correct; the subjunctive usually adds doubt
you don’t state it: it is possible, probable or doubtful

Ask yourself: am I stating it or not? “Seguro que llueve”: you state it (indicative). “Es posible que llueva”, “Dudo que llueva”: you don’t (subjunctive). And remember the two special cases: “A lo mejor llueve” (always indicative) and “Quizás llueve / llueva” (both).
It will probably be cold tomorrow.
Maybe we’ll go to the cinema tonight.
I’m sure your sister is right.
I’m not sure the restaurant is open on Mondays.
I may be a bit late for the meeting.
Sara, Irene’s sister, is preparing an important meeting with some clients at her office. She isn’t sure of anything. Transform her sentences.

Three more expressions. “Seguramente” does not mean “surely” (100%): it means “probably”, and works the same way. “Lo más probable es que” takes the subjunctive. In conversation, especially in Spain, “igual” = a lo mejor, with the indicative. And a preview to recognise: “Estará en el tren” = she’s probably on the train (the future of probability, class 161, level B2).
“Seguramente Elena llega a las doce” means…
Most likely the fair will end at half past four.
Mateo isn’t answering. Maybe he’s asleep.

You can now choose the mood by how sure you are: “Seguro que llueve”, “Es posible que llueva”. In class 095 you learn another important decision: when to use the infinitive and when “que” + subjunctive, depending on who does the action: “Quiero salir” (I) / “Quiero que salgas” (you). It is the natural next step: you already know many expressions with “que” + subjunctive, and now you see when you don’t need “que”.

In Guadalajara, Mariana and Rodrigo Salas are planning a surprise party: their parents are celebrating 35 years of marriage. There is a lot to decide: who cooks, who invites people, what aunt Beatriz allows in her garden. In classes 089 to 094 you learned many verbs with que + subjunctive. Today you bring it all together in one decision: infinitive or que + subjunctive?
I want to cook the mole.
I want Rodrigo to cook the mole.
Who cooks?
How many people are there?
In English: “I want Rodrigo to cook”. In Spanish…
Is the person who wants (or feels) the same person who does the action?
I hope to pass the exam. / I hope you pass the exam.
I’d rather stay at home. / I’d rather you stayed at home.
We need to rest. / We need the children to rest.
Rodrigo needs to look for the old photos.
Mariana needs Rodrigo to look for the old photos.
I’m afraid Mum will suspect something.

With verbs like alegrar, molestar or encantar, the person who feels is in the pronoun: me, te, le. That is the person you compare with the second action. With judgements (es importante, es mejor) there is no person in the first verb: speaking in general, use the infinitive; with a specific person, que + subjunctive.

With “quiero” you don’t say “quiero que yo cocine”, because you are the one who wants. But “es mejor”, “es importante” and “es necesario” have no person, so “Es mejor que yo cocine” is perfectly correct.
Mum loves dancing.
It annoys me that my brother plays on his phone at the table.
It’s better to send the invitations by text.
Our aunt wants us to play music.
Our aunt lets us play music.
Which verbs take an infinitive with another subject?
The doctor forbids Dad to eat sweets.
My parents don’t let me use their car.
I’ll let you go out, but be back before twelve.
The doctor advised me to rest for a week. (past: the infinitive is the easy option)
Which one is NOT correct?
The venue forbids us to use candles on the tables.
Who rests?
Rodrigo brings the photos to make a video.
Rodrigo brings the photos so that everyone can see them.
Purpose follows the same logic: same person, para + infinitive; another person, para que + subjunctive. Today you only recognise it: you work on it in class 099.
Mariana wants to arrive early.
Our aunt lets us use the chairs from her house.
“Mariana sends a voice message so that everyone knows the time.” Who knows the time?
We’d rather celebrate at home.
I need you to help me with the tables.
Mari, it’s a month until Mum and Dad’s anniversary. What do you have in mind?
A surprise party. I want to organise it in aunt Beatriz’s garden, and I want you to talk to her this week.
OK, I’ll call her tomorrow. But I’m not cooking, all right? I’d rather we hired someone.
Fine. I hope to find a mariachi band at a good price. And above all, I hope Mum doesn’t suspect anything.
Tricky: Mum finds out about everything. Listen, our aunt doesn’t let us play music after eleven, because of the neighbours.
Then we start early. Another thing: the doctor won’t let Dad eat sweets, so the cake will be sugar-free.
Sugar-free? Poor Dad… Well, I’m glad he’s finally taking care of himself.
Me too. And when are you arriving?
Friday night. And I’m bringing the old family photos to make a video.
What a good idea! I’m glad I’ll be able to see you for more days. And bring the printed photos too, so the guests can see them.
Done. One last thing: it’s important that nobody tells them anything. Will you write to the cousins?
Yes, tomorrow I’ll send them a voice message. And I’m going to ask them to arrive at seven sharp.
What does Rodrigo prefer for the food?
Why will the cake be sugar-free?
Who plays the music?
After the call, Mariana writes notes on her phone. Sort each note: one person (infinitive), another person (que + subjunctive) or a verb of influence with the infinitive?
“Rodrigo, I want you to design the invitations.”
“I want to leave early on Friday, before the traffic.”
It annoys Dad when guests arrive late.
Our aunt doesn’t let us park the car in the garden.
“Rodrigo, it’s better if you buy the cake: the bakery is near your hotel.”
“I’m afraid of eating too much and not being able to dance.”
Look at the first verb and at who does the second action. Does the sentence take the infinitive, que + subjunctive, or both?
I hope Mum doesn’t suspect anything.
Our aunt lets us use her garden.
I’m glad you’re coming from Monterrey.
Why does Mariana send the message?
What time do the cousins have to arrive?
Who is going to get everything ready?
Why are they starting early?
What would Mariana like them to bring?
Same person: infinitive
Another person: que + subjunctive
No specific person: infinitive
Verbs of influence: infinitive or que + subjunctive
Preview: purpose follows the same logic

Ask yourself: who wants or feels? Who does it? Same person: infinitive. Another person: que + subjunctive. And with permitir, prohibir, dejar, aconsejar, the pronoun (te, nos) already points to the other person, so the infinitive works too.
After the party, Rodrigo goes back to Monterrey. He shares a flat with Iván, and the landlord has rules. Rodrigo tells Mariana about them.

Three more cases. “Obligar” takes “a”: te obligan a llevar casco / a que lleves casco. On signs and rules, with no person, se prohíbe / se permite + infinitive. And with a first verb in the past, the infinitive is the easy option: “me aconsejó descansar” (the “que” form uses another subjunctive tense, which you will see at B2).
“Here they make you wear a helmet.”
“Smoking is forbidden in the rooms.”
“The doctor advised me to rest for a few days.”
“I’m happy to see the whole family together.”
“I need someone to help me with the chairs.”

You can now choose between the infinitive and que + subjunctive depending on who does the action. The natural next step: passing a request from one person to another, like a messenger: “Tell him to come”, “Ask them to wait here”. There is always another person, so the subjunctive appears in every sentence.

Today is the opening night of a play at Teatro La Lumbre, a small theatre in Guadalajara. The director, Marisol Peña, gives orders to everyone. Her assistant, Iván Soto, passes them on to the technician, Raúl, and to the actors, Lucas and Celia. At five the theatre owner, doña Amparo, arrives with guests. Today you learn to give orders with tú, usted and ustedes and to pass on what someone else asks: “Tell him to come”.
Iván, come to the stage.
Lucas, don’t come late today.
Doña Amparo, come this way.
Why “venga” and not “ven”?
Which order uses a form you already know from the subjunctive?
Where do commands come from?
Celia, wait a moment. / Celia, don’t wait any longer.
Sir, please wait here. / Don’t wait at the door.
Guys, wait in the dressing room. / Don’t wait in the corridor.

In the River Plate region and much of Central America, the affirmative vos command is the infinitive without -r, stressed at the end: vení, esperá, decí, hacé; ir becomes andá. With pronouns: decile, decímelo. In the negative the most widespread form is the tú form: no vengas, no me lo digas (you also hear “no vengás”). Usted and ustedes do not change.
Guys, don’t make noise behind the curtain.
Raúl, go to the lighting booth, please.
Sir, don’t give the ticket to anyone.
How do I pass on what Marisol asks for?
Marisol: “Iván, tell Raúl to check the lights.”
Iván: “Raúl, Marisol says you should check the lights.”
Raúl: “Marisol is asking me to check the lights again.”
Tell Lucas (that) Celia is coming at six.
Tell Lucas to come at six.
“Marisol says you should call her later.”
Tell Raúl the curtain makes a strange noise.
Iván, tell Celia to hand out the tickets to the press.
Can I use que + subjunctive without another verb?
“Doña Amparo is at the door.” “Show her in! / Let her in!”
“What’s Raúl saying? I can’t hear him.” “(He says) to go up to the booth.”
“Sorry?” “(I said) don’t touch the curtain, please.”
I hope everything goes well tonight!
“Show them into the small room!”
“What are you saying?” “(I said) wait for me at the door.”
“Good luck! / Hope it goes really well!”

The rule from class 065 works for every person: in an affirmative command, the pronoun goes after the verb and joined to it; in a negative command and after “que”, it goes before the verb. With two pronouns, le / les + lo, la, los, las becomes se: dáselo, no se lo des.
A relayed order has two verbs: the first is an imperative with the pronoun after it (dile); the second is a subjunctive with the pronouns before it (que me lo dé).
The end of the play? Don’t tell me! I want to see it tonight.
Doña Amparo, if you have a question, ask me.
Lucas has the blue jacket. Tell him to give it to Celia.
Gentlemen, sit here.
Marisol is asking you to wait for her.
Iván, it’s three hours till opening night. Come here a moment, please.
I’m here. Tell me, what do I do first?
Tell Raúl to check the lights for the second act. Yesterday one wasn’t working.
OK. Oh, Lucas is asking me to open the dressing room for him at half past five.
Open it for him, of course. But don’t give him the key: it’s the only one we have.
Got it. Listen, Raúl says the curtain is making a strange noise.
I know. Don’t tell anyone, please. We’ll fix it tomorrow.
Don’t worry. Look, doña Amparo is already at the door with two guests.
So early! Show them into the small room. And ask them to wait there for a few minutes.
Good afternoon, doña Amparo. Come in, please, and sit down here. Don’t worry: Marisol is coming right away.
Thank you, Iván. Tell her there’s no hurry. Oh, and she mustn’t forget the photos for the press.
Marisol, doña Amparo says there’s no hurry, but she asks you not to forget the photos.
What does Raúl have to do?
What doesn’t Marisol want?
“Tell her there’s no hurry.” Doña Amparo…
Iván writes down everything he hears this afternoon. Is each sentence a direct order, a relayed order or information?
“Lucas, don’t touch the curtain, please: it’s broken.”
“Good afternoon, sir. Come this way, please.”
“Guys, switch off your phones before going on stage.”
“Tell Celia to call me as soon as she arrives.”
“Marisol says Celia is arriving a bit late today: she has a doctor’s appointment.”
“(He says) to go up to the booth.”
Ask them to wait here.
Don’t tell Marisol.
Tell Lucas to bring it to me.
Why does Marisol send the message?
What does Raúl have to check?
Who is going to call?
What time do the actors have to arrive?
What do doña Amparo’s guests have to do?
What does Iván have to do with the press tickets?
Affirmative tú: its own form, pronouns attached
Negative tú, usted, ustedes: present subjunctive
Relayed order: que + subjunctive, with person and pronoun changes
Information: indicative
Que + subjunctive alone: order for someone else, repetition, wish

Ask yourself two things: am I speaking directly to the person who has to act? If so, use the imperative (its own form only with affirmative tú). If the order goes through someone else, use que + subjunctive. And does anyone have to do anything? If not, it’s information: indicative.
Sonrisa dental clinic, Monday morning. Dr Lidia Campos gives instructions to the receptionist, Mónica, and Mónica talks to a patient, Mr Paredes (usted).

When we report an order in the past (“me dijo”, “nos pidió”), the subjunctive changes to another form, the imperfect subjunctive: “Marisol me dijo que viniera” (she told me to come). You will study it later; today you only need to recognise it. Compare: “Me dijo que venía” (indicative) is information: she was coming.
What does it mean?
Who had to wait?
Which sentence reports the order “Don’t touch the curtain” in the past?

You now use the present subjunctive to give orders, pass them on and wish things. The natural next step: the present perfect subjunctive (haya llegado, hayas terminado), to react to and evaluate, from now, something that has already happened: “I’m glad you’ve come”, “I hope Raúl has checked the lights”.

Gabriel is going to Lima for ten days for work. His neighbour Nuria is going to look after his dog, Tula, and his plants. It’s Sunday afternoon and Gabriel gives her the keys and explains everything. In lesson 213 you used cuando + present for your routine; in lesson 088 you learned the present subjunctive. Today you put the two together to talk about the future.
When I get home, Tula waits for me at the door. (every day)
When I got home yesterday, Tula was asleep. (it happened)
When you arrive tomorrow, Tula will say hello. (not real yet)
“When you arrive tomorrow, Tula will greet you.” Is Nuria already at Gabriel’s place?
Which sentence is about a habit?
What happens at a future moment?
When you get to Lima, text me.
When I get back, I’ll take you out for dinner.
When you have time, will you send me a photo of Tula?
When Gabriel gets back, Nuria will give him the keys back.
Tomorrow, when I get to the airport, I’ll send you a message.
Usually, when I take Tula to the park, she plays with other dogs.
Do they work like cuando?
I’ll write to you as soon as I know the flight time.
Stay at home until the technician arrives.
While you’re away, I’ll water the plants.
As soon as I get home, Tula starts jumping. (every day)
Don’t take Tula off the lead until you’re inside the park.
Yesterday, as soon as Nuria opened the door, Tula ran towards her.
Next week, while Gabriel is in Lima, Nuria is going to collect his post.
What if there are two different people?
Water the plants before it gets hot.
I always take Tula out before it starts to rain. (a habit, but still subjunctive)
After the technician leaves, turn off the gas.
Before you go out, close the bathroom window. (you go out, you close it)
Before I leave, I’ll leave you the keys.
Before you leave, I’ll make you a coffee.
With hasta and the same subject, both forms are correct. With antes de and después de, if the subject is the same, the infinitive is the normal choice.
Gabriel wants to talk to Nuria before she picks up the keys.
Before leaving, Gabriel turns off all the lights.

“Avísame cuando vuelvas” means let me know when you get back (at that moment). “Avísame cuándo vuelves” means tell me the date you’re coming back: an indirect question, with an accent and the indicative. The accent changes the meaning.
Nuria asks: “When are you coming back from Lima?”
Water the plants in the morning, before the sun gets high.
I’ll give you the book back as soon as I finish it.
After eating, Nuria washes Tula’s bowls.
Thanks for coming, Nuria. Here, these are the keys. When you arrive tomorrow, Tula will be in the kitchen.
Perfect. And what time does she eat?
At eight in the morning and seven in the evening. When I get home, I first give her fresh water and then her food.
Great. And the walks?
Two a day. But careful: don’t let her off the lead until you’re inside the park. She loves running after bikes.
Got it. Hey, when exactly are you coming back?
Wednesday next week, at night. I’ll text you as soon as I know the flight time.
And the plants? Last time, when you went away in March, they nearly dried out.
Ha ha, that’s true. Water them twice a week, in the morning, before it gets hot.
OK. And while you’re away, can I bring my nephew over to play with Tula?
Of course! She loves it. Oh, and before you leave, close the bathroom window properly, because it opens by itself.
Don’t worry. Have a good trip! And when you get back, you tell me everything.
What does Gabriel do when he gets home?
When is Gabriel going to write to Nuria?
What happened in March?
When Tula sees the lead, she gets really happy.
As soon as you get back from the walk, wipe Tula’s paws.
Gabriel always goes running before the traffic starts.
Yesterday, when I opened the door, Tula hid under the sofa.
Leave the hall light on until it gets dark.
When you get home, text me.
I’ll call you as soon as I know something.
I’m not leaving until you get back.
Take Tula out before it rains.
What is the main idea?
What will Tula do as soon as she sees Nuria?
When does Nuria have to take Tula out at night?
What shouldn’t Nuria do while Gabriel is away?
Until when does Nuria have to stay at the flat on Thursday?
not real yet; never the future tense after the connector
it always happens, it already happened, or it’s a question
two different subjects
one person does both actions
Always ask: is it real yet? If not (future): subjunctive. If it always happens or already happened: indicative. And never the future tense after cuando.
I’ll give you your suitcase back when you get back from your holiday.
As a child, when we went to my grandparents’ house, we always ate paella.
Finish the report before the meeting starts.
“When are your parents arriving?” “On Saturday.”
I won’t be at ease until the doctor gives me the results.
Óscar starts at a travel agency tomorrow. His colleague Alba explains what his first day will be like. Choose the right form.
Alba: “When you get to the office, ask for me at reception.”
Alba: “As soon as you have your password, you can open your email.”
Alba: “I always check the bookings before answering the emails.”
Alba: “You’ll work with me until you learn to use the software.”

When you report in the past a plan that was in the future at that moment, the subjunctive changes to the imperfect subjunctive (llegara). You will study it at B2; for now, just recognise it. Two more formal connectors work like en cuanto: tan pronto como (as soon as) and una vez que (once).
“Nuria promised Gabriel she would call him as soon as the technician arrived.” When was Nuria going to call?
“Gabriel asked her not to let Tula off the lead until she was in the park.” What did Nuria have to do?

You can now talk about future moments. In lesson 099 you use the same logic for purpose: same subject, para + infinitive; another person, para que + subjunctive. It is the natural next step: a goal, like a future moment, is not real yet.

Marina Ferrer runs the La Semilla community garden. On Saturday there is an open day, and Gabriel, a new volunteer, is coming to help. Marina explains what each thing is for: “I water early to use less water.” “I put up posters so that the neighbours know what we do.” Today you learn to say the purpose of an action.
I water early to use less water. (Same person does both.)
I put up posters so that the neighbours know what we do. (Two different people.)
In “Riego temprano para gastar menos agua”, who uses less?
In this sentence, the verb “sepan” is in…
Is the person who acts the same one who gets the goal?
Gabriel comes on Saturdays to learn how to grow things.
We cover the soil so as not to lose moisture.
Marina calls don Ernesto to ask him for seeds.
Does another person (or thing) get the goal?
I’ll explain compost to you so that you understand it well.
We water in the evening so that the plants don’t dry out.
Open the gate so the children can come in.
Marina puts up a sunshade so the volunteers don’t get hot.
Gabriel buys a book to learn more about tomatoes.
I’m leaving you the key so that you can open the shed tomorrow.
Are you asking about the purpose?
What is this tarp for? — To cover the soil.
What do you want so many pots for? — So the children can plant flowers.
Gabriel doesn’t know what the green box is for.
Do you go, come or go out somewhere to do something?
Gabriel is coming to help on Saturday.
Lucía goes out to put up the posters.
I’ll go down and open the door.
“Porque” gives the cause and takes the indicative. “Para que” gives the purpose and takes the subjunctive. They answer different questions: why? / what for?
What are you keeping these empty bottles for?
Tomorrow I’ll come and plant the lettuces with you.
We’re not watering today because it rained last night.
Are you writing a letter, a report or an official notice?
We are writing to you in order to request a grant.
We will open the garden on Saturday so that local residents can get to know the project.
We arrange the tables so that everyone can see the demonstration.
With the subjunctive, “de modo que” expresses a purpose (so that). With the indicative it expresses a result (so, therefore). You study results in class 116.
We attach the budget so that you can study it.
We are meeting on Monday in order to organise the shifts.
Put the tall plants at the back so that they don’t shade the small ones.
Lucía leaves early to catch the eight o’clock bus.
Explain to people what the donations are for.
Hi! I’m Gabriel, the new volunteer. I’ve come to help with Saturday’s open day.
Great, welcome! Look, first we’re going to cover the tomatoes so they don’t get scorched by the sun.
OK. And that green tarp? What is it for?
It’s for covering the soil when it rains a lot. That way the seeds don’t get washed away.
And these posters? Shall I put them up in the local shops?
Yes, please. We put them up so the neighbours know what we do here. Lots of people walk past and don’t know about the garden.
And where do we put the tables on Saturday?
In a circle, so that everyone can see the demonstration. Don Ernesto explains how compost is made.
Great! Hey, and what is the donation box for?
We want to buy a tank to collect rainwater. And on Monday I’m sending a letter to the district board to ask for a grant.
Very good. Tomorrow I’m going out to buy seeds. Shall I get you anything?
Yes, some small gloves, so the children can plant without getting dirty.
What is the green tarp for?
Why are they putting the tables in a circle?
What does Marina ask Gabriel for?
We use drip irrigation to save water.
I’m leaving the gate open so the neighbours can come in without knocking.
What is this tiny shovel for?
Lucía is going to the market to put up the last posters.
We organise workshops so that children learn to look after plants.
I put out fresh water so the birds can drink.
I’m coming to water Marina’s plants.
What is this tool for?
We are writing to the board in order to ask for a grant.
Why does Marina send the voice message?
Why is Lucía putting the posters up in the shops?
What is Gabriel coming at nine to do?
Why do they need to water on Friday evening?
What is the donation money for?
the same person acts and gets the goal
someone or something else gets the goal; never indicative
the same rule, in letters and official texts
the purpose of a movement; and “¿para qué…?” + indicative
Ask yourself: who gets the goal? If it is the same person who acts: para + infinitive. If it is someone else: para que + subjunctive. In the question itself, indicative: “¿Para qué ahorras?”
I speak slowly so that my students understand me.
Ana gets up at six to go to the gym.
What do you need so many chairs for?
The bank sends this notice so that its customers update their details.
This afternoon I’m going down to take the rubbish out.
Gabriel also helps at the neighbourhood library, which is setting up a book club. Join the ideas on the poster with “para”, “para que” or “a fin de que”.

When the main verb is in the past, “para que” takes another form, the imperfect subjunctive (class 128): “Marina put up posters so the neighbours would know what they did.” Today you only need to recognise it: it ends in -ra. And one nuance: with verbs like give, leave, bring + someone, the infinitive is also possible with a different subject: “I’m leaving you the key to open the shed” (you open it).
Marina prepared some worksheets so that families would learn to plant.
“I called Gabriel so that he would come and help me.” When did it happen?
“I gave Lucía a key to open the shed.” Who opens the shed?

You can now explain what you do things for: “I put up posters so the neighbours know what we do.” In class 100 you use the subjunctive in another place: to describe something you are looking for and don’t know yet: “I’m looking for a volunteer who knows about compost” versus “I have a volunteer who knows about compost.” It is the natural next step: the same subjunctive for what is not yet real.

Irene Salas is looking for an apartment in the centre. Today she visits one with her friend Gabriel: it is on the fourth floor with no lift, and the rent is higher than she wanted to pay. But it gets lots of light and it is a ten-minute walk from her work. Irene goes up, looks around and says: “Even though it’s expensive, I like it.” Today you learn to admit a real drawback without changing your decision.
Even though it’s expensive… (a real fact she accepts; normally it would stop her)
…I like it. (the decision stands: the obstacle is not strong enough)
In “Aunque es caro, me gusta”, is the apartment expensive?
Even though there is no lift, Irene wants the apartment.
What drawback do you admit? And what happens anyway?
Although the kitchen is small, it has everything you need.
Although it was raining, Irene went to see the apartment.
Irene signed the contract, although the owner didn’t lower the price.
Although it was very hot yesterday, Irene climbed the four floors.
Which sentence has the right punctuation?
Even though it’s expensive, I like it.
It’s expensive, but I like it.
It’s expensive. However, I like it. (more formal, typical in writing)
It’s expensive. Even so, I like it. (stresses that you know and don’t care)
“Aunque” and “pero” don’t go together in the same sentence: choose one. With “pero” you can add “aun así” to insist: “It’s expensive, but even so I like it.”
The kitchen is small, but it has an oven and a new fridge.
Agency report: “The building has no lift. However, it is in an excellent area.”
Gabriel: “It’s nine hundred a month, Irene.” Irene: “I know. Even so, I’ll take it.”
What comes next: a noun, a verb or a full clause?
In spite of the price, Irene wants the apartment.
Despite living on the fourth floor, Irene doesn’t need a lift. (same subject: Irene)
Even though the building is old, the windows are new.
In spite of the street noise, the bedroom is quiet.
Despite being an architect, Gabriel didn’t notice the damp problem.
Even though the kitchen is small, Irene cooks every day.
Which sentence is correct?
As it gets a lot of light, Irene works in the living room.
Well, this is the apartment. I know it’s four floors with no lift. However, look how much light comes in.
It’s lovely! Even though I got to the top out of breath, it’s worth it.
The living room is very spacious, although the kitchen is quite small.
It’s small, but it has everything you need: an oven, a fridge and a new washing machine.
And how much is the rent, Mrs Molina?
Nine hundred a month, water included.
It’s more than you wanted to pay, Irene… Even so, you look very happy.
It’s true. Even though it’s expensive, it’s a ten-minute walk from the studio. I save on the bus.
And the noise? This street is full of bars.
Despite being right in the centre, this apartment is very quiet: the bedroom faces the courtyard.
Look, in spite of the stairs, I love it. I’ll take it. When can we sign?
What problems does the apartment have?
Why is the apartment quiet?
What does Irene decide?
Even though the rent is high, I’m going to sign the contract.
The building is old. However, the windows are new and no noise comes in.
In spite of the stairs, Irene’s mother goes up without stopping.
Despite being very tired, Irene puts the bed together that same night.
The owner didn’t want to lower the price. Even so, I signed the contract.
Although it’s small, I love the balcony.
In spite of the rain, we did the move.
Irene sleeps well although she lives in the centre.
What is the main idea?
What did the owner do?
How was the visit with Irene’s mother?
What does Irene say about the kitchen?
What problem does Irene have for Saturday?
the drawback you admit; in front or after, with a comma
they go with the result; never “aunque…, pero…”
del = de + el; infinitive when the subject is the same

Ask: where is the obstacle? “Aunque” (+ verb) or “a pesar de” (+ noun or infinitive) go with the obstacle. “Pero”, “sin embargo” or “aun así” go with the result. One obstacle, one connector. And if it is a reason rather than an obstacle, use “como” or “porque”.
Although I don’t speak German well, I work for a company in Berlin.
In spite of the traffic, we got to the airport on time.
The hotel was expensive. Even so, we booked it.
Although I studied a lot, I didn’t pass the exam.
Despite being tired, we finished the project.
A few months later, Gabriel is offered a job in another city. He has doubts, but he accepts. Rewrite his sentences.

Today you use “aunque” with the indicative: the obstacle is a fact you state (“Aunque llueve”: it is raining). You will also hear “aunque” with the subjunctive: “Aunque llueva mañana…”: you don’t know if it will rain, and it doesn’t matter. You will study this at B2 (class 137); for now, just recognise it. In conversation you also hear “y eso que” + indicative after the main idea, roughly “and that’s despite the fact that…”.
Irene, on Friday: “Even if it rains tomorrow, we’re starting at eight.” What does Irene know?
Irene, on Saturday, looking out of the window: “Even though it’s raining, we’re starting at eight.” What does Irene know?
“Irene’s mother went up without stopping, and she’s seventy.” What does it mean?

You can now admit a real drawback and keep your decision. In class 102 you look to the future with another relation between two ideas: the condition. “If I finish early, I’ll call you.” It is the natural next step: after saying what happens in spite of an obstacle, you learn to say what happens if a real condition is met.
