Lucía Herrera is going to Lima for work tomorrow, for ten days. Her neighbour Raúl is going to look after her cat, Canela, and her plants. She leaves him a note in the kitchen with things that may happen and what to do in each case. You already know “si + present” (class 078). Today you see everything that can go in the other half of the sentence.
What may happen?
If Canela doesn’t eat, call me.
If I come back earlier, I’ll let you know.
If she hears the doorbell, Canela hides under the bed.
If you go out, you have to double-lock the door.
If I have time tomorrow, I’ll water the balcony plants.
In “Si Canela no come, llámame”, does Lucía know whether Canela will eat?
The condition hardly changes: “si + present”. The result does: it depends on what you want to do with the sentence. Look at Lucía’s note.
For predictions both are correct. “Ir a” sounds closer and more conversational, and is very common when you can already see the signs. The future sounds a bit more neutral and is typical of promises.
“Si Canela oye el timbre, se esconde.” The result expresses…
Lucía wants to give an instruction: “If the basil’s leaves are drooping, give it water.”
Condition first: comma after it. Typical of notes and instructions.
Result first: usually no comma. The condition comes at the end, like a detail.
Which sentence has the usual punctuation?
“Call me if Canela doesn’t eat.” = …
If I come back earlier, I’ll tell you. (maybe)
When I come back, I’ll bring you a present from Lima. (it will happen)
Lucía doesn’t know if she’ll finish early: “If I finish early, I’ll go and see the sea.”
If I come back before Monday, I’ll write to you.
If Lucía comes back on Sunday, we’ll go and pick her up.
I don’t know whether Lucía will come back on Sunday. Here the future is fine.
Raúl isn’t sure: “I don’t know whether Canela will play with me.”
The basil doesn’t need direct sun, but rather a lot of light.
Which sentence is correct?
Thanks again, Raúl. Here are the keys. I’m leaving you a note in the kitchen with everything.
Perfect. And Canela? Is she difficult?
No, she’s very calm. But if she hears the doorbell, she hides under the bed. It’s normal, don’t worry.
And how much does she eat?
A bit in the morning and a bit at night. If she doesn’t eat all day, call me, please.
All right. And the plants? I don’t know much about plants…
It’s easy. The basil, water every two days. The cacti, hardly any: if you water them a lot, they’re going to rot.
Got it. Anything else?
Yes: if you go out, you have to double-lock the door. Oh, and if you want, you can use my bike.
Great! And when are you coming back? Monday the 14th?
Yes, if all goes well. But if I change my flight, I’ll let you know. I don’t know yet whether I’ll be able to change it.
Don’t worry. And if anything happens here, I’ll write to you straight away.
What does Canela do if she hears the doorbell?
What is going to happen if Raúl waters the cacti a lot?
In which case will Lucía let Raúl know?
If the basil has drooping leaves, it needs water.
If Canela doesn’t eat in the morning, give her a bit of wet food.
If I lose the key, I won’t be able to get in.
If all goes well, Lucía will come back on Monday the 14th.
If you want to use the bike, you have to put some air in the back tyre.
If she hears the doorbell, Canela hides.
Call me if Canela doesn’t eat.
If you water the cacti a lot, they’re going to rot.
I don’t know whether I’ll be able to call you tomorrow.
What is the main idea?
What happens on Thursday at ten?
What happens if Raúl can’t be at home?
What does Canela do if she gets bored?
When might Lucía come back?
What can Raúl do with the basil?
something possible; never future or subjunctive after “si”
what always happens in that case
what will happen
what to do, or what you may do

The condition hardly changes: si + present indicative. You choose the result by what you want to say: habit (present), prediction or promise (future, ir a), instruction (imperative, puedes, tienes que). Watch out for two traps: “cuando vuelva” (certain) but “si vuelvo” (possible); and “no sé si volverá” (whether) does take the future.
If water reaches a hundred degrees, it boils.
If you can’t find the keys, ask the doorman.
This bike isn’t Raúl’s but Lucía’s.
When I finish the course, I’ll look for a job in Lima.
Inés, Raúl’s cousin, rents a room to a student, Bruno. She writes him the house rules. Turn her notes into sentences with “si”.

In formal notes, signs or contracts you will read other ways to set a condition: en caso de que + subjunctive (= si, more formal: “in case / if”) and siempre que + subjunctive (= only on that condition: “as long as”). Careful: siempre que + indicative means “whenever”. For now you only need to understand them.
“In case Canela doesn’t eat, call the vet.” = …
“You can use my bike as long as you leave it inside the building.” = …
“Whenever it rains, Canela sleeps on the sofa.” = …

You can now set real conditions: “Si Canela no come, llámame”, “Si vuelvo antes, te avisaré”. In class 103 you learn the simple conditional: to advise without ordering, to ask politely and to imagine. It is the natural next step: from what is possible and real to what you would do.

Natalia Ferrer runs “La Escalera”, an amateur theatre group at her neighbourhood cultural centre. On Thursday they had the dress rehearsal and nothing went to plan: “We were about to start when it started to rain and the power went off.” Today you learn to say how something starts: neutrally, suddenly, or just before it starts.
It started to rain as we left the theatre.
Suddenly it started raining.
We were about to start.
“Estábamos a punto de empezar” means…
Which sentence stresses a sudden start?
In “Empezó a llover”, after “empezó” comes…
When does an action or a process start? The neutral option, valid with any verb.
The group started rehearsing the play in September.
Little by little, Rodrigo began to understand his character.
Centre notice: “On Monday we will begin selling tickets.”
Does something start suddenly, or does someone get down to doing it?
At seven o’clock sharp it started pouring.
Marcos started looking for torches all over the theatre.
Tonight I’m getting down to going over the script.
Yesterday Rodrigo got down to studying at eleven at night, after dinner.
Over time, Elena began to feel more confident on stage.
Does an emotion or a movement start suddenly, almost out of control?
In the saddest scene, Rodrigo burst out laughing.
When the rain came, the neighbours broke into a run towards the doorway.
Elena read the last letter and burst into tears.

“Ponerse” + adjective is a change of state (class 061): I got nervous, she went red. “Ponerse a” + infinitive is the start of an action: I started shaking. In one sentence: “Rodrigo got nervous and started talking very fast.”
When she saw her name on the poster, Elena burst into tears of joy.
On Thursday at seven it started raining very hard.
After dinner, Marcos got down to checking the lights calmly.
The actors are about to go on stage.
Elena is going to come on in the second act.
Two minutes to curtain-up: the actors are about to go on.
Rodrigo nearly fell off the ladder, but Marcos held him.
Next year Elena is going to study Drama.
The script is long, but last night I got down to reading it.
Which sentence is correct?
Natalia! How was the dress rehearsal? I heard there were problems.
Oh, you can’t imagine. We were about to start when it started pouring and the power went off.
Seriously? And what did you do?
Marcos started looking for torches, and Rodrigo took it upon himself to fix the fuses without knowing anything about electricity.
How dangerous! And then?
Luckily, at half past seven the power came back and we started rehearsing. But in the hospital scene, Rodrigo burst out laughing.
In the saddest scene of the play?
Yes, it was nerves. Suddenly we all burst out laughing with him. I nearly stopped the rehearsal.
And Elena? She’s always so calm.
Elena was perfect. At the end she read her character’s letter and burst into real tears. Nobody moved.
How lovely. And now? The opening night is tomorrow.
Tonight I’m getting down to going over my notes, and tomorrow we’re going to start at six sharp. Rodrigo is already starting to feel calmer.
What happened just before the rehearsal?
What did Rodrigo do in the hospital scene?
What is Natalia going to do tonight?
At five the actors started doing their make-up in the dressing room.
When Rodrigo saw the full theatre, he started shaking.
Elena was cold and started doing exercises to warm up.
There were two minutes left and the play was about to start.
In the second act, the audience began to understand the story of the two brothers.
It suddenly started raining.
We all burst out laughing.
I was about to leave when the phone rang.
What is the main idea?
What happened when they were about to start?
How did the group react when Rodrigo burst out laughing?
What did Natalia nearly do?
What will they do tomorrow after warming up their voices?

Natalia says “Empezamos por calentar la voz”. “Empezar por” + infinitive is not about the start of an action: it says what we do first in a sequence. Compare: “we start warming up our voices” and “we start by warming up our voices”.
the neutral start; also for states and slow processes
a sudden or deliberate start; activity verbs
an abrupt start, almost out of control; few verbs
before the start: imminent, interrupted, or nearly

They all take “a” + infinitive (and “estar a punto de”). “Empezar a” is neutral and always works. “Ponerse a” adds surprise or determination, but not with states. “Echarse a” is for laughing, crying, running and shaking, with no extra “se”. And before the start: “estaba a punto de… cuando” (interrupted) or “estuve a punto de” (nearly).
We had been on the beach for ten minutes when the sky began to cloud over.
The little girl saw the dog and burst into tears.
After lunch, my father got down to fixing the bike in the garage.
Ana was about to leave home when her boss called her.
What a scare: I nearly missed the plane, but I arrived just in time.
A month after the opening night, Elena gives her first interview on a local radio station. Afterwards she tells Natalia about it. Transform her sentences.

More ways to express a start. “Romper a” + crying, raining, talking: a sudden, intense start; rather literary. “Meterse a” + infinitive (colloquial): to take on something you are not qualified for, or that nobody asked you to do. “Comenzar a” is the usual choice in formal texts. And in many parts of Latin America, “estar por” + infinitive means “to be about to”: “It’s about to rain.”
“On reading the letter, the old woman burst into tears.”
“He knows nothing about electricity, but he took it upon himself to fix the socket and now there’s no power.”
“The registration period will begin on 1 March.”
“Take the umbrella: it’s about to rain.”
Which sentence sounds appropriate?

You can now say how something starts: “Empecé a ensayar”, “Se puso a llover”, “Estaba a punto de salir”. In class 107 you look at what happens after the start: the action continues (“Sigo ensayando”), is repeated or stops. It is the natural next step: from the beginning of an action to how it carries on.

Raquel Benítez has presented “Buenos días, barrio” on a community radio station for twenty-five years. Today, Friday, is her last show. Before going into the studio, she tells Hugo, the producer: “I’ve just arrived. I’ll finish clearing my desk and we’ll start. And from Monday, no more early mornings.” Today you learn to talk about the end of an action: what has just happened, what you finish, what you stop doing and how a story ends.
Raquel has just arrived at the station.
First she finishes clearing her desk.
From Monday she stops getting up early.
“Raquel acaba de llegar” means…
Which sentence is about a habit that ends?
In “acabar de”, “terminar de” and “dejar de”, what comes after “de”?
Did it happen a moment ago, just before now or just before another moment in the past?
Just a moment, I’ve just walked into the studio.
The listeners have just sent more than a hundred messages.
When Hugo came to the station, he had just finished his degree.
—Hugo, are you free? —Yes, I’ve just recorded the interview.
“Ayer acabé de leer la novela a las doce” means…
Does an activity or habit stop? Or, on the contrary, does it never stop?
In 2015 the neighbourhood stopped having a cinema.
The listeners keep on writing messages.
If you go to Oaxaca, be sure to try the mole.
From Monday Raquel stops setting the alarm for five.
For a year now the director hasn’t let us eat in the studio.
If you visit the station, be sure to say hello to Hugo.
Are you completing a task that had already started?
Hugo finished editing the show at midnight.
Hang on, I’ll finish writing this email and we’ll go down.
I’ve just read your message.
I’ll finish reading the script and call you.
I stopped reading the novel on page fifty.
Raquel read half the novel and gave up: she stopped reading it.
—Can we eat now? —Yes, I’ve finished cooking.
How does a story end: with a high point or with an unexpected result?
Over the years, Raquel came to know almost every neighbour by name.
The interview went on so long that Hugo never got to play the last song.
Hugo came to do an internship and ended up working here.
At first he didn’t want the job, but he ended up accepting it.
Raquel planned to work at the station for a year and ended up staying twenty-five.
The show was so popular that it even made it onto national television.
Wait a minute: I’ll finish checking the script and pass it to you.
—And tomorrow’s script? —I’ve just finished it.
Raquel was afraid of the change, but she ended up accepting it.
Good morning, Raquel. How are you? Nervous?
A bit. I’ve just arrived and the phone hasn’t stopped ringing. It’s the listeners.
Of course: it’s your last show. Have you finished clearing your desk?
Almost. Look what I found: a photo of my first day. I had just turned thirty-eight.
Twenty-five years at this station! Did you never think of quitting?
Yes, once I went as far as writing my resignation letter, but I didn’t hand it in and in the end I stayed.
And what are you going to do with so much free time now?
First of all, stop getting up early. I’ve been getting up at five for twenty-five years.
And are you going to stop listening to the radio too?
Never! I’m going to listen to you every morning. And you, be sure to call me if you have any questions.
Promise. Right, it’s five to nine: finish your coffee, we’re about to start.
Coming. I’ve just realised it’s the last time I’ll say “Buenos días, barrio”.
Why does the phone keep ringing?
What happened to Raquel’s resignation letter?
What does Raquel ask Hugo to do?
—Where’s Raquel? —She’s just gone out: she’s at the door with the neighbours.
When the director arrived, the guests had just cut the cake.
Doña Carmen got emotional and didn’t stop crying all afternoon.
Hugo, be sure to come to dinner on Saturday: I want to see you.
In twenty-five years, Raquel interviewed as many as three thousand neighbours.
I’ve just spoken to Raquel.
Be sure to listen to the show.
I came for a year and ended up staying.
What is the main idea?
Who is the last message of the day from?
What was Raquel’s life like when she started at the station?
What is Raquel going to stop doing from Monday?
What does Raquel ask the listeners to do?

Raquel says “I’m going to keep listening to the radio” (class 107). With the same meaning she could say “I’m not going to stop listening to the radio”. Seguir + gerund presents the continuity neutrally; no dejar de + infinitive stresses it: it doesn’t stop.
just done; in the preterite or future it means “to finish”
to complete a task already under way
to stop; with “no”, to keep on or “be sure to”
the high point; the final result

“Acabo de” = just now; “termino de” = I complete the task; “dejo de” = I don’t do it any more. Without “de”, “dejar” + infinitive means to let. With “no”, “no dejar de” means to keep on or to be sure to. And to tell how a story ended: “llegar a” + infinitive (how far it went) and “acabar” + gerund (how it turned out).
—Is there any coffee? —Yes, Lola has just made it.
When we got to the cinema, the film had just started.
My grandmother stopped driving at eighty: she couldn’t see well any more.
If you go to Lima, be sure to visit the Barranco district.
I didn’t like jazz, but over the years I ended up loving it.
A year later, Raquel lives on the coast and writes to Hugo. Transform her sentences.

“No acabar de” + infinitive means “not quite”: “I don’t quite understand this change”, “The idea doesn’t quite convince me.” In many parts of Latin America, “recién” + preterite works like “acabar de”: “Recién llegué” = I’ve just arrived; in Spain, “recién” goes mainly with past participles: “freshly baked bread”. “Terminar” + gerund is as normal as “acabar” + gerund, and very common in Latin America. And in formal notices and letters, “dejar de” announces changes (“The service will stop working”) and “no deje de” is a polite invitation.
“Sorry, but your proposal doesn’t quite convince me.”
“Where are you? —I’ve just arrived, I’m at the entrance.”
“Line 4 will stop running on Sundays from January.”
“If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us.”
“I went to look at shoes and ended up buying myself a coat.”

You can now talk about the end of an action: what you have just done, what you finish, what you stop doing and how a story ends. In class 109 you see what happens when something you stopped starts again or is repeated: “I started getting up early again”, “I’ll call you again tomorrow.” It is the natural next step: after stopping something, sometimes we take it up again.

Lucía Reyes is a translator who works from home. She rents an apartment, and the washing machine leaks: the first time was three weeks ago, and since then it has happened again twice. Today, Wednesday, Lucía tells her sister Marta: “Óscar, the guy from the agency, called me again yesterday.” Today you learn to talk about things that happen again and to promise that something will not happen again.
On Monday Lucía came back home at eight.
Óscar called her again yesterday.
This is not going to happen again.
“Óscar volvió a llamarla” means…
In “Lucía volvió a casa”, “volver” means…
“Esto no va a volver a pasar” is…
Is an action happening again? Conjugate volver, add a, then the infinitive.
The washing machine is making a strange noise again.
On Friday Ramiro came to the apartment again.
Tomorrow I am going to call the agency again.
On Thursday Ramiro will check the washing machine again.
Lucía was fed up: the washing machine had already failed again twice.
The washing machine leaked again.
Where do I put lo, la, me, se…? Two positions are correct, but you use only one.
Lucía read the contract and then read it again.
Óscar called me again yesterday.
The part broke again.
“Lo volví a leer” ✔ · “Volví a leerlo” ✔ · “Lo volví a leerlo” ✘. Pick one place for the pronoun. If you attach it to the infinitive, you sometimes need an accent: “volver a explicárselo”.
Which sentence is correct?
“Me volvió a escribir” = …
Ramiro came again. (adverbs: they work with any verb)
Ramiro repeated the same repair.
Lucía reread the contract.
Which sentence is NOT correct?
Lucía read the contract again = Lucía reread the contract.
On Friday Ramiro repeated the first day’s repair.
Is something never going to happen again, or did it never happen again?
Óscar promises: “This won’t happen again.”
Marta, to her son: “Don’t leave the door open again.”
After that winter, the heating never failed again.
Óscar stopped calling his clients on Mondays. (a habit ended)
The neighbour called once and never called again.

With “se” and an adjective, volverse means to become (a change of character): “With so many breakdowns, Lucía became very distrustful.” It also means to turn around: “Se volvió y me miró.” You will study it with the verbs of change; today you only recognise it. Careful: “la pieza se volvió a romper” is not volverse: it is “romperse” + volver a.
Ramiro, to Lucía: “I’m sorry. This won’t happen again.”
Lucía to Marta, who left the tap running: “Don’t leave it running again!”
The previous technician came once and never showed up again.
Lucía had to wash all the clothes again.
Good afternoon, Ms Reyes. I listened to your message. Has the washing machine leaked again?
Yes, again. Last night I got back home at eight and the kitchen was full of water. It’s the third time this month.
I’m very sorry. But Ramiro fixed it on Friday, didn’t he?
Yes, he came again on Friday and changed a part. But yesterday I ran the washing machine and the floor filled with water again.
I see. First thing tomorrow I’ll call the repair company again. And I’ll forward you Ramiro’s email, in case you want to talk to him.
Thanks. Also, I had to wash all the clothes again by hand. I don’t want to go through this again.
I apologise again. I promise you this is not going to happen again.
That’s what you told me last time… If it happens again, I’ll look for another apartment.
You’re right. In the meantime, please don’t use the washing machine again until the repair.
All right. And if I don’t hear anything tomorrow, I’ll call you again.
Perfect. Until tomorrow, Ms Reyes.
How many times did the washing machine leak this month?
What is Óscar going to do tomorrow?
What does Óscar ask Lucía to do?
Three weeks ago the washing machine leaked. Last week it leaked again.
In my old apartment, the heating would break down again every January.
I called on Monday night because the water had reached the hallway again.
Óscar promised me: “This won’t happen again.”
Let’s hope the washing machine doesn’t fail again.
Don’t use the washing machine again.
What is the main idea?
Who did Óscar talk to this morning?
What is Ramiro going to do on Thursday?
What happens if the washing machine leaks again after Thursday?
What does Óscar say about the downstairs neighbour?
again, in any tense; the pronoun before volver or attached to the infinitive
never again: promises, warnings and wishes
repetir takes a noun; re- does not work with every verb
after “a” comes a place, not an infinitive

Look at what comes after “a”: if it is an infinitive, volver a = again (“volvió a llamar”); if it is a place, volver = return (“volvió a casa”). With “no” or “nunca”, volver a = never again (“no volverá a pasar”). Only volver is conjugated, and the “a” never disappears.
I forgot the password and had to create it again.
My brother broke my favourite mug. I told him: “Don’t touch my things again!”
I went to that restaurant in 2019, the food was very bad and I never went again.
I liked the novel so much that I reread it in the summer.
What does “Con los años, mi jefe se volvió muy exigente” mean?
Marta, Lucía’s sister, works in an office. The printer is giving her trouble too. Transform her sentences with volver a.

With a verb of movement, “a” + infinitive can also express purpose: “I left home, but I went back to get the umbrella.” Context decides. To avoid doubt, name the place: “volví a casa a buscar el paraguas”.
Formal email from the agency: “We once again apologise for the inconvenience.”
“I left the apartment, but I went back for the keys.” What is most likely?
News: “The eight o’clock train arrived late again.”

You can now talk about what happens again and what must not happen again: “volvió a llamarme”, “no volverá a pasar”. In class 110 you continue with verbs that take a fixed preposition before the infinitive: “I got used to living far away”, “I try to arrive on time”, “I’m thinking of moving house”. It is the natural next step: just like in “volver a”, the preposition is part of the verb and cannot disappear.

Valeria Ríos is an architect from Guadalajara, Mexico. Six months ago she moved to Valparaíso, Chile, to work for a studio that restores old houses on the hills. When she talks about her new life she says: “I got used to living far away”, “I try to call my mum every week”, “I think about my family a lot”. Today you learn verbs that always go with the same preposition.
I’ve got used to the wind now.
I try to call my mum.
I think about my family.
My cousin married a Chilean man.

These prepositions don’t carry a meaning you can work out: the verb requires them. So learn them together as one unit. The preposition stays in front of whatever follows: a noun, a pronoun, an infinitive or a clause with “que”.
“I think about my family a lot.”
In “I got used to living far away”, the “a”…
How do you say “She married a Chilean man”?
Adapting, daring, learning, helping or refusing: these verbs take “a”.
Valeria got used to climbing stairs every day.
I still don’t dare to drive on the hills.
This year I learned to cook fish.
Catalina helped me look for a flat.
The landlord refused to lower the rent.
Trying, remembering, forgetting, complaining, falling in love or realising: these take “de”.
I try to talk to the neighbours every day.
Do you remember the first day at the office?
Yesterday I forgot to call my mum.
My brother complains about the heat in Guadalajara.
Valeria fell in love with the city on the first day.
At first I didn’t dare to speak in meetings.
Do you remember the studio’s address?
My neighbour helped me look for a home.
Thinking about, trusting, noticing, taking time, insisting or agreeing: these take “en”.
At night I think about my friends in Guadalajara.
I trust Catalina: she never lets me down.
Look at the colours of the houses.
It took me three months to get used to it.
Emilio and I agreed to talk on Sunday.
Dreaming of, counting on or marrying: these take “con”.
Valeria dreams of restoring a whole house.
If you need anything, count on me.
My cousin married a guy from Lima.
The bus took twenty minutes to arrive.
Last night I dreamt about the sea.
Don’t worry, you can count on me for the move.
I always think about my grandmother.
What do you think of Valparaíso? — I think it’s beautiful.
In July I’m planning to go to Guadalajara.
I usually have dinner at nine.
I got used to eating late.
I’m used to the cold now.
“What do you think of my new flat?” “I think it’s very bright.”
Next summer I’m planning to visit the south of Chile.
At first the noise from the port bothered me, but I’ve got used to it now.

The standard norm keeps the preposition the verb requires, also before “que”. Dropping it (“queísmo”) is common in casual speech in many areas but avoided in careful language. Adding “de” where the verb doesn’t need it (“dequeísmo”) is also avoided. Trick: replace the “que” clause with “eso”: if you need “de eso”, write “de que”.
What are you thinking about? Who did she marry?
Spanish never leaves the preposition at the end, as English does.
The same happens with relative clauses, which you’ll study in class 112: “Catalina is a friend I can count on.” For now you only need to recognise it: the preposition goes first, never at the end.
Suddenly I realised that I had lost my keys.
I think Valeria is going to stay in Chile.
What do you dream about?
Which sentence is correct? (I forgot the bank closed today.)
Which sentence is correct? (I trust my team.)
Hi, Vale! You’ve been there six months now. Have you got used to Valparaíso yet?
Almost. I climb hills all day and I love it, but I can’t get used to the afternoon wind. And I still don’t dare to drive on those streets.
Hey, Mum complains that you don’t call her.
I know! I try to call her on Wednesdays, but with the time difference I always forget what time it is there.
And at work? Have you made friends yet?
Yes, I can count on Catalina for everything. She helped me find the flat. And the other day I realised I already say “al tiro”, like Chileans do.
Ha! You suddenly look very serious. What are you thinking about?
About you all. I think about the family every time I see the boats leaving.
Oh, Vale… Well, what do you think about coming in July?
I’m planning to go, but don’t tell Mum anything. I dream of surprising her.
Perfect. So we’ve agreed to talk on Sunday to look at dates.
Yes. And don’t worry: it doesn’t take me long to find cheap tickets.
…+ en + infinitivo: el tiempo que necesitas para hacer algo.
What hasn’t Valeria got used to yet?
Why doesn’t she call her mum as often as she wants?
What does Valeria want to do in July?
The client refused to pay for the roof repair.
Restoring a house like that takes months.
I met him at a concert and fell in love with him that same night.
Look at this window: it’s original, from 1890.
For the presentation, can I count on you?
I got used to living far away.
Who did your cousin marry?
Catalina helped me paint the kitchen.
I never remember his birthday.
What is the main idea?
Why shouldn’t Mariana take long to look for a flat?
Who helped Valeria understand the new words?
What did Valeria realise after a month?
What was the hardest thing for Valeria?

In Chile, “tomar once” is an early-evening meal: tea or coffee, bread, avocado, cheese… Many people have it instead of a big dinner. Valeria “took a month to realise” this: a good example of verbs with prepositions chained in one sentence.
getting used to, daring, learning, helping, refusing
trying, remembering, forgetting, complaining, falling in love, realising
the mind, trust, attention, time taken, an agreement
wishes, support and partners; con + mí = conmigo

Learn each verb with its preposition. The preposition stays in front of a noun, an infinitive or “que”, and goes at the start of a question. Don’t add “de” where the verb doesn’t take it: “pienso que”, “creo que”. And remember: “pensar en” (in your mind), “¿qué piensas de…?” (opinion), “pienso ir” (a plan).
My grandfather refuses to use a mobile phone: he says he doesn’t need one.
When I saw the photo, I realised it was my old teacher.
What are you complaining about now?
My sister married a classmate from university.
I agree with you: I think the project is too expensive.

A year later, Valeria is interviewing a young architect for the studio. Before the interview, she writes down her questions. Turn her notes into direct questions, with the preposition in the right place.

More frequent verbs with a fixed preposition: depend on (de), consist of (en), work as / devote yourself to (a), regret (de). And with emotions: “alegrarse de que” + subjunctive (class 092): “I’m glad you came.” Notice: English uses a different preposition or none, while Spanish keeps its own.
The final price depends on the materials the client chooses.
The job consists of checking plans and visiting old houses.
“What does your brother do?” “He’s a music teacher.”
I don’t regret moving: it was the best decision.
That’s great, Mariana! I’m glad you like Lima.

Today you used many pronouns after a preposition: “I think about you”, “count on me”, “I trust her”. In class 111 you work with personal pronouns in the sentence: when to say “A mí me encanta”, “A Valeria la conocí en Chile”, and why the pronoun appears twice. It’s the natural next step: from the preposition a verb requires to the pronouns that go with it.

Sofía Vidal runs a small language school. She is back after two weeks at a conference, and her assistant, Raúl Molina, tells her what has happened. Raúl starts many sentences with the topic: “The invoices, I paid them on Thursday”, “Julia, I met her on Tuesday”. Today you learn to put the topic first and pick it up with a pronoun, to add emphasis with “a mí, a ti”, and to answer with “lo es”.
Raúl paid the invoices on Thursday.
The invoices? I paid them on Thursday.
Julia seems serious, but she isn’t.
In “Las facturas las pagué el jueves”, what does “las” do?
Which sentence best answers “And the report?”
In “Parece seria, pero no lo es”, “lo” means…
Do you start the sentence with the thing or person you are talking about? Then a pronoun must pick it up.
The new timetable I already have; the books I don’t have yet.
I’ll see the teachers tomorrow at the meeting.
I haven’t seen that film, but people say it’s good.
Raúl has the key to classroom three.
Which sentence follows the general norm?
Is there a person who receives something (a message, a present, an explanation)? Spanish usually names that person twice.
I wrote to Julia yesterday to welcome her.
I sent the students the calendar on Friday.
Raúl loves organizing; I don’t, not so much.
I explained the course programme to the new teachers on Monday.
Which sentence is incorrect?
Do you want to highlight or contrast a person: me, not you? The tonic form never goes alone; it always comes with me, te, lo, la, le…
Sofía didn’t call Raúl: she called me.
I owe you a coffee, at the very least.
I know her brother, but I don’t know her.

In many parts of Spain people use “le” for a man as a direct object: “A Raúl le vi ayer”. The RAE accepts it only for one man. You don’t need it: “A Raúl lo vi ayer” is correct everywhere. For a woman, always “la”.
Julia didn’t tell Raúl: she told me.
Which sentence is correct?
Are you answering about a quality or a job without repeating it? “Lo” replaces it after ser, estar and parecer.
“Is Julia an English teacher?” “Yes, she is, and French too.”
The students look nervous, and they are: the exam is tomorrow.
Classroom four looks small, but it isn’t.
“Are your colleagues punctual?” “Yes, they are.”
“Is Raúl tired?” “A bit, yes, he is.”
“Is the director happy?” “Yes, she is.”
Good morning, Raúl! I’m back. So, tell me: what about this month’s invoices?
Don’t worry: I paid the invoices on Thursday, all of them.
Perfect. And the new teacher? Have you met her yet?
Yes, I met Julia on Tuesday. She seems very serious, but she isn’t: the students already love her.
Great! And the exam calendar?
I sent the calendar to the B2 students on Friday. The B1 students get it today.
And Mr Ortega’s contract? I need it for Thursday’s meeting.
I don’t have that contract yet. I wrote to Mr Ortega yesterday, but he isn’t answering.
Oh dear. Well, I’ll call him myself this afternoon. Hey, and you? You look tired.
A bit, yes, I am. This week everyone has asked me: where the key is, when the course starts…
Well, I owe you a coffee, at the very least. And this afternoon I’ll welcome Julia.
Deal. But not the one from the machine, OK? I don’t like it at all.
What happened to the invoices?
What is Julia like, according to Raúl?
What is the problem with the contract?
Raúl printed the posters yesterday afternoon.
We sent the students’ families an invitation on Monday.
The key to the staff room: have you got it, Raúl?
Julia didn’t ask the technician for help: she asked me.
“Is the director nervous?” “Yes, she is, but she doesn’t say so.”
The report, I finished it yesterday.
Julia loved the open day.
It looks easy, but it isn’t.
What is the main idea?
What is the Monday group like?
What did Julia do with the practice exams?
Who did she give the marks to?
What does Julia ask Sofía for?

Julia says “Las notas se las di hoy a Raúl”. Three things happen at once: the topic first (the marks), its pronoun (“las”) and the person who receives them (le becomes “se”, as in class 064). It sounds very natural: topic first, then the rest.
the pronoun is a must; after the verb, the direct object is not repeated
optional but very common; always with gustar; plural → les
to highlight or contrast; the tonic form never goes alone
picks up a quality; always “lo”

If the object comes first, a pronoun picks it up: “El informe lo terminé”. If it comes after the verb, the direct object is not repeated, and the indirect object usually takes le / les. “A mí, a ti, a ella” always come with their clitic. And for a quality, invariable “lo”: “Sí, lo es”.
My brother bought the concert tickets.
We gave my grandmother a trip for her birthday.
“Are your neighbours friendly?” “Yes, very.”
Elena and her partner, Gonzalo, are moving house on Saturday. Elena goes through the list and answers a friend who wants to help. Transform her sentences.

Four cases to go further. 1. In the River Plate area, people often double a person direct object after the verb too: “La conocí a Julia”; the general norm says “Conocí a Julia”. 2. In many parts of Spain, “le” for a man: “A Raúl le vi” (accepted only for one man). 3. With a bare noun (no article) first, there is normally no pronoun: “Coffee, I haven’t got.” 4. With “estar” + place there is no “lo”.
“Have you got any sugar?” “Sugar, I haven’t got, but I have honey.”
“I’ve known your brother for years.” In the general norm, it would be…
Which sentence does the norm NOT accept?
“Is Sofía in the office?” “Yes, she is.”

You can now organize information: put the topic first and pick it up with a pronoun (“A Julia la conocí el martes”). In class 112 you go one step further to talk about people and things already mentioned: the relatives quien, el que, el cual (“Julia is the teacher I work with”). It is the natural next step: from picking up with a pronoun to linking sentences with a relative.

Inés Robles is a new member of the Peñas Altas hiking club. On Saturday there is an outing to Valdelagua, a village with an old mill. Inés doesn’t know many people yet, but she says: “I already know the person who organized the visit: it’s Nerea, the guide.” Today you learn to talk about people and things with quien, el que / la que and, for reading formal texts, el cual.
I know the person who organized the visit.
I know who organized the visit / the person who did.
In this sentence, “quien” means…
Why doesn’t “quien” have an accent here?
Where can I use “quien”?
The person who has the keys to the mill is don Ramiro.
Don Ramiro is the man I spoke to on the phone.
The members I share a car with live in my neighbourhood.
Nerea, who knows the village well, is going to guide us.

You will hear and read sentences like “Quien quiera, que venga” (whoever wants to, let them come) or “Quien llegue tarde, que tome el otro autobús”. Here quien means “anyone who” and takes the subjunctive because we don’t know who it will be. Today you only need to recognize it; you work on it in depth in class 169.
The person who took the photos on the last outing is Óscar.
The friends I do the routes with are from university.
When do I use “el que”, “la que”…?
Alicia is the friend I travelled to Peru with.
Valdelagua is the village we are going to on Saturday.
This is the backpack I carry the first-aid kit in.
The one who organized the visit is Nerea.
Those who came last year already know the way.
This is the walking pole I climbed the mountain with.
Which sentence is correct?
The hikers who were wearing new boots ended up with blisters. (only those)
The hikers, who were all wearing new boots, ended up with blisters. (all of them)
“My colleagues, who speak English, helped the tourists.” How many speak English?
The club has thirty members and only six have a car. Which sentence is right?
What is “el cual”?
The cooperative we work with produces goat’s cheese. (formal)
The mill, which dates from the 18th century, has been restored. (formal)
Where are you most likely to read this?
The mill we are visiting is two hundred years old.
Welcome to the club, Inés. How did you find us?
Through Alicia, the friend I travelled to Peru with last year. She has been a member for years.
Alicia! She’s the one who has done the most kilometres this year.
Listen, about Saturday, who do I talk to? The person who organizes the routes?
Better with Nerea, the guide, who knows the village like nobody else. She organized the visit to the mill.
Oh, then I already know the person who organized the visit! Alicia introduced her to me on Tuesday.
Great. And don Ramiro, the man we always call, opens the mill for us at eleven.
Do we need to bring walking poles? The way down looks long.
If you like. Last year, those who had poles came down with no problems. And Óscar, who was wearing brand-new boots, ended up with blisters.
Well, I’m taking my old boots, which I climbed Machu Picchu in.
“Con las cuales”… how formal! Here we say “con las que”. Oh, and whoever wants to can stay for dinner in the village.
Who is Alicia?
Last year, who came down without problems?
Why does Julián say “how formal!”?
Nerea is the guide who knows the area best.
The person who is bringing the first-aid kit this Saturday is Alicia.
The members I share a car with arrive at a quarter to eight.
That is the water bottle I carry the water in.
The village we’re going to has only a hundred inhabitants.
The person who organized the visit is Nerea.
This is the friend I travelled with.
Óscar, who was wearing new boots, ended up tired.
The village we are going to is small.
What is the main idea?
What happens to people who arrive late?
Who is don Ramiro?
Who should bring walking poles?
Why does Nerea thank Inés?
only people; never right after a noun without commas
people and things; the preposition goes in front
it selects: only some
it adds a detail: all of them

“Quien” is only for people and goes with no noun before it, after a preposition or between commas. “El que / la que” works for everything and agrees. The preposition always goes in front: “la amiga con la que viajé”. Without commas you select (only some); with commas you add (all). “El cual” is formal: recognize it when you read.
My colleagues, who are very nice, gave me a backpack.
The person who finished the route first was Alicia.
Let me introduce the neighbours I organize the street party with.
It’s the shop where I bought these boots.
“The students who passed the exam went on a trip.” What does it mean?
On Monday Inés goes back to her job at a library. There is a new colleague and Inés introduces her to everyone. Join the sentences.

In formal texts (official letters, leaflets, news) you will read “el cual / la cual / los cuales / las cuales”, mostly after a preposition or between commas. And in everyday language you’ll hear “hay quien” + verb: “Hay quien prefiere caminar solo” (some people prefer to walk alone).
We thank you for your support, without which this visit would not have been possible.
The cooperative, which is over forty years old, produces goat’s cheese.
What does “Hay quien prefiere caminar solo” mean?

You can now talk about people and things with “quien” and “el que / la que”: “Conozco a quien organizó la visita”, “la amiga con la que viajé”. In class 113 you move on to ideas: “Lo que me dijo Nerea” (what Nerea told me), “lo de la cena” (the dinner thing). It is the natural next step: from the article that agrees (el que, la que) to neuter “lo”, which refers not to a person or a thing but to an idea.

On Thursday there is a residents’ meeting in the building on calle Olmo. Lucía Ferrer chairs it and is preparing the topics. In her notebook she writes: “What worries me is the roof terrace”, “And the lift business?”, “The good thing is that the insurance pays half”. In class 067 you saw “lo que más me gusta…”. Today you go further: with lo you talk about ideas, known topics and aspects of a problem without repeating nouns.
What worries me is the roof terrace.
And what about the lift (business)?
The good thing is that the insurance pays half.
“¿Y lo del ascensor?” Lucía means…
In this sentence, “lo bueno” means…
Which thing? (without naming it)
What we need is a reliable technician.
What bothers me most is the building work so early.
Pilar told us everything that happened in her kitchen.
I don’t understand what the property manager is saying.
What Hugo proposes is to use the room in the courtyard.
Lucía wrote down everything the neighbours said.
Which matter are we talking about? (both people already know)
What happened in the end with the lift business?
What happened yesterday was a scare: water got into Pilar’s kitchen.
Are you still thinking about moving?
Pilar’s problem is sorted now: the insurance is paying.
Yesterday’s thing was a scare.
What happened yesterday was a scare.
Have you heard about the roof terrace? There’s water again.
What the technician said isn’t very clear.
Which part of the topic? (the good, the bad, the important one)
The good thing is that the technician is coming this week.
The worst part was the noise in the morning.
The important thing is to have two quotes.
“The noise bothers me.” “Same here.”

If you report a fact, use the indicative: “Lo malo es que el ascensor no funciona”. If you give advice or judge something that hasn’t happened yet, it works like “es importante que” (class 091): subjunctive. “Lo importante es que vengan todos.” For general advice, the infinitive is easiest: “Lo mejor es esperar”.
Which neighbour? The new one, the one on the fifth floor.
What’s new is that we have a quote now.

Sometimes you will hear lo + adjective + que: “¡No sabes lo difícil que es encontrar un técnico!”. It means “how difficult it is”, with emotion. Today you only need to understand it; you practise it in class 192.
The best thing about this building is the light: every flat gets lots of sun.
Hugo thinks the same as Pilar: the roof terrace needs fixing now.
The technician who came yesterday didn’t fix anything.
Which lift? The one at the back.
What the technician said isn’t clear.
What did the technician say?
After saber, entender, preguntar or explicar, both are correct: “No sé qué quiere” and “No sé lo que quiere”. In other sentences, the rule above works.
“Which proposal do you prefer?” “The one Hugo made.”
What Hugo did on Saturday was clean the room.
The neighbour who lives on the fourth floor is called Pilar.
What I don’t like is having the meeting so late.
How’s the plan to change the front door going?
Good evening, everyone. First topic: the lift. It broke down again on Monday.
Well, what worries me is the roof terrace. And yesterday was a real scare: water got into my kitchen.
The same thing happened two years ago, didn’t it?
Exactly. I have two quotes for fixing the roof terrace. The good thing is that the insurance pays half.
And the bad part?
Well, the bad part is that the work starts at half past seven in the morning.
Ugh. I work nights, so what I’m asking is to start a bit later, at nine.
I’ll write that down. Last topic: the bikes. Hugo, you explain it.
Lots of us have bikes and there’s no space. So what I’m proposing is to use the empty room in the courtyard.
Which room? The one with the green door? It’s full of old boxes.
That one. And the important thing is to empty it. If you like, we can all clean it together on Saturday.
Sounds great. I’ll send everything we decided today to the group tonight.
What happened at Pilar’s place yesterday?
What does Hugo ask for regarding the building work?
What is the good thing about fixing the roof terrace?
What worries the residents most is the roof terrace.
Hugo explained the bike plan.
Lucía sent the group everything they decided.
There are two quotes. The residents prefer the one that is cheaper.
What worries me is the timetable.
The important thing is to empty the room.
We did everything we could.
What is the main idea?
When is the lift technician coming?
Why are they fixing the roof terrace?
What time does the building work start?
What do the residents have to bring on Saturday?
a thing or idea with no noun; the focus goes last
a matter we already know about; no conjugated verb after it
one side of the topic; adjective in masculine singular
if there is a noun, don’t use lo

Ask yourself: is there a noun? If there is, que or el que / la que. If not: with a conjugated verb, lo que (“lo que pasó”); with a noun, an infinitive or “ayer”, lo de (“lo de ayer”); with an adjective, lo + adjective (“lo bueno”). And to put the focus: “Lo que necesito es…”.
What I find hardest about my job is getting up early.
So what happened in the end with your sister’s situation? Did she find a job?
Of all the cafés in the area, the one I like best is the one on the corner.
The best thing about this course is that the classes are short.
It isn’t fair: she always does everything they ask her to.
Another meeting, this time in an office. Sara presents her team’s problems. Help her say them with lo: put the focus or introduce the topic.

An extra step, if you have time. If the verb takes a preposition (hablar de, pensar en, estar de acuerdo con), the preposition goes in front: “Eso es de lo que hablamos”. And in more formal texts, lo que can refer back to a whole sentence: “El técnico llegó tarde, lo que molestó a todos” (and that annoyed everyone). You will see more of this at B2.
I agree with what Hugo said.
That isn’t what we talked about at the meeting.
The technician arrived two hours late, which annoyed everyone.
What does this sentence mean?

You can now present topics, problems and proposals without repeating nouns: “lo del ascensor”, “lo que me preocupa es…”, “lo bueno es que…”. In class 114 you take the next step in giving opinions: you add nuance and contrast with ni… ni, aunque and sin embargo. It is the natural next step: “Lo bueno es que el seguro paga la mitad; sin embargo, lo malo es el ruido”.

Elena Vidal runs La Lámpara, the theatre group at the Las Acacias cultural centre. Opening night is on Friday, but on Tuesday, during rehearsal, the lights stop working. That afternoon Elena hears the same cause told in three ways: between colleagues, in a neutral way and in an official notice. You already know porque and como (class 077). Today you learn to choose the connector by register and by what you want to say about the cause.
“Why aren’t we rehearsing?” “Well, there’s no light.” (a quick spoken excuse)
We’re not rehearsing because there’s no light. (works almost everywhere)
Due to a fault, the rehearsal is cancelled. (an official text: the cause is a noun)
Which sentence is for the sign on the theatre door?
Hugo arrives late and tells Elena: “Sorry, it’s just that the bus took ages.”
Why? And how do I start the sentence?
“Why are you so late?” “Because there were roadworks on the avenue.”
As there was no light, Elena cancelled the rehearsal.
Is the cause already known? Is the text formal?
Since the electrician isn’t coming until Monday, we’re postponing the premiere.
The premiere is postponed, since the hall has no lighting.
Given that there are only three days left, we’re letting the audience know today.
“Why is the hall closed?” “Because there’s a fault.”
Email from the cultural centre: “Since the hall has no lighting, Wednesday’s rehearsal is cancelled.”
Elena to Hugo: “Since you’re here, will you help me move the sofa on the stage?”
Is the cause a noun or an infinitive?
Hugo arrived late because of the roadworks on the avenue.
Because of the rain, the fair was held indoors.
Sorry for not replying yesterday.
Thanks to the neighbours, there are fifty more chairs.
We were left without lighting because of an old cable.
Due to a fault, the premiere is postponed.

In English you say “because of the rain”. In Spanish, porque always goes with a verb: “porque llovía”. With a noun, use por, a causa de or debido a: “por la lluvia”. “Porque de la lluvia” does not exist.
There was no dress rehearsal because of the fault.
Thanks to Nuria, the stage lights are now new.
Hugo apologises for being late.

In speech, es que introduces an explanation or an excuse, almost always in reply to a question, a complaint or an invitation: “Are you coming to the cinema?” “Well, I start work early tomorrow.” It is very common across the Spanish-speaking world, but in a formal email or a notice it sounds too informal.

To reject a false reason and give the real one: “We’re postponing the premiere, not because we aren’t ready, but because there’s no lighting.” The reason you reject usually goes in the subjunctive (estemos); the real one in the indicative (hay). Today you only need to recognise and understand it.
WhatsApp message to a friend: “I can’t come to your party, I’ve got the premiere, you see.”
“We don’t rehearse so much because we enjoy it, but because we want to do it well.” Why do they rehearse so much?
Which connector is the most formal?
Which sentence is correct?
Because of the train delay, we missed our connection.
Sorry, Elena! The bus took ages, you see.
Don’t worry. As you weren’t here yet, we started with scene two.
It was because of the roadworks on the avenue: all the traffic goes down my street.
Elena, we’ve got a problem: the lights aren’t working because there’s a fault in the wiring.
And can’t it be fixed this week?
No, since the centre’s electrician can’t come until Monday. And without lights there’s no dress rehearsal.
Well, since we’re here anyway, we can rehearse the lines sitting down.
Good idea. But we can’t open on Friday. Given that there are only three days left, we need to tell the audience today.
What bad luck! All because of an old cable.
At least, thanks to the neighbours, we now have fifty more chairs.
Yes. And in the notice I want to make one thing clear: we’re postponing the premiere, but not because we aren’t ready, but because we want to do it properly.
Then start like this: “Due to an electrical fault, the premiere is postponed to Friday the 14th.”
Why was Hugo late?
Why can’t the fault be fixed this week?
According to Elena, why are they postponing the premiere?
We can’t test the sound today because the sound technician is ill.
As the new date is Friday the 14th, we’re going to change the posters.
Friday’s performance is postponed due to technical problems.
Sorry for not replying sooner, I was at rehearsal.
In the end, the rehearsal finished at eleven because of the fault.
As there was no light, we rehearsed sitting down.
The premiere is postponed due to a fault.
Since you’re here, help me with the chairs.
Hugo arrived late because of the roadworks.
What is the main idea?
Why can’t they use the lights and sound?
According to Elena, is the play ready?
What happens if someone can’t come on the 14th?
What is the good news?
“porque” answers why; “como” only at the start
front or after; ya que is also common in speech
gracias a = good result; por culpa de = bad; debido a = neutral
a spoken excuse; not in formal texts

Ask two questions. Clause or noun? With a clause: porque, como, ya que, puesto que. With a noun: por, debido a, gracias a. Who are you talking to? With friends, “es que” and “porque”; in a notice or a formal email, “debido a”, “ya que”, “puesto que”. And remember: “como” always goes first, and never “porque de”.
As today is a public holiday, the library is closed.
Airport notice: “The flight is delayed due to fog.”
“Why didn’t you come to dinner?” “I had a temperature, you see.”
Thanks to my sister, I found an apartment in a week.
I got a fine for going too fast.
A group of friends is organising a trip to the mountains, but the plan changes. Rewrite the sentences with the connector given.

The same cause changes shape with the register: from the corridor, to neutral, to an official notice. In formal texts it is common to turn a clause into a noun: “is ill” → “the illness”; “it’s raining” → “the rain”.
“I’m not calling because I want something from you, but because I miss you.” Why is the person calling?
Email from the university: “Since the building is under renovation, Monday’s classes will be online.”
“Since you’re going to the market, will you buy me some bread?” Here “ya que” means…
Which version is best for an official sign?

You can now present the cause with the right connector: “Como no había luz…”, “Debido a una avería…”, “Es que…”. In class 116 you look at the other side of the same relationship: the consequence, with “así que”, “por eso” and “de modo que”. It is the natural next step: first you explain why something happens; now you say what happens as a result.

Rocío Medina and Julián Ferrer work at a small children’s book publisher. On Friday they were travelling to a book fair in Granada, but there was a problem at the station. Rocío texts her director, Elena: “The train was cancelled, so we took a taxi.” Today you learn to express results: in a conversation, in an email and in a formal complaint.
Since the train was cancelled, we took a taxi. (the connector marks the reason)
The train was cancelled, so we took a taxi. (the connector marks the result)
In this sentence, which part does “así que” introduce?
There was a lot of traffic, so we got to the station late.
Are you telling a friend or a colleague what happened?
There were no tickets left, so we went by bus.
Julián got sick on buses. That’s why he preferred the train.
The train doesn’t leave until four, so we’re looking for another option.
Are you writing a complaint, a report or an official email?
The service was cancelled due to a breakdown; therefore, we request a refund of the ticket.
The fair changed its opening hours; as a result, the publishers opened their stands later.
There were roadworks on the road, so we arrived late.
Rocío writes to the rail company: “The train didn’t leave; therefore, I request a refund.”
Rocío talks to Julián: “The taxi is expensive, so we’ll split it.”
“We arrived late. That’s why we didn’t see the opening.” What does “eso” refer to?

In conversation, “así que” can open your turn to draw a conclusion from what the other person has said: “So the hotel was full?” It is very natural in speech. In formal writing, though, it is better not to start a sentence with “Así que”: use “Por lo tanto,” or “Por eso”.
Which sentence is correctly punctuated for a formal email?
Elena hears: “We slept in a hostel.” She answers: “So there were no rooms in the hotel?”
Which of these sentences is NOT correct?
We put the posters at the entrance, so all the visitors saw them. (a real result)
Put the posters at the entrance, so that everyone sees them. (an aim)
The hotel was far from the fair, so we took a taxi every morning.
Speak more slowly, so that the children understand you.
Turn the cause into a result: “Since there were no taxis, we walked.”
My phone had no battery, so I didn’t call you.
There was a taxi strike, so we went by metro.
Rocío! Julián already told me about the train. So in the end you got to Granada by taxi, right?

Yes. They announced there were no more trains until four and that, therefore, the company would refund the money. But the opening was at twelve, so we shared a taxi with people from another publisher.
Very good idea. And did you get there on time?
Not quite. There were roadworks, so we arrived at half past one. That’s why we weren’t at the opening.
Well, never mind. And the boxes of books?
They didn’t fit in the taxi, so Julián sent them by courier. As they arrived on Saturday, on Friday we only had a few copies.
So on Friday you didn’t sell much.
Very little. But on Saturday we put big posters at the entrance, so lots of people came to the stand.
Great! For the next fair we’ll send the boxes two days earlier, so that they arrive on time.
Yes, please. Today I’m writing the complaint to the rail company, since the train was cancelled because of a breakdown on their side.
Perfect. The cancellation wasn’t your fault; consequently, they should also pay you back for the taxi. I’m saying it like in an official letter, eh?
Why didn’t they wait for the four o’clock train?
Why weren’t they at the opening?
What are they going to change for the next fair?
Nobody offered us other transport; therefore, we had to pay for a taxi.
We didn’t have the boxes, so we put the few copies we had on the table.
Put the new books at the front, so that people see them first.
We put the new books at the front, so people saw them first.
Elena: “So on Sunday you had nothing new at the stand?”
There were no rooms left, so we slept in a hostel.
We arrived late. That’s why the stand opened at four.
The service was cancelled; therefore, we request a refund.
We put posters at the entrance, so a lot of people came to the stand.
What is the main idea?
Why don’t they wait for the next train?
Who are they going to share the taxi with?
What happens to the boxes of books?
What does Julián ask Elena to do?
the most common in speech; «¿Así que…?» draws a conclusion
letters, reports, complaints; with a semicolon and a comma
a real result
an aim, not a result (class 099)

All of today’s connectors come after the cause and introduce the result. To start with the cause, use “como” (and nothing before the result). Choose the register: “así que”, “por eso”, “entonces” in speech; “por lo tanto”, “en consecuencia” in formal writing. And check the verb after “de modo que”: indicative = result; subjunctive = aim.
My flight left at six in the morning, so I slept at an airport hotel.
Speak louder, so that the people at the back can hear you.
The museum was closed for works; therefore, the guide moved the visit to Monday.
I lost my keys. That’s why I waited for my flatmate in a bar.
There was a metro strike, so I went by bike.
A month later, Elena flies to a publishers’ conference. She is not lucky either. Transform the sentences: from cause to result, and from everyday to formal register.

In formal writing you will read other result connectors. Today you only need to recognise them: “por consiguiente” (= therefore, very formal), “así pues” (to draw a conclusion at the end of an argument) and “Así,” at the start of a sentence (= in this way, as a result). And a preview: when the result depends on an intensity (“There were so many people that you couldn’t get through”), Spanish uses “tan / tanto… que”: you study it in class 154.
“Demand rose; consequently, the publisher printed more copies.” Which connector means the same?
In which text is “así pues” most natural?
“There were so many people at the fair that we couldn’t get through.” What does the part with “que” express?

You now link causes and results with “así que”, “por eso” or “por lo tanto”, in conversation and in formal writing. In class 117 you add arguments and compare ideas with “además”, “incluso” and “en cambio”. It is the natural next step: with causes, results, additions and contrasts you can defend an opinion or write a well-organised report.

The town council wants to close calle Mayor to cars for six months, as a trial. On Thursday there is a residents’ meeting at the community centre. Héctor Ríos, a teacher and father of two, is in favour. Nuria Campos, who owns the bookshop on the street, has doubts. To defend an opinion, “and” and “but” are not enough: today you learn connectors to add arguments, highlight the unexpected, compare two things and correct an idea.
The street will be quieter; besides, it will be safer. (another argument, same direction)
My whole building is in favour, even Mr Gil, who drives every day. (the least expected case)
Héctor walks to work; Nuria, on the other hand, needs her van. (two different people side by side)
In this sentence, “además”…
In “Everyone came, even the councillor”, “incluso” highlights…
My street is noisy; yours, on the other hand, is quiet. What does “en cambio” do?
Do you have another reason that points the same way?
Without cars, the street will be quieter. Besides, the air will be cleaner.
The children will also be able to cycle to school.
There are already few parking spaces and, on top of that, they want to remove twenty.
The trial doesn’t bother me; in fact, I think it’s necessary.
The bus was late and, on top of that, it was full.
I don’t think it’s a bad idea; in fact, I think it’s urgent.
As well as closing the street, the council is going to plant trees.
What is the most surprising case?
Lots of residents came, even the transport councillor.
Even my grandmother, who is eighty, is going to the meeting.
Nobody talked about the noise, not even Héctor.
Everybody read the project, even Nuria.
Nobody read the project, not even Silvia.

Before the verb, without “no”: “Ni siquiera llamó” (he didn’t even call). After the verb, with “no”: “No llamó ni siquiera una vez”. It works like “nadie” or “nunca”. And watch out for “hasta”: “until” as a limit, or “even” when it means “incluso”.
She was so tired that she didn’t even have dinner.
In “Even the baker is in favour”, “hasta” means…
Which sentence is correct? (Not even Héctor came.)
Are you comparing two people, places or groups?
Héctor walks to work; Nuria, on the other hand, needs her van for deliveries.
Parents want more play areas, whereas shopkeepers are asking for loading zones.
The noise hasn’t gone down; on the contrary, it has gone up with the roadworks.
My street is noisy; yours, on the other hand, is quiet.
My street is noisy. However, I like living here.
To compare, the clearest form is “mientras que” (whereas). “Mientras” without “que” mainly expresses time: “while”, at the same time.
The restaurants are happy with the trial; the greengrocer’s, on the other hand, has doubts.
The street is very pretty. However, nobody wants to live on it: it’s too noisy.
I live in the centre, whereas my parents live in a village.
Is the first idea false, and does the second one replace it?
It isn’t a closed street, but a pedestrian street.
The council isn’t removing the car park; instead, it’s moving it to the station.
The idea is good, but it comes late.
The meeting isn’t on Tuesday, but on Thursday.
Nuria didn’t close the bookshop; instead, she moved it to another street.
The premises are small, but they get a lot of light.
Which sentence is correctly punctuated? (The square is big; besides, it has trees.)
Héctor presents his last argument: “Finally, the trial only lasts six months.”
Good evening. Today we’re talking about the calle Mayor trial: six months without cars. First, we’ll hear from Héctor; then, from Nuria.
Thank you. I’m in favour. Without cars, the street will be quieter; besides, it will be safer for children.
I’ve talked to many residents and almost all of them agree, even Mr Gil, who drives every day.
Thank you, Héctor. Nuria, you have the bookshop on calle Mayor. What do you think?
I find the idea interesting, but I have doubts. Many customers come by car and, on top of that, there are roadworks on the avenue right now.
And it’s not just me. Young residents walk everywhere; older people, on the other hand, need the taxi at the door.
I understand. But the project doesn’t close the street to everyone, only to private cars. Taxis and ambulances can get through.
And the parking on the street? Are they going to remove it?
The council isn’t removing it; it’s moving it to the station car park, five minutes away. What’s more, residents will pay half price.
Well, that’s good news. The bad thing is that they haven’t even asked us shopkeepers.
You’re right. We parents have had three meetings with the council, whereas the shops haven’t had a single one.
Finally, a proposal: we hold a meeting just with the shops. Even the councillor has said she wants to come.
What two arguments does Héctor give in favour of the trial?
Why does Nuria have doubts?
What happens to the parking on the street?
The trial will last six months; besides, it will be free for residents.
Many residents support the idea, even some who own a car.
The restaurants want more terraces, whereas the chemist’s is asking for a loading zone.
The next meeting isn’t in the library, but at the community centre.
Nobody voted against, not even Mr Gil.
The street is quiet; besides, it’s clean.
Nuria didn’t sell the premises; she rented them out instead.
Nobody complained, not even Raúl.
Héctor walks, whereas Nuria uses the van.
What is the main idea?
Who went to the meeting?
What changes in the plan?
Which shop still has doubts?
What does Nuria complain about?
another argument in the same direction
the case you least expect
two different things; not the same as “sin embargo”
sino replaces; pero adds a limit

Before choosing the connector, ask yourself what you are doing: adding (además), highlighting the unexpected (incluso, ni siquiera), comparing two things (en cambio, mientras que) or correcting something negated (sino, sino que)? And punctuate: “; además,”, “, en cambio,”, “, sino que”.
The flat is very bright; besides, it has a huge terrace.
My brother sleeps eight hours, whereas I sleep six.
I didn’t call Ana; I sent her a message instead.
He was so nervous that he didn’t even have breakfast.
The restaurant is expensive, but the food is excellent.
Silvia and her partner are choosing a summer camp for their children. They compare two options: the lake camp and the mountain camp. Join the ideas with the given connector.
Do you want to add, giving more weight to the second idea?
The trial not only reduces noise, but also helps local shops.
Not just the residents came, but the shopkeepers too.
Traffic has not decreased; on the contrary, it has risen by ten per cent.
Sales on the street have not fallen; on the contrary, they have risen by five per cent.

You can now defend an opinion with ordered arguments: “además”, “incluso”, “en cambio”, “no… sino”. After a meeting, the natural thing is to tell others what each person said: “The councillor said that the trial would last six months”, “Nuria asked us to…”. In class 118 you learn to report other people’s words: the natural step after a debate.

Lima, Rumbo Sur travel agency, Monday morning. Daniel Ortega is back from a business trip. His colleague, Rocío Vargas, tells him what happened on Friday: a client, Clara Molina, who is travelling in Cusco with her husband Javier, called. Today you learn to report in the past what someone else said, asked or requested: “She said she was tired”, “She asked me to call her”.
“I’m very tired and it’s very cold here.”
Clara said she was very tired and that it was very cold there.
Clara says she’s very tired.
What changes in Rocío’s sentence?
“Clara says she’s tired.” Why doesn’t “está” change?
Which tense do I use after “dijo que”?
“Javier has a temperature.” → Clara said Javier had a temperature.
“I lost my suitcase.” → She said she had lost her suitcase.
“We’ll come back on Tuesday.” → She said they would come back on Tuesday.
Clara said they had booked a tour.
She said they were going to go to Ollantaytambo the next day.
Javier said he would ask for another room.
Clara said she lived in Miraflores.
Clara said she lives in Miraflores (and she still does).

Today is Monday and Clara is coming back tomorrow, Tuesday. Rocío can say “Clara said they’re coming back on Tuesday” (it still lies ahead) or “that they would come back on Tuesday”. But on Wednesday, when they are already back, only “dijo que volverían” works.
Which sentence is NOT correct today?
“Clara said she would come back on Tuesday, and she did.”
Yesterday Elena said Clara is our best client. It is still true today. What is possible?

Rocío is not speaking from Cusco or on Friday: she is speaking from Lima, on Monday. So the people (I → she), the possessives (my → her) and the place and time words that depend on where and when you speak also change.

Before reporting, think about where and when you are speaking. If Rocío reports the morning call on Friday afternoon, she says “Clara said they were going to Machu Picchu tomorrow”: tomorrow is still tomorrow. If she reports it on Monday, she says “the next day” or “on Saturday”.
She said she had visited the cathedral that day.
Clara said her husband was at the hotel.
She said it was raining a lot there.
How do I report a question?
“Can you change my flight?” → She asked whether we could change her flight.
“Where is the airline office?” → She asked where the office was.
How do I report a request in the past?
Clara asked me to call her that afternoon.
Elena asked Daniel to come to the office early.
Javier told me to make him a booking for Monday.
Clara told me she would call in the afternoon.
Clara told me to call her in the afternoon.
Javier asked whether there was a lift in the hotel.
Clara asked what time the train left.
“Elena asked me to come early.”
Javier asked how much the excursion cost.
Rocío said Elena had called her the day before.
Morning, Rocío. Did anything important happen on Friday?
Yes, Clara Molina called from Cusco. She said she was exhausted and that it was terribly cold there.
And the trip? Everything OK?
More or less. She told me she had lost her suitcase at the airport.
What bad luck! Did they find it?
Not yet. She said they were going to go to Machu Picchu the next day, that is, Saturday, and that they would come back to Lima on Tuesday.
And what did she need from us?
She asked me if we could change her return flight. And she also asked where the airline office was in Cusco.
And did you change it for her?
Yes. But she asked me to call her that same afternoon and I couldn’t: I was in a meeting with Elena.
Then I’ll call her now. Anything else?
Yes. Elena said Clara is our oldest client, so treat her really well.
What happened to Clara at the airport?
Why didn’t Rocío call Clara on Friday?
Why does Rocío use the present tense?
Daniel writes down what other clients said on the phone on Friday. How will he report each sentence: with “dijo que”, with “preguntó si / dónde…” or with “pidió que”?
“Mr Ramos said his wife was ill.”
“The Fuentes said they had already paid for the hotel.”
“Hugo said he would arrive on Thursday, but he arrived on Friday.”
“The client asked if we accepted cards.”
“Mr Ramos asked me to make the booking that same day.”
Clara said she was tired.
She asked me if we could change the flight.
She asked me to call her.
Why does Rocío send the message?
What did Clara say about her suitcase?
When were Clara and Javier going to arrive in Lima?
Why does Rocío send a voice message instead of calling?
Where is Thursday’s meeting going to be?
Present reporting verb: same tense; past reporting verb: the tense moves back
Tense shifts; optional when the content is still true or pending
People, possessives, place and time words adapt to where and when you speak
Questions: si for yes/no, the question word (with its accent) for the rest
Past requests: pidió que + -ra (three fixed forms for now)

Before reporting, ask yourself three questions: does the person inform, ask or request? (dijo que / preguntó si / pidió que); am I reporting in the past? (then the tense moves back, unless it is still true); and where and when am I speaking? (then I adapt I, my, here, tomorrow).
Los Pinos building, in Arequipa. On Saturday the building manager, Óscar Medina, spoke to a neighbour, Lucía. On Monday Lucía tells her husband, Mateo.

Besides decir, preguntar and pedir, some verbs show how the person spoke: prometió que (+ conditional), avisó de que, explicó que, contestó que and, in formal registers, comunicó que or informó de que. In conversation you will also hear “me preguntó que si…”: it is spoken and informal, and means the same as “me preguntó si”.
Clara promised she would give it back the next day.
What does it mean?
The airline warned us that the flight was leaving late.
Formal email: “The guest informed us that he was not satisfied with the room.”

You can now report what a specific person said, asked or requested. The natural next step: talking about what is done without saying who does it, with “se”: “Tickets are sold here”, “People say the hotel is very good”, “People work hard at this agency”.
